He had been a scholar of Oriel College, Oxford. The book is given to the Marquis of Dufferin and Ava. Morris calls him the most distinguished Irishman of his time. A Greek line from Sophocles and an old proverb head the title page.

Chapter one surveys Ireland in 1901. Its heads trace a revolution in the Victorian age. Dublin and Belfast grew, and homes and churches improved. Yet agriculture declined, and progress lagged behind England and Scotland. The land system draws hard words: late laws did some good but were unjust. Ireland, Morris argues, is divided into three peoples, and Catholic Ireland stays disaffected.
37862-saul-of-tarsus-a-tale-of-the-early:
Elizabeth Miller wrote a tale of the early Christians printed at Indianapolis in 1906, with pictures by Andre Castaigne. Miller had written The Yoke. Saul of Tarsus opens the chapters, then a prudent exception and the first martyr. The bankrupt, Agrippa in repertoire, and Marsyas assuming a charge follow. The bondman of hate and an Alexandrian trait fill the early pages.

As an army with banners, the house of defense, scattering the flock, and a trust fulfilled lead on. For a woman's sake, the false balance, a matter handled wisely, and a word in season come next. The ransom, the deliverance, the feast of Flora, and the fining fire raise the stakes toward sanctuary. With foot as rapid and noiseless as a fox among the tombs, the Levite crosses into the gloom in the shown scene. Paul's world is rebuilt in fiction.
38152-the-girl-scouts-rally-or-rosanna-w:
The Girl Scouts Rally, or Rosanna Wins, is a book for girls by Katherine Keene Galt. It is the second book of a set of girl scout tales. The set list at the front names three books in all. It was put out in the mid west in nineteen twenty one. A front plate shows a man at a talk with the girls of the tale.

The tale opens in a great town of the south. Three small girls sat in a row on the top step of a fair home. At the right was a dark haired child, like a small fay. A soft cap of the French chief kind sat pert on her cut hair. Her dark eyes were round and deep in thought as she gazed at naught. A small line stood past her black brows.
3829-love-among-the-chickens:
P G Wodehouse built this comic novel from a friend's real adventures on a Devonshire chicken farm, as the dedication owns. The narrator goes down to join the scheme and finds hens, hopes, and hard work in comic disorder. His friend, full of plans and short of cash, treats every setback as a trifle, while the narrator falls for the professor's daughter and must win her regard despite the farm's chaos.

A boating scene shows the method, as Mr Hawk plunges, the boat turns over, and the professor swims with energy but little skill. Wodehouse keeps the tone sunny and the dialogue brisk. Readers who like light romance with farming farce will find an early Wodehouse in full feather, before Jeeves and Wooster took the stage.
38452-lord-chatham-his-early-life-and-co:
Lord Rosebery's Chatham, His Early Life and Connections was published by Arthur L Humphreys in London in 1910, and this copy is a second impression. Rosebery dedicates the book to Bevill Fortescue of Dropmore and Boconnoc, saying it owes everything to him.

The first chapter skips the pedigree at length and keeps to one stem of the Pitts. William Pitt's great-grandfather was vicar of Blandford in Dorsetshire, and his grandfather Thomas, Governor Pitt, sought his fortune in the Golden East and found it. Rosebery traces in the governor, an interloper who defied the East India Company's monopoly for over twenty years, some germs of his grandson's intractable qualities.
38498-the-code-of-the-mountains:
The Code of the Mountains is a Kentucky feud novel by Charles Neville Buck, printed at New York in 1915. Buck also wrote The Call of the Cumberlands. Gage drew its illustrations. The story opens on the forks of Troublesome Creek, where a boy gets his name back.

The name is Spooner, and in the talk of the Cumberland ridges it stands for violent law-breaking. It is a synonym, the narrator says, for poison meanness. Generations of Spooners have carried it into feud and ambush. Back in Bloody Breathitt a sunken grave on a steep mountainside bears witness to the record. A girl called Newty asks why the boy does not shake the dirt of the place off his feet. Buck writes the mountain code of honour and revenge from inside.
38571-hero-tales-and-legends-of-the-serb:
Woislav Petrovitch, late attaché to the Serbian royal legation in London, gathered the hero tales and legends of the Serbians. A preface by Chedo Miyatovich is dated at Belgrade on June 28, 1914. Thirty-two colour illustrations accompany the text. The book is inscribed to Nicholas Pashitch, the Serbian statesman.

An introduction and historical retrospect lead into Serbian beliefs and customs, then the national epic poetry. Kralyevitch Marko, the royal prince, takes the longest chapter, followed by Tsar Doushan the Mighty and Tsar Lazarus. Ballads such as The Building of Skadar and folk tales from Pepelyouga to Bash Tchelik fill the rest. A glossary closes the volume.
38601-l-histoire-des-vaudois-from-authen:
Authentic Details of the Valdenses, dated 1827, abridges Milner's church history and Bresse's Histoire des Vaudois, with etchings. The book is dedicated by permission to Charles, Lord Bishop of Llandaff, in hope of aid for pure Christianity and her distressed professors abroad. A Llandaff quotation calls the Waldenses the middle link between the primitive Christians and the reformed.

The historical details trace the Valdenses' past sufferings in Piedmont and other countries, drawing on scarce manuscripts of Peyran, Henri Arnaud and Bresse. Earlier writers named include Allix, Jones, Gilly and Acland, whose works the compiler supplements rather than replaces.
38816-poor-relations:
Compton Mackenzie wrote Poor Relations, a novel dated nineteen nineteen and published in February nineteen twenty. Mackenzie had earlier written Sylvia Scarlett and Plashers Mead. He framed the book as a theme in C major with variations, for a major he had served under in war.

The tale opens as the liner Murmania leaves New York for Liverpool in October. Kisses rain at the gangways and cloths wave from the quay. Ladies hand costly bouquets to their stewards, and men don bold caps at sea. Bright girls in jumpers fall in fast with a young officer. Shipboard life starts the comedy.
39094-two-boy-gold-miners-or-lost-in-the:
Frank Webster wrote this tale for boys, copyrighted by Cupples and Leon in New York in 1909. A plate shows a fire burning fiercely in spite of drenching rain, by its caption. Hard times open the contents, and after the runaway comes the gold miner in the early chapters.

A curious story, more hard luck and the gold strike follow in the list. Off for the West, a bucking bronco, big game and rapids fill the journey. At the gold fields, on a new trail, their first gold and lost in the mountains carry the subtitle's promise, with a bear cornering the boys along the way.
39116-unicorns:
Unicorns is a book of essays by James Huneker, printed at New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1917. Huneker calls it a book of spleen and gossip, and inscribes it to his friend Edward Ziegler. The pieces were first printed in newspapers and magazines between 1906 and 1917.

An Emerson line fronts the book: I would write on the lintels of the door post, Whim. Huneker was a critic of music, drama and books, known for a rich and wayward style. In these pages he writes as he pleases on the arts and the men who make them. The book is a fair door into his world, where taste is law and every piece starts from a whim.
39127-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This volume is slice six of volume thirteen of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, running from Home to Hortensius. Transcribers' notes explain the marks for roots, Greek letters and subscripts. A list corrects slips in the articles on Homer, Honduras, Horace and Hornby.

The entries mix lives, places and things in strict letter order. Daniel Dunglas Home, the spiritualist, stands near John Home and the Home Office. Homer and the painter Winslow Homer both appear. Long articles treat Honduras, Hong-Kong, Honolulu and homicide law. Horn gets three entries: a hero, the animal part and the wind instrument. The slice shows the dictionary plan at full breadth.
39140-a-racial-study-of-the-fijians:
Norman Gabel wrote A Racial Study of the Fijians, published in 1958 as volume twenty, number one of the University of California's Anthropological Records. The paper runs to forty-four pages with fifteen plates and cost one dollar. A simplified map shows the four regional divisions of Fiji's population that Gabel made. His study belongs to physical anthropology as the field was then practised: measuring bodies to sort out racial history.

The contents show the method in detail. Gabel measured weight, stature, span, and the trunk, then the arms and legs bone by bone. The head gets the closest attention: circumference, length, breadth, the cephalic index, and features down to lip thickness and ear length. An introduction sets out the problem, the habitat, and Fiji's history. Modern readers use such studies with care, as records of a science whose frame has since been rebuilt.
39164-the-pocket-gophers-genus-thomomys-:
Stephen Durrant wrote this study of the pocket gophers of Utah for the University of Kansas in 1946. It opens volume one of the Museum of Natural History publications, at pages 1 to 82. One figure in the text supports Durrant's account, the contents note in the volume's list.

The volume collects papers from 1946 to 1950, printed at Topeka in 1950. Other papers treat a skink's status, tadpoles of a toad and reptiles of Kansas and Oklahoma. Durrant sorts Utah's Thomomys gophers by kind and range, a careful piece of mammal work for museum and field students alike.
39196-the-expositor-s-bible-the-epistle-:
Rev Professor G G Findlay of Headingley College, Leeds, wrote a commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians for The Expositor Bible, edited by Rev W Robertson Nicoll. Hodder and Stoughton in London issued the third edition in MDCCCXCVIII. The series title page names Nicoll, editor of The Expositor. Findlay treats the letter verse by verse in chapter essays. Ephesians is the subject throughout.

Findlay was a Wesleyan scholar known for plain, warm exposition. The commentary opens with the salutation and the great thanksgiving of the first chapter. The church as the body of Christ stands at the centre of his reading. Jew and Gentile made one, the household of God, and the whole armour of God fill later chapters. Preachers and students get a beloved Victorian commentary, learned but readable, in the Expositor manner.
39310-on-the-age-of-maya-ruins:
On the Age of Maya Ruins, by Charles Bowditch, was reprinted from the American Anthropologist in 1901. Putnam of New York issued the pamphlet that year. Its text turns on an inscription lately found at Chichen Itza. Edward Thompson, the American consul at Merida, found that inscription.

The stone holds an Initial Series of glyphs, Bowditch notes with care. It gives, so far as he knows, the only initial date found in northern Yucatan. Doubt hangs on what date the long count of the Maya truly marks. Bowditch weighs the glyphs to fix the age of the ruins. His paper is a founding shot in the long Maya calendar debate. Scholars still argue the correlation he probed here.
39549-the-carved-lions:
Mrs Molesworth wrote a story for girls, illustrated by Leslie Brooke and published at London in 1895. The narrator opens in old days. It is a long time since she was a little girl, and the remembrance of childhood comes over her so vividly that she can scarcely believe herself as old as she is. Children, she hopes, are like each other in heart across the years.

The contents move from a happy evening through coming events and an unpromising beginning to a new world. Gathering clouds, a chapter called Nobody, a flight out in the rain, refuge, and kind friends follow, before good news closes the tale. The pictures promise magic amid the schoolroom: the brother lions rose into the air. Boarding-school sorrow with a touch of wonder is the fare.
39664-the-hansa-towns:
Helen Zimmern's The Hansa Towns, issued in London by T Fisher Unwin in 1889, stands twentieth in the Story of the Nations series. Zimmern believes it to be the first history of the Hanseatic League. The impetus to write it came from the United States, at the suggestion of her friend G H Putnam of New York.

Her preface reads the Hansa as an early representative of the federal spirit. Federation, she argues, is best understood in America, and the Old World has much to learn from the successes and failures of the past. She thanks Doctor Otto Benecke, keeper of the state archives of Hamburg, among her helpers.
39830-memoranda-on-poisons:
Thomas Hawkes Tanner wrote a small handbook on poisons for doctors and students. Lindsay and Blakiston printed this third edition at Philadelphia in 1872. The book was fully revised, and the editor calls it almost a new book. Tanner also wrote a practice of medicine and a treatise on the ills of infancy and childhood.

Tanner aimed to give the working doctor a compact guide for cases of poisoning. This edition gives more weight to the drug side of the work. It sets out the best tests for each poison, and ways to part a poison from the flesh it hides in. The old threefold sorting of poisons is dropped. New groups run from plain corrosives and irritants to agents that act on the nerves.
39977-illustrations-of-universal-progres:
Herbert Spencer wrote Illustrations of Universal Progress, a series of discussions, printed in New York in 1865. A notice of his new system of thought goes with the volume. That notice sets out the plan. Spencer has begun the issue of a new scheme of thought, it says, so fresh and wide as to deserve the heed of all earnest inquirers.

He proposes nothing less, the notice goes on, than to unfold a complete account of nature, bodily, living, mental, and social, as science has now first made possible. If carried out, it will mark a great step in the progress of thought. His scheme is to span five works, each a distinct treatise, yet all closely joined in plan. A list at the front prices his other books from the same house.
4012-the-dutch-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote this children's book about Dutch twins, a boy and a girl who live with their parents in Holland. The sampled scenes show home work done with song, as their mother churns butter and the twins drink buttermilk at dawn.

Each chapter follows a small task or holiday, from butter making to market days, with the twins learning the ways of their village. Perkins wrote the book for young readers, with simple words and homely detail. It suits children first meeting another country's daily life, and adults who enjoy a gentle, old-fashioned school story.
40200-exultations:
Ezra Pound's Exultations, printed at London by Elkin Mathews in 1909, gathers early poems steeped in Provence, Italy, and older song. The contents list a Sestina: Altaforte, a Ballad of the Goodly Fere, and hymns from the Latin.

The opening poem voices Guido Cavalcanti inviting a voyage: he leaves Lappo and Dante behind and would sail the seas with his friend alone. Night Litany turns to Venice, praying God to purify hearts amid the shadow of the city's beauty on the waters. Other pieces treat Piere Vidal, Francesca, Plotinus, and a planh for the young English king. Pound thanks the English Review and two London papers for leave to reprint pieces first printed there.
40345-a-song-of-the-guns:
Gilbert Frankau wrote A Song of the Guns, issued at Boston and New York in 1916 by Houghton Mifflin. A note tells the odd birth of the poem. Frankau served in Flanders and was at the battle of Loos. In a lull, as gunners slept like tired dogs under their guns, he jotted its main theme.

The poem was done at Ypres in long trench war. Its last three stanzas were writ at midnight in brigade headquarters. German shells screamed over into the ruined town as he wrote. Parts hold the voice of the slaves, gun teams, eyes in the air, and signals. Observers and the ammunition column get parts too. The guns are called slim grim masters in the pit. The verse speaks for the men who served them.
40448-the-child-s-book-of-the-seasons:
Arthur Ransome's The Child's Book of the Seasons was published by Treherne at London in 1906, with illustrations by Frances Craine. Ransome, author of The Stone Lady, dedicates it to Robert and Phyllis. Four chapters follow the year: spring, summer, autumn, winter. Spring begins the morning the Imp, in a bright pink nightgown, rushes in with a sprig of almond blossom from outside his window.

The children keep a notebook of firsts: the first brimstone butterfly, the first primrose, the first bird's nest. The Imp and the Elf desert their nurse, who loves fairy tales but not flowers, and thunder on the narrator's door. They beg Mister Ogre to walk, and three pairs of eyes go open into the fields. Ransome writes nature for children in the voice of a family friend, long before the Swallows and Amazons made him famous.
40548-the-rival-campers-or-the-adventure:
The Rival Campers is a boys' adventure tale by Ruel Smith, published at Boston by Page and Company in 1905. Shute drew its illustrations. The book is dedicated with love to the author's small son. The contents promise a full summer of camp war. A camp is pitched, a rescue made, and a night spent with Henry Burns. A hidden cave and a haunted house fill the mid chapters. A trap is set, and a cruise round the island follows. A storm drive stands near the end.

The tale opens at Southport, a fishing village on Grand Island in Samoset Bay. The daily steamboat's whistle wakes the town from its nap. Loungers at the grocery rouse themselves and stroll to the wharf. Into this quiet world the campers come, and with them the rivalry of the title. Smith writes the wholesome outdoor tale of his day.
40549-the-private-life-of-the-romans:
Harold Whetstone Johnston, professor of Latin at Indiana University, wrote The Private Life of the Romans, published by Scott, Foresman and Company in Chicago in 1909. Johnston also edited selections from Cicero and wrote on Latin manuscripts. The book is a textbook of Roman private antiquities, set out in numbered sections.

An introduction fixes the scope and lists the sources. The chapters then take up the family: the household, kin by blood and marriage, adoption, and the father's power. The Roman name, with its three parts, follows. Marriage and the position of women, the dowry, and the wedding day get a full chapter. Children and education come next, with nurses, playthings, and the ceremony of the bulla. The book served Latin students who needed the daily world behind the texts.
40799-an-address-to-free-coloured-americ:
An Address to Free Colored Americans was issued by an Anti-Slavery Convention of American Women held in New York in May 1837. William Dorr printed the pamphlet at 123 Fulton Street that year. It opens with the words Beloved Brethren and Sisters.

The women say sympathy for their enslaved fellow-citizens called them together to devise the best means of bringing the country to a sense of her transgressions. They describe slavery as a system of irresponsible power, violence and injustice, quoting a Southern gentleman's address of 1830 on its horrors. The address dwells most on the mental and spiritual degradation of the enslaved, made a chattel and denied self-improvement and marriage.
4086-the-scotch-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote this children's book about Scotch twins, a boy and a girl growing up in a Scottish village. A sampled scene finds the mother baking scones when three boys burst in, one dripping wet from head to heel, mud and water running in streams.

Jean throws up her hands at the mess on her clean floor, in the book's homely, humorous manner. Each chapter follows small tasks, holidays, and mishaps, teaching young readers about Scottish home life. Children who enjoyed the Dutch Twins will find the same gentle pattern here, with scones, kilts, and kind neighbors.
4091-the-french-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote this children's book about French twins, a boy and a girl living near a cathedral in wartime France. The Abbe asks Pierre to fetch two large Red Cross flags for the towers, since wounded may arrive at any moment.

The Red Cross, he says, will guard the cathedral from shell fire, for not even Germans would destroy a hospital. The twins run off with careful directions and a note for the shopkeeper. The book mixes daily French life with the Great War, in Perkins's gentle manner for young readers learning about another country.
4092-the-monikins:
J. Fenimore Cooper's satire The Monikins sends its narrator among a race of intelligent monkeys, whose society mirrors human folly. A chapter on palpable sublimity and practical ideas opens with intense feeling disturbing the narrative, as new sources of happiness break on the writer's mind.

Cooper uses the monkey world to mock politics, law, and social climbing, in the manner of Swift. The satire is odd, wordy, and often funny, with the author's earnest moral voice behind the jest. Readers who enjoy strange, old-fashioned satire will find a curious Cooper work, far from his frontier tales.
40938-wigwam-and-war-path-or-the-royal-c:
Wigwam and War-Path, or The Royal Chief in Chains, is Meacham's account of the Modoc conflict and its peace commission. Meacham had been Superintendent of Indian Affairs and chairman of that commission. John Dale of Boston issued this second, revised edition in 1875.

Portraits illustrate the book: the author, General Canby, Thomas, and the Modoc leaders Captain Jack and Schonchin. Others pictured are Scar-Faced Charley, Black Jim, Boston Charley, and Tobey and Riddle. Eleven engravings show scenes from Modoc life, witnessed by the author. A preface by the reviser explains that he rearranged the manuscript and its contents. He says he kept the author's eloquent style, making only immaterial changes. The result is a participant's history of a war he had tried to end by treaty.
4096-verses-and-translations:
A book of verses and translations gathers light, witty poems, including lines that tease a fellow poet's quoting. The speaker notes that if he had said beginning, the line might do, but he dislikes quoting wrong, and Cowper wrote middle for beginning.

Other verses turn on abstinence from malt, on Greek minds and their injurious liquors of wine, water, and temperance drinks. The collection favors humor, craft, and classical play over grand feeling. Readers who enjoy clever verse and translation will find a pleasant, old-fashioned book of short poems.
40969-the-mating-of-the-moons:
The Mating of the Moons is a science fiction story by Kenneth O'Hara, printed in the magazine Orbit in 1953. Its heroine, Madeleine, has come to Mars in search of something she cannot name, to give her life a meaning. A note in the margin promises that she found it, in a way.

The opening places her among the ruins of Taovahr. The sun glares, the thin air feels friendless and empty, and the plains of sand begin to waver before her eyes. Even the ruins strike her as false, lacking the dress of dream she had given them on lonely nights back on Earth. A handsome young guide-host drones through his set lecture on the ruins. The narrator calls him the biggest piece of falseness on Mars, a sharp start to a tale of longing on a dead world.
41098-the-vinland-champions:
Ottilie Liljencrantz wrote The Vinland Champions, copyrighted in 1904 and illustrated by the Kinneys. A prologue precedes three parts. Part first, The Brood of the Wind-Raven, opens concerning Alrek of the Viking camps.

The boys of the Wind-Raven consider the chances of finding a Skraelling, and one is found on the Cape of Crosses. The sword-bearer is reminded he has broken the law, the storm-giant blusters, and a strange find is made on Keel Cape. Thorfinn Karlsefne the lawman enters. Part second brings the hall of the Vinland champions and trade with the Skraellings coming to a mysterious end. Readers get a Norse America romance built on the Vinland sagas, boys and chiefs in the first western world.
41127-rose-in-bloom-a-sequel-to-eight-co:
Louisa Alcott published Rose in Bloom at Boston in 1876, as the sequel to Eight Cousins. In her preface Alcott insists there is no moral to the story and that Rose is not designed as a model girl. The sequel, she says, was written to fulfill a promise, with hopes of amusing other roses getting ready to bloom.

The first chapter, Coming Home, puts three young men on a wharf on a bright October day, waiting for an ocean steamer. The Campbells are there for their cousin Rose, who has been abroad for several years with her uncle, the Doctor. Handsome Prince Charlie, as the family calls him, rescues a small boy from among the piles while they wait. Ahead lie old friends with new faces, thorns among the roses, Phebe's story, and the polishing of Mac. Readers get the Campbell cousins grown up, facing love and choice.
41192-animal-proteins:
Hugh Garner Bennett wrote this handbook on animal proteins for the applied chemistry series of Baillière, Tindall and Cox. It appeared at London in 1921. Bennett had lectured in the Leather Industries Department of the University of Leeds and belonged to the Society of Leather Trades' Chemists. His earlier book was The Manufacture of Leather. The series preface sets the plan: each volume surveys one industry from the chemical standpoint, not the engineering one.

The war had sped the growth of applied chemistry, the preface argues, and the empire had raw materials waiting for science. Bennett's subject covers the proteins behind leather and its allied trades. Formulae, ions, and the chemistry of hides run through the text. The book addresses the works chemist rather than the laboratory student, comparing methods across the chief producing countries.
41242-the-americans:
The Americans, a drama by Edwin Davies Schoonmaker, was published by Mitchell Kennerley at New York in 1913 and dedicated to his father and his brother Frank. The author's note places the play third in a series of racial dramas.

The Saxons treated man's struggle for religious liberty; The Slavs, postponed, will treat political liberty; The Hindoos will close with spiritual unfoldment. The Americans takes the industrial conflict now raging. Its persons include J Donald Egerton, lumber king and mill-owner, Sam Williams the strike leader, a militia general, a bishop, and the state governor.
41263-the-mediterranean-its-storied-citi:
Six writers, among them T G Bonney, H D Traill, and Grant Allen, wrote The Mediterranean, its storied cities and venerable ruins. James Pott published it at New York in 1907 with photogravures. Contents open with the Pillars of Hercules, portals of the ancient world.

The first chapter tours the bay of Tangier at sunrise, Tarifa, and the Rock of Gibraltar, with its fortifications, the Alameda gardens, and the view from the highest point. The great siege and Ceuta, the Spanish stronghold on the Moorish coast, follow. Algiers, a pearl set in emeralds, comes next. Readers get an Edwardian grand tour in one volume, port by storied port around the inland sea.
41272-speaking-of-prussians:
Irvin Cobb wrote Speaking of Prussians, published by Doran in New York in 1917 and dedicated, by permission, to President Woodrow Wilson. Cobb was a Kentucky humorist and one of America's best-known magazine writers. This is a wartime book, not a funny one: a picture called Turning the Eagle Loose fronts it.

Cobb begins by calling the writing his patriotic duty as an American citizen. He is not setting up as teacher or preacher, he says. His claim to speak is chance: he happened to be one of four or five American newspapermen in Europe when the Great War began. From what he saw of the German armies and their work, he builds his case against Prussian militarism for American readers, in the year the United States itself entered the war.
41356-letty-and-the-twins:
Letty and the Twins, by Helen Sherman Griffith, was issued at Philadelphia in 1917, copyrighted in 1910, with pictures by Frances Jones. Griffith wrote many Letty books, from Letty of the Circus to Letty at the Conservatory. Chapter one brings the children to a farm.

Jane cries that it is just fun, her rosy, chubby face beaming at how fast they go. Her twin Christopher, called Kit, scoffs that it is not so fast. He would like sixty miles an hour. Later chapters name Sunnycrest, a sprained ankle, green apples, and the circus. Letty sings a lullaby, Christopher goes for the mail, and then he is lost. Measles, a cablegram, and good news follow. Readers get a warm farm tale for girls.
41471-callias-a-tale-of-the-fall-of-athe:
Callias, a tale of the fall of Athens, is a historical novel by Alfred Church, professor of Latin in London, issued in America in 1891. A Latin motto from Cicero says Athens outlived her conqueror but fell when Socrates was killed. A picture of Socrates with Alcibiades faces the title. The contents open with a new play, then news from the fleet.

A stranger named Hippocles, a council, and a run through the blockade follow in quick heads. The sea fight of Arginusae and its bloody aftermath at Athens form the heart of the tale. The murder of the generals, a rescue, and the figure of Socrates carry the story to the city's fall. Church wrote such tales to bring Greek and Roman history alive for young readers.
41635-among-the-tibetans:
Isabella Bird wrote this travel book on Tibet, illustrated by Edward Whymper in this Dover edition. Five chapters carry the journey: the start, Shergol and Leh, Nubra, manners and customs, and climate and natural features. A frontispiece portrait shows Usman Shah, one of her party on the road.

The plates list camps at Gagangair and Sonamarg, a hand prayer-cylinder and a Tibetan girl. Leh, a lama, monastic buildings at Basgu and a yak all appear among the views. Chang-pa women and chiefs, the castle of Stok and a Tibetan farm-house fill out a record of high mountain travel.
41676-armour-weapons:
Armour and Weapons, by Charles Ffoulkes, is a handbook printed at the Clarendon Press, Oxford, in 1909. Viscount Dillon, curator of the Tower Armouries, wrote the preface and lent many illustrations. Ffoulkes built the book from his lectures before the University of Oxford in the Lent term of 1909.

He calls it a short guide to the craft of the armourer, not a full history. Chapters follow the age of mail from 1066 to 1277, a transition period, and the wearing and construction of armour. Plate armour from 1410 to about 1600, horse armour, and the decadence of armour follow, with a closing chapter on weapons and an index.
41781-the-country-house-with-designs:
Lady Mary Fox edited The Country House, with Designs, a volume of friendly contributions printed by Murray of London in 1843. The preface explains a change of dress. Earlier contributions came out in a small volume. To do justice to the beautiful designs in this one, the book had to grow.

The designs come from De Chateauneuf, the Hamburg architect known for his Architectura Domestica and his plan for the new Royal Exchange. He supplies the observations on the style fittest for domestic architecture, the description of the proposed house, and the drawings. Eastlake adds a letter on the principles of interior decoration. Subscribers got a model country house wrapped inside a gift book of letters and essays. Builders of 1843 could study plan, style, and furnishing in one volume.
41802-frank-in-the-mountains:
Frank in the Mountains is a boys' adventure tale by Harry Castlemon, one of the Rocky Mountain Series. It was published at Philadelphia by Porter and Coates, and entered in 1868. The contents open with a foot-race and its fruits. Frank learns something, a trapper is taken prisoner, and Archie finds a new uncle. A medicine man, a friendly grizzly, and a panther hunt fill the mid chapters. Adam Brent tells his story along the way.

The scene is the far west, on a journey from Fort Yuma to the headwaters of the Missouri. Frank and his cousin Archie ride with trappers across the plains. A buffalo hunt and a chase of wild horses break the ride. Frank wins praise for his rifle work. Archie wins it for his dogged try at a wild steed. The tale is frontier schooling for boys of its day.
41850-the-expositor-s-bible-the-second-e:
The Second Epistle to the Corinthians is a word book in the Expositor Bible set. James Denney wrote this book of the set, out at London in eighteen ninety four. Robertson Nicoll, head of The Expositor sheet, led the set as a whole. Each book of the set sold at one price in cloth form. Lists of past set books crowd the front leaves by year rank.

Denney starts from the close tie of the two Corinth notes we hold. How Paul stood with that church is the start point of all search here. Books by Maclaren, Dods, and Farrar stand in the set rank list. Psalms, Kings, and the John tale fill ranks of that same list. Crown size cloth is the form note for the whole set line.
41915-hossfeld-s-spanish-dialogues-and-i:
Hossfeld's Spanish Dialogues was revised by Cornett. Hirschfeld Brothers published the new edition in London in 1915. It stands among Hossfeld's pocket manuals for languages. A front list names the firm's Spanish works. Grammars, dictionaries, readers, and commercial letters fill it. The preface explains what the revision changed. Pronunciation pages were rewritten and enlarged. The verbs were augmented too. Vocabularies grew, and several were rearranged. Idioms and proverbs, set in alphabetical order, replace weaker matter. Hints on letter-writing are added for good measure. A full course in letters is left to a sister volume, the preface says.

The dialogues themselves drill the phrases a traveller needs. Their aim stands in the title: a rapid grasp of Spanish. Cornett keeps the old book's plan while refreshing its stock.
41919-camp-venture-a-story-of-the-virgin:
Camp Venture: A Story of the Virginia Mountains, by George Cary Eggleston, was published by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard Company at Boston in 1901. W A McCullough illustrated the book, and Eggleston also wrote A Carolina Cavalier and The Last of the Flatboats.

The chapters build a cabin camp in the mountains under a Doctor's plans. Moonshiners, a Sunday discussion, an armed negotiation, and a midnight alarm follow. Tom leaps upon a mountaineer's back in the frontispiece, and the tale ends with the capture of Camp Venture and its final dissolution.
42026-english-bisaya-grammar-in-twenty-e:
Pedro Jimenez, a Recoleto father, shortened grammars by the Recoleto fathers Guillen, Nicolas, and Zueco into an English Bisaya grammar in twenty eight lessons. It was printed at Cebú in 1904 for the use of the American people. A licence from the church governor of the Cebu diocese stands at the front. Two friars of the order had censored the book and judged it fit to print.

Lessons give singular and plural forms with Bisaya equivalents. A letter is rendered as usa ca sulat, and a dog as usa ca iro. Proper names take their own article forms, shown through the name Peter. Notes explain uses for companions and terms of affection.
42096-the-king-of-the-mountains:
Edmund About wrote this novel of Greece, translated from the French by Mrs Kingsbury and published by Rand, McNally in 1897. It opens on a July morning in Athens, where the narrator is watering his flowers.

A young German botanist, Hermann Schultz, enters the garden with gold spectacles and a huge porcelain pipe, carrying About's own book and praising it warmly. He has come to complete his herbarium and study the country, the animals, and the people. Talk turns, as talk in Greece must, to brigandage. Schultz gravely reports fifteen days in the hands of Hadgi-Stavros, nicknamed the King of the Mountains, and offers to tell the tale. Readers get About's famous brigand romance, half satire and half adventure.
42119-the-trapper-s-daughter-a-story-of-:
Gustave Aimard wrote a story of the Rocky Mountains published at London in 1861. A preface signed by his translator lists the order of the linked tales: Trail Hunter first, then Pirates of the Prairies, this volume third, and the Tiger-slayer after. Each, the preface insists, is complete in itself.

The first chapter, The Jacal, opens about three in the afternoon on the banks of a stream running to the Gila. A horseman in Mexican dress gallops hard, hand on his weapons, urging his horse by shouts and spur. Contents promise the Apaches, a war stratagem, a fight with a grizzly, and lynch law. Red Cedar, Bloodson, and White Gazelle people the cast.
42284-love-among-the-ruins:
Warwick Deeping writes a romance of war in Love Among the Ruins, printed in New York in 1904. Deeping had writ Uther and Igraine, as the title page notes. Benda draws the plates, and one shows Flavian of Gambrevault bound before a lady.

Part one opens on a wild night in a great forest. Winter stands like a pale queen with her crown at the steel sky. A tower burns amid the woods and hurls spears of light. Black battlements wave in the glare of the fire. Vast shades leap and writhe in the still night. The scene sets a grim, high tale of love in a land laid waste by war.
42304-the-gist-of-japan-the-islands-thei:
R B Peery wrote The Gist of Japan, its islands, people, and missions. Fleming H Revell Company issued it in 1897. Fuji San fronts the book in a plate. Peery gave the book to his wife in thanks. Her sympathy made its value, he says. Sixteen chapters fill the contents in all.

The Land of Japan opens the survey. Its chain runs from Kamchatka to Formosa, he says. More than 1500 miles stretch that chain. Width runs 100 to 200 miles across. The area counts 146,000 square miles, less Formosa. Two Dakotas would match that size, he notes. History, character, and customs fill early chapters. Religions of Japan take the seventh in turn. First Christian coming and modern missions follow. Methods, hindrances, and outlook close the book. A missionary's whole Japan in one gist shows the 1890s church reader his field, from jinrikishas to temple bells.
42340-sermons-of-christmas-evans:
Joseph Cross presents these sermons of Christmas Evans, Englished from Welsh. Leary and Getz printed the book at Philadelphia in 1857. A memoir and portraiture of the preacher join the sermons here. Two hands translated the sermons and the journal extracts apart.

An opening note warns the styles differ and asks reader pardon. Evans was a Calvinistic Baptist, Cross notes in the preface note. His sermons lean to that creed, yet stay free of sect bias. Spiritual Christians of all creeds may profit, Cross contends there. A portrait of the Welsh preacher stands at the front of the Leary edition shown.
42350-the-new-hand-book-to-lowestoft-and:
A handbook to Lowestoft and its environs was drawn from older histories of Suffolk. T Crowe printed the work at Lowestoft in the Roman year MDCCCXLIX. Steel engravings show the town and its marine esplanade. Sources named are Gillingwater's History and Suckling's Antiquities of Suffolk.

Lowestoft stands on the most easterly point of land in England, the guide opens. A lofty cliff, dry soil, and keen, bracing air make it a healthy resort. The main street runs three-quarters of a mile down the hill's brow. Visitors gain a proud, full guide to a rising watering place.
42390-the-myths-of-the-north-american-in:
Lewis Spence wrote a book of the myths of the native folk of North America. The book came out in London in 1914. Thirty-two color plates by James Jack aid the text. Spence had wrote on the myths of Mexico and Peru. He also made a word book of myth lore.

Tales of gods, beasts, and first men fill the book. A front plate shows a spirit who takes the form of a wood bird. Spence sets tale by tale in tribe and land order. He treats the tales as both art and past. Fans of old tale lore get a wide, rich store. The plates make far worlds feel near and real.
42399-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Volume thirty-one of The Philippine Islands, 1493 to 1898 was published by the Arthur H Clark Company at Cleveland in 1905. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series, with a historical introduction and further notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. The volume is dated 1640.

Its main piece continues Diego Aduarte's Historia de la provincia del Sancto Rosario, printed at Manila in 1640 and translated here by Henry B Lathrop. The instalment covers pages 167 to 384 of the first book. Chapter thirty-eight treats the advance the Indians of Nueva Segovia had made in virtue, and their attendance upon the sacraments, once idolatry was ended.
4244-among-the-tibetans:
Isabella L. Bird, writing as Mrs. Bishop, recorded this journey from Kashmir into the high valleys of Ladakh and Tibet. The opening chapter leaves the Vale of Kashmir, a resort of tourists and traders, and moves toward Shergol and Leh, through country governed harshly and served by mission schools and hospitals.

Bird traveled with porters and guides, noting the people, monasteries, and daily life of a region few Europeans had reached. Her eye is practical as well as curious: she records roads, food, shelter, and the costs of travel, alongside the customs of a Buddhist land on the edge of British India. The book remains a vivid Victorian travel account.
42458-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson put in order The Philippine Islands, a vast set of old texts in English. Book 32 came out at Cleveland in 1905, with a first part and notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. The set runs from 1493 to 1898. It shows the isles as told in books and hand texts of their own age.

Book 32 holds the close of a work by Diego Aduarte, a friar of the Order of Preachers. His tale of the Province of the Holy Rosary was first set down at Manila in 1640. Maps of the East Indies from 1635 and from near 1660 serve as plates. A copy of the hand mark of Aduarte, from the state vaults at Seville, closes the book. Lists of sources let scholars trace each text to its root.
42466-facts-and-fancies-in-modern-scienc:
Dawson gave these lectures on science and faith at Crozer Seminary in 1881. The American Baptist Publication Society printed them in Philadelphia in 1882. Dawson aimed to show a fair view of science and Christian belief. He denies that science based guesses can replace religion at all.

He calls such bids a fancy of the age in his preface. They yield only systems like Positivism and Nihilism, he argues. Truth in nature and truth in spirit run in parallel, he holds. The lectures clear false clashes and point to deep accord. Dawson gave the talks as the Crozer lectures for 1881.
42483-at-home-with-the-patagonians:
George Chaworth Musters, a retired naval commander, wrote At Home with the Patagonians, published by John Murray in London in 1871. The book records a year of wanderings over untrodden ground, from the Straits of Magellan to the Rio Negro. A map and illustrations, including Wáki killing a puma, accompany the text.

Musters warns readers who want exact science that instruments could not be carried or safely used on the journey. His route was laid down by compass, and the map, if incomplete, is not imaginary. Nor does he promise hair-breadth escapes. His aim is a faithful record of life with the Tehuelche people, all the year round. The book made English readers at home with a people then almost unknown to them.
42517-historic-inventions:
Historic Inventions is a book of invention stories by Rupert Holland, published in Philadelphia by Jacobs in 1911. Holland had written Historic Boyhoods and Historic Girlhoods. A frontispiece shows Gutenberg taking the first proof from his press.

Sixteen chapters pair each invention with its maker. Gutenberg and the printing press open the book. Palissy and his enamel, Galileo and the telescope, and Watt and the steam engine follow. Arkwright's spinning jenny, Whitney's cotton gin, and Fulton's steamboat mark the industrial age. Davy's safety lamp, Stephenson's locomotive, and Morse's telegraph come next. McCormick's reaper, Howe's sewing machine, and Bell's telephone fill the later chapters. Edison and the electric light, Marconi and the wireless, and the Wrights and the airship close the march. Holland wrote history as a parade of makers for young readers.
42572-the-adopted-daughter-a-tale-for-yo:
The Adopted Daughter is a moral tale for young persons by Miss Sandham. Harris published the second edition at London in 1822. Sandham had written The Twin Sisters and other approved works. A line at the head of the first chapter runs: you took me up a tender flower.

In her preface Sandham owns that her people are too near perfection for real life. The tale means to show what people ought to be, she writes. Few with a fortune would use it as her heroine does. The heroine, Mrs Meridith, is heiress to two great estates. She lost her mother at birth and her husband early. Sorrows turned her from town glitter to quiet country scenes. She settles at Rosewood, near the village where she was nursed. There she takes up a child to raise as her own.
42645-the-expositor-s-bible-the-epistle-:
The Reverend Professor G G Findlay wrote a study of The Epistle to the Galatians for The Expositor's Bible, issued in New York in 1893. Findlay taught at Headingley College, Leeds. He calls Paul's letter to the churches of Galatia a precious work without peer in its kind. The text used is the Revised English Version, or its margin.

Thirty chapters follow the letter in order, from the address and salutation to the brand of Jesus. Early parts treat Paul's gospel, his divine call, and his clash with Peter at Antioch. Middle parts weigh Abraham's blessing, the law's curse, and the story of Hagar. Later parts turn to the fruit of the Spirit, sowing and reaping, and the perils of liberty.
42668-matins:
Matins is a volume of poems by Francis Sherman, published at Boston by Copeland and Day in 1896 and dedicated to the poet's father. Some thirty short lyrics are gathered, with titles like At the Gate, Ave, Easter-Song, The Kingfisher, The Builder and Te Deum Laudamus. The sequence moves between prayer, nature and dream.

The opening poem asks a great gate to swing wide so the speaker may enter fearless. The wind among the stars, he says, taught him of life, not of death and sin. The second poem, A Life, runs a whole career in three sonnets. Pride of rule is checked by a gray rose falling in the king's garden. The closing sonnet turns westward, to sleep and the sun's gold. Sherman's manner is the lush, archaic lyric of the eighteen nineties.
42753-the-expositor-s-bible-the-epistles:
James Denney wrote The Epistles to the Thessalonians for The Expositor's Bible, the commentary series edited by Robertson Nicoll. Hodder and Stoughton published it, with the Doran company in New York. The volume expounds both of Paul's letters to the church at Thessalonica, chapter by chapter.

The contents map the argument. For the first epistle: the church of the Thessalonians, the thanksgiving, the signs of election, and conversion. Denney then prints Paul's defense of his own ministry, and the impeachment of the Jews. Absence and longing, personal purity, and charity and independence follow. The great themes come late: the dead in Christ, and the day of the Lord. The second epistle takes up suffering and glory, the man of sin, and the restraint and its removal. A chapter called The Christian Worth of Labour closes the exposition. Preachers got Paul's earliest letters read with a scholar's care.
43013-animal-analogues-verses-and-illust:
Robert Williams Wood, who wrote How to Tell the Birds from the Flowers, made this book of verse and plates on like-named beasts and plants. Paul Elder printed Animal Analogues at San Francisco and New York in 1908. Sound, not sense, links each pair.

The Bee meets the Beet, and the Beetle joins them on page one. The Ant greets the Pheasant, the Bunny the Tunny fish. The Eel pairs with the Elephant, the Puss with the Octopus. The Gnu stands by the Newt, and more such puns march on. Wood, a famed hand at light verse and a grave man of science by day, plays here with words pure and simple.
43082-stromboli-and-the-guns:
Francis Gribble collected eight tales in Stromboli and the Guns, issued by Ward, Lock and Company at London in 1904. Henry Austin drew the pictures. The title tale opens in the old days of a famous anarchist club near Tottenham Court Road.

An evening paper sent Gribble to write about the club, and an Italian waiter took him in as a guest. There he met Stromboli, full name Jean Antoine Stromboli Kosnapulski, an old white-bearded exile. Other tales treat a hunted Pole, a counter revolution, a secret society, and a visit to a holy man. Talk, plots, and sudden fights fill the set, with plates of teacups hurled and doors assailed.
43106-not-without-thorns:
Mrs Molesworth wrote a novel in an edition dated 1873, opening with a chapter titled Sweet Seventeen. A foggy evening in early December settles over Wareborough, a low, flat manufacturing town. Fog hangs in air loaded by tall chimneys, and street traffic struggles. A young man rides in a rattling fly and shudders at the town.

He wonders how anyone can spend a life in such a place. The driver stops where no houses can be seen in the fog. A gate stands by his passenger, with a path to three houses. Mr Dalrymple's house is the middle one, the driver says. The young man must walk up and have the bell rung.
43122-silverthorns:
Silverthorns is a children's novel by Molesworth, illustrated by Noel-Paton. Hatchards of London published the edition of 1887. The story opens in the school-room of a London family, the Waldrons.

The room, at Number 19, Norfolk Terrace, looks out on a plain back garden. Four boys and a girl live and work there, with two nursery children besides. Charlotte and her brother Jerry, the eldest, keep what order exists. The boys call themselves invisibly tidy: they know where their things are. Yet boats are rigged, skates oiled, and stamps and autographs spread about. Charlotte answers that, but for Jerry and herself, the tidiness would not last. Her mother's inspections, she hints, would soon find the cupboards out.
43167-how-to-know-the-ferns:
Frances Theodora Parsons wrote How to Know the Ferns, a guide to the names, haunts, and habits of our common ferns, with copyright in eighteen ninety nine. Charles Scribner Sons in New York issued the edition of nineteen fifteen. Marion Satterlee and Alice Josephine Smith made the illustrations. Parsons had earlier written How to Know the Wild Flowers. A Thoreau quote heads the dedication to J R P.

Early chapters treat ferns as a hobby, when and where to find ferns, and an explanation of terms. Fertilization, development, and fruiting follow, then notable fern families. A guide key leads into fern descriptions in six groups. Indexes to Latin names, English names, and technical terms close the book. To be affected by ferns, Thoreau says, so that they signify something to you, is not so easily accomplished. Nature lovers get a beloved field guide in plain words.
43206-the-breaking-crucible-and-other-tr:
James W Alexander turns German hymns into English verse in a book issued by Randolph at New York in 1861. The title hymn comes from F Hartmann. Its German first line stands above the translation.

Now the crucible is breaking, the hymn begins. Faith takes its seal, like molten gold unhurt by fire. Verse two reads grief as the Lord's moulding hand. He shapes our dust now, and the inner man later. Sorrows quell our insurrection, verse three says. They gather home the senses, lest they stray after idols. Sorrow strings the harp for everlasting singing. It makes faith lowly, childlike, and confiding. Alexander, a Princeton divine, gave American churches a set of stern, tender German songs in plain English dress.
43216-zut-and-other-parisians:
Guy Wetmore Carryl writes of Paris in Zut and Other Parisians, printed at Boston and New York in 1903. Houghton Mifflin made the book, out in September of that year. Carryl had also writ The Lieutenant Governor and Grimm Tales Made Gay.

Zut leads the set of tales, a long first piece. Caffiard follows, then The Next Corner and The Only Son of His Mother. The tales treat Parisians of the day, in the light, deft manner of a humorist at home in the city. A warm French dedication to a friend fronts the book, in thanks for shared fine days and sound advice. Readers of sprightly short fiction get a tour of Paris types, told with a wink and a quick turn.
43326-joe-miller-s-jests-with-copious-ad:
Frank Bellew edited this fattened heir of the most famous joke book in English. Joe Miller's Jests first came out in 1739, in the name of a dead comic actor. The Northern Magazine's office printed this copy at New York in 1865, with copious additions.

The first title page stands copied at the front. The Wit's Vade-Mecum, it calls itself: the most brilliant jests, the politest repartees, the most elegant bon mots in the tongue. Elijah Jenkins, the actor's lamentable friend, claims to have taken many from Miller's own mouth. Captains, Pope, and a kettle-drummer share the dedication's odd roll. For a century, a Joe Miller meant any stale joke; this book is why.
4340-the-british-barbarians:
Grant Allen called this a hill-top novel, a story written from a height above the common run of fiction. In an introduction he asks readers to read it first, and he dedicates the book to all with heart, brain, and soul enough to understand it. A hill-top novel, he explains, raises a protest in favor of purity.

Allen complains that recent fiction has been flooded with stories of evil tendencies, while writers of higher aims struggle to earn bread and find publishers. His novel answers with a stranger's view of British manners, judging them as a visitor from a simpler world might. The book is a satire of 1895, earnest in its moral purpose.
43403-seaward-an-elegy-on-the-death-of-t:
Richard Hovey wrote Seaward, a long poem of grief for the poet Thomas William Parsons. D Lothrop Company issued the poem in Boston in eighteen hundred ninety three. Lines from Dante, Emerson, and Parsons face the title page. A sea view stands at the head of the text.

Hovey watches the tide fill the marshes of Massachusetts Bay. He feels far marshes in Nova Scotia call to him too. Parsons stands by him in mind, shy and quiet. The dead poet sang for love of song alone, Hovey says. Few fans could find his lone retreat in life. Now kelp men haul their boats while surf cries far off. Sea, grass, and loss blend in each slow verse.
43526-cremorne-and-the-later-london-gard:
Cremorne and the Later London Gardens, by Warwick Wroth, was published at London in 1907. Wroth was assistant keeper of coins in the British Museum at the time. Elliot Stock issued the book with twenty five illustrations in its pages. He had written earlier on the London pleasure gardens of the eighteenth century.

Cremorne Gardens fills the first and longest section of the survey. Manor House baths and gardens at Chelsea come next in the contents. A hippodrome and a famed symposium at Kensington follow in the roll. The Hippodrome at Notting Hill, the Royal Oak at Bayswater, and Chalk Farm continue the tour. Tea gardens, tavern grounds, and dance halls of a vanishing London are the matter here. A waterside entrance at Cremorne, etched in 1871, fronts the volume.
43550-the-bible-of-bibles-or-twenty-seve:
Bible of Bibles, or Twenty Seven Divine Revelations, is a critical work by Kersey Graves, issued at Boston in 1879. Colby and Rich published this fourth edition of the book. Graves is named as author of The World Sixteen Crucified Saviors and The Biography of Satan. Lydia Graves is credited as assistant author on the title page.

The full title promises a description of twenty seven Bibles in its scope. It also promises an exposition of two thousand Biblical errors in science, history, morals, religion, and general events. Notes for the third edition correct points on geology, on the reign of Ahaziah, and on the anointment of Christ. One note concedes that Unitarians believe in hell only as a state or condition, not as a place. The book is a freethought assault on the unique authority of the Christian Bible, argued by catalogue and comparison.
43809-benjamin-franklin-and-the-first-ba:
Benjamin Franklin and the First Balloons is a paper by Abbott Lawrence Rotch, reprinted from the Proceedings of the American Antiquarian Society. It was printed at Worcester, Massachusetts, in nineteen hundred seven. Rotch notes that the bicentenary of Franklin's birth had revived interest in balloons. Franklin's accounts of the first ascents were almost unknown, he says.

Five letters from Franklin to Sir Joseph Banks, president of the Royal Society, are presented in the paper. They were written in seventeen eighty three, when Franklin was minister to France. In Paris he watched the first balloons rise and reported them with wit and care. Rotch rescues those letters from neglect among Franklin's papers.
43912-practical-italian-recipes-for-amer:
Practical Italian Recipes for American Kitchens, held in 1917, was sold to aid the families of Italian soldiers. No author is named on the title page shown here. A contents list was added for the reader, as the first book had none. Each dish is named in English and in Italian.

Soups lead the book with brown stock, bean soup, pea soup, and soup with little hats. Rice dishes hold Milanese rice and rice with peas. Greens, eggplant, celery, and potatoes fill the next part. Eggs, corn meal dishes, and polenta close the part shown here. The book adapts Italian home cooking to American kitchens and goods.
44029-mind-and-body-or-mental-states-and:
Mind and Body, or Mental States and Physical Conditions, by William Walker Atkinson, was published in London and Chicago in 1910. Atkinson was a leading voice of the New Thought movement. His first chapter takes up the subconscious mind, known to the new psychology by many names. Writers called it the subjective, involuntary, subliminal, or unconscious mind, he notes.

Later chapters treat the sympathetic system and what he calls the cell minds of the body. The mental basis of cure comes next, with a history of psychotherapy. Faith cures, the power of the imagination, and belief and suggestion each get a chapter. Atkinson argues that the hidden mind holds sway over the body's functions and sensations. His methods chapters show how that sway might heal. The book is a clear, plain statement of mind cure teaching at its height.
44163-london-in-the-sixties-with-a-few-d:
London in the Sixties is a memoir of town life by one of the old brigade. That pen name hides a man who knew the town in that age first hand. The book first came out in the year nineteen hundred and eight. Cheap prints of the work kept it in reach for years past that date.

Parts roam the Tower, dance halls, night dens, and low streets of the age. Race booths, card fevers, and a last public rope rite fill sharp heads. Inns, stage plays, money lenders, and odd fish of men earn their turn. A trip east and a quack queen of beauty close the tour of the town. Bright recall and broad chat mark the keen old hand tone.
44188-boys-second-book-of-inventions:
Boys' Second Book of Inventions is a book of science for boys by Ray Stannard Baker, first published in 1903. Marconi stands as its frontispiece. The first chapter takes up the miracle of radium. It tells of the Curies and their new element, its marvels and its dangers. Flying machines come next, with the steerable balloons of Santos-Dumont. The earthquake measurer of Professor Milne fills a third chapter. Electrical furnaces, and how the hottest heat is made, fill a fourth.

Harnessing the sun and its solar motor get a chapter of their own. The inventions of Peter Cooper Hewitt close the list: his mercury arc light, his converter, and his interrupter. The plates show the men and their machines at work. One shows radium used as a test for true diamonds. The book feeds a boy's wish to know how the new age was built.
44360-the-amenities-of-book-collecting-a:
The Amenities of Book-Collecting and Kindred Affections is a book of essays by Edward Newton. Lane published the work at London in 1920, with pictures. Newton dedicates the book to his wife, his partner in bookish bliss for twenty eight years. A caricature of Thackeray and Dickens faces the title page.

In an opening essay Newton says his book is written for the tired business man. He tells how a partner urged him to take a holiday in 1913. A magazine number on Egypt charmed him into a trip up the Nile. From such starting points the essays wander among books and collectors. Newton writes as a wealthy amateur glad to share his shelves. The tone stays genial, with stories of finds, prices, and fellow lovers of books.
44445-bessie-among-the-mountains:
Bessie among the Mountains is a children's story by Joanna Mathews. Robert Carter and Brothers published it in New York in 1872. It is the fourth of the Bessie books. Bessie at the Seaside, Bessie in the City, and Bessie and Her Friends came first. Press notices praise Bessie as a charming specimen of little girlhood. They call the series a lovely picture of home and nursery life. One notice credits the author with a delightful grasp of child character.

The motto on the title page bids readers overcome evil with good. That line from scripture sets the book's moral aim. The series shows bright, merry children under gospel influences. Reviewers noted its simplicity and naturalness of style and incident. This volume takes Bessie from home settings to the mountains. It was written for family reading in a Christian home.
44581-the-stoneground-ghost-tales-compil:
E G Swain wrote The Stoneground Ghost Tales, compiled from the recollections of the Reverend Roland Batchel, vicar of the parish, published at Cambridge in 1912. He dedicates the book to Montague Rhodes James, provost of King's College, Batchel's friend for twenty pleasant years and the indulgent parent of such tastes as these pages indicate.

Nine tales fill the book: The Man with the Roller, Bone to His Bone, The Richpins, and The Eastern Window. Lubrietta, The Rockery, The Indian Lamp Shade, The Place of Safety, and The Kirk Spook follow. The first opens on the edge of the Fens at a village called Stoneground. Readers get quiet, antiquarian ghost stories in the James manner.
44605-man-and-his-migrations:
R G Latham wrote Man and His Migrations, a study of the world’s peoples. John Van Voorst issued the book in London in eighteen hundred fifty one. Six lectures at Liverpool’s Mechanics’ Institution ground the work. Latham here lays them out in fuller, more ordered form.

Bodily history of man and his civic tale part at the start, he shows. Herodotus leads the ancients; Buffon and Linnaeus lead the new school. Blumenbach coined the term Caucasian in his scheme of kinds. Tongue study serves the race hunter as a chief sharp tool, he holds. Leibniz and Klaproth shine in that linked field of old words. One stock or many first homes for man: that great doubt stands posed. Tongue loss and tongue keeping test each claimed kinship of tribes. Sea wanderings close his wide map of how peoples spread.
44628-nineteenth-century-questions:
Nineteenth Century Questions is a volume of essays by James Freeman Clarke, printed at Boston in 1897. Clarke also wrote Ten Great Religions and Common Sense in Religion. Houghton Mifflin published the book from the Riverside Press. The essays mix religion, history, and biography, as their author's career did.

The contents take up the two Carlyles, weighing Carlyle past and present. Buckle and his theory of averages get an essay of their own. Voltaire and Ralph Waldo Emerson follow, and Harriet Martineau closes the biographical run. Clarke was a Unitarian minister who wrote for the general reader, not the study alone. His questions are the century's own: faith against science, the great man against the average, and the shape of belief to come.
44934-captives-among-the-indians:
Horace Kephart edited Captives among the Indians, printed at New York in 1915. The book gathers first hand narratives of Indian wars, customs, tortures, and habits of life in colonial times. It is number three in the Outing Adventure Library.

Four tales stand here. Colonel James Smith tells of life among the Delawares from 1755 to 1759. Father Bressani writes of his captivity among the Iroquois in 1644. Mary Rowlandson's tale comes from Massachusetts in 1676, and Mercy Harbison's capture and escape from 1792. Smith, taken at eighteen and adopted by a tribe, was well treated, Kephart notes. His tale contrasts with the harsher ones that follow.
45110-beautiful-ferns:
Beautiful Ferns is a plate book of fern kinds, from first hand water hue drawings made from life. Two artists made the plates. The text that tells of each kind is by Eaton, a teacher of plant science at Yale College. The book came out at Boston in the mid eighteen eighties.

Its list of plates runs from the maiden hair and ostrich ferns to beech ferns, wood ferns, lip ferns, and cliff brakes. A walk leaf fern and a spleenwort stand in the set as well. Each kind is then told in turn in tight plant terms: its root stock, stalks, and fronds, with size and build in full. The book weds fine art prints to hard plant facts for the fern fan.
45251-how-to-know-the-ferns:
S Leonard Bastin wrote a guide to knowing ferns, with thirty-three pictures. Methuen and Company issued How to Know the Ferns in London, first in 1917. Fourteen chapters run from fern kin and life tales to gathering and growing ferns. Bracken, male fern, lady fern, and polypodies each get a full part.

Bastin starts low, with green algae that film damp ground with no stem or root. Mosses add stems and leaves but lack true roots, he notes. Ferns, horsetails, and club mosses form the next great group in his scale. Walkers gain a clear aid for naming fronds in woods and lanes.
4530-precipitations:
Evelyn Scott published this book of poems in 1920, drawing pieces that had first appeared in journals such as Poetry, The Dial, and The Egoist. Many poems take New York as their subject: Manhattan streets, the Brooklyn Bridge, Central Park at dusk, crowds, riots, and night lights. Others turn to home life, illness, children, and love, in short, sharp lyrics rather than long narratives.

Scott's title suits her method, since feeling falls suddenly, like weather, over city scenes and private moments. The poems are modern in image and free in form, yet they stay close to sights a reader can picture. Readers who like early modern verse will find a vivid city book, with tenderness and unrest running side by side through its pages.
45346-sea-spray-verses-and-translations:
Sea Spray is a book of verses and translations by Thomas Rolleston, published in Dublin by Maunsel in 1909. Rolleston was an Irish man of letters, steeped in the old literature of Ireland. Some of the poems had appeared in the Spectator, the Irish Homestead, and the Westminster Gazette.

The contents open with the title poem and March Winds. Then comes Midir the Proud inviting Queen Etain to fairyland, from the old Irish tales. A song of Maelduin, the grave of Rury, and the Shannon at Foynes follow. One piece is a ballade of the Cheshire Cheese, the London inn of writers. The translations close the book: the battle of Salamis from the Greek, the dead at Clonmacnois, and a song of Finn. Irish myth, Irish rivers, and classical war stand together in Rolleston's small harvest.
45436-mosby-s-war-reminiscences-stuart-s:
John Mosby wrote these war reminiscences of Stuart's cavalry campaigns, printed in New York in 1898. Chapter heads sum up each episode in full. The first chapter tells of the opening of the war and of Stuart showing the qualities of a great leader of cavalry. Picket line adventures and the capture of a Federal wagon train follow.

Christmastide raids come next, when Union cavalrymen once left their turkeys behind. Later chapters harass the Army of the Potomac and dodge plans to capture Mosby's command. A sergeant of the Fifth New York Cavalry deserts and joins Mosby in one tale. Chancellorsville, wagon trains, and railroad guards fill the later heads, with red tape blamed for ills in the Confederate service.
45506-flatland-a-romance-of-many-dimensi:
Flatland, a romance of many dimensions, was printed by Seeley in London in 1884, with illustrations by the author, who signs himself A Square. The dedication addresses the inhabitants of Space in general, hoping that citizens of three dimensions may aspire to the secrets of four, five, or even six.

Part one describes this world: a vast sheet of paper on which lines, triangles, squares, pentagons, and hexagons move freely about. They have no power to rise above the surface or sink below it. They are like shadows, only hard and with luminous edges. Sections treat the climate and houses, the women, methods of recognition, the suppression of a colour sedition, and the priests. Part two turns to other worlds: a vision of Lineland, a stranger from Spaceland in the form of a sphere, and a journey upward into the third dimension.
45520-stories-about-indians:
Stories About Indians is an anonymous children's book published by Merriam and Merrill in 1854. It opens with a plain account of Indian life. The Indians, it says, were formerly lords of the soil we now occupy, living by hunting and fishing in villages of fifty to five hundred families. Their wigwams were poles bent together and covered with bark, with a hole at the top for the smoke of the centre fire.

The people sat and slept on skins and mats, wore clothes of skins with the fur turned inward in winter, and loved trinkets, feathers, and polished shells. Anecdotes follow, including one of a Pawnee brave, son of Red Knife, who at twenty-one was ranked the bravest of the braves. The book belongs to the schoolroom shelf of its decade: short, illustrated lessons about Native peoples for white children.
45617-redskin-and-cow-boy-a-tale-of-the-:
G A Henty sends a young hero west to the cattle plains in a tale first issued in 1891. Charles Scribner's Sons printed the New York edition of 1896. Alfred Pearse drew twelve full-page pictures.

Henty's preface speaks straight to his boy readers. He grants the tale is not history. Still, he swears the cowboy life shown can be trusted. He took its risks and work from a near relative who lived that life. Texas, he notes, was the great ranch state twenty-five years back. The type now holds on in New Mexico and the northern states. Henty pairs ranch craft with the wars of the plains Indians. His books taught empire and grit to a age of schoolboys, and this one shows his method at full stretch.
45658-the-mystery-of-the-downs:
Mystery of the Downs is a detective novel by Watson and Rees, authors of The Hampstead Mystery. The New York and London edition is dated nineteen eighteen. A notice at the front quotes a Philadelphia paper on their earlier book. Care in writing and a complicated plot lift it above the common run, the quote says.

Chapter one opens in a storm that sweeps in from the sea. Rain and lightning blot out the country side under a pall of blackness. Harry Marsland rides down a cliff road on the downs, bent over his horse's neck. He trusts the animal's sure feet to keep them from the breakers below. A slip might plunge them both into the sea, the tale says. He is miles from shelter on a lonely road.
45714-practical-cinematography-and-its-a:
Frederick Talbot's Practical Cinematography and Its Applications came out in London in 1913 from William Heinemann. Talbot had already written Moving Pictures: How They Are Made and Worked. The front of the book shows a trick of the trade. A dummy cow of papier-mache, fifteen feet high, lets a camera man stand inside and film wild beasts in safety.

Chapters take up the camera and its works, how to use it, and hand-camera work. Developing the film and printing the positive get their own full treatment. Later pages slow fast motion down, speed slow motion up, and join the camera to the X-ray tube and the microscope. The book is a working guide to a young craft.
46037-a-revision-of-the-treaty-being-a-s:
Revision of the Treaty is a sequel to The Economic Consequences of the Peace, by John Maynard Keynes. The New York edition is dated nineteen twenty two. A portrait of Lord Keynes serves as frontispiece. Contents run to seven chapters and an appendix of documents. The first chapter treats the state of opinion. The second runs from the treaty's ratification to a London ultimatum.

Side studies treat coal and the legality of occupying Germany east of the Rhine. Later chapters weigh the burden of the London settlement and the reparation bill itself. Pensions and inter ally debt earn chapters of their own. Statesmen talk as much folly as the public demand, Keynes writes in the part shown. They practise no more of it than fits their words, he adds.
46080-earliest-years-at-vassar-personal-:
Earliest Years at Vassar, personal recollections by Frances Wood, the college librarian, was printed by the Vassar College Press at Poughkeepsie in 1909. Wood warns that the personal element makes the early times almost unwritable: a note taker among them would not have been tolerated, and she kept no journal.

Her picture is of life and customs, not of catalogues. The course of study, she notes, matched what was prepared for brothers in men's colleges, with the same proficiency required to enter. One running joke survives: the word female, carved over the entrance and not yet struck from the spoons, defended at length in an 1860 newspaper against prudish antipathy. A Latin student who always demanded the exact date of every event also survives, gently mocked.
46106-the-scottish-parliament-before-the:
Robert S Rait, a fellow of New College, Oxford, wrote The Scottish Parliament before the Union of the Crowns. Blackie and Son in London, Glasgow, and Dublin issued the book in nineteen oh one. The core of the book won the Stanhope Prize at Oxford in eighteen ninety nine. Parts had run in the English Historical Review in April and July nineteen hundred. Two main parts and an appendix fill the volume.

Part one treats the start of the Scottish Parliament, its members, and its ways of work. Part two weighs the sway of Parliament in Scottish life. The main tale closes with the Union of the Crowns in sixteen oh three. A brief sketch then runs to the Union of the Kingdoms in seventeen oh seven. Students of Scotland get a short, clear frame for a lost body of rule.
46210-the-retreat-from-mons:
Field Marshal Lord French adds a preface to a short account of the retreat from Mons, issued in Boston and New York in 1917. The pamphlet belongs to a series on the British Army's work in the war then still raging. French calls the piece a summary or chronology of leading events, not a full history.

French stresses that the unexpected is what happens in war and that British training taught officers never to be caught by surprise. Germany's sudden march through a neutral country wrecked all prior plans, he says, and left the British on the open flank. Yet the men fell back in good order, trusting their leaders, with no collapse of spirit. Readers get the army's own early telling of a famed retreat, written while its war was far from over.
46229-the-life-of-george-stephenson-and-:
The Life of George Stephenson and of His Son Robert Stephenson is Samuel Smiles's biography of the railway pioneers, published in New York in 1868. This revised edition prefixes a history of the invention and introduction of the railway locomotive, including a memoir of Richard Trevithick that the preface calls more complete than any yet printed.

Smiles measures the decade since the book first appeared. Railway mileage in Europe has grown from eighteen thousand miles to more than fifty thousand. France, Germany, Spain and Russia are all extending lines, and Italy is using her new liberty to build. The statistics frame the lives: the Stephensons' engines, and the world those engines remade within one generation, are the joint subject of the book.
46232-the-boy-s-book-of-new-inventions:
The Boy Book of New Inventions, by Harry Maule, was published at New York in 1912. Doubleday, Page and Company issued it at Garden City with many illustrations. A plate honours Wilbur Wright, who with Orville invented the first practical aeroplane. Wilbur death of typhoid fever in 1912 was a loss to aviation, it notes.

A dedication gives the book to the author mother for her broad interest in the world. Thanks are due to many persons and journals for photographs and data in the front. Aeroplanes, wireless, submarines, and moving pictures fill such a survey for boys. The newest machines of 1912 stand explained with pictures for young readers. Invention as the romance of the age is the pitch of the whole book.
46251-old-continental-towns:
Walter Gallichan wrote Old Continental Towns, one of a uniform series of illustrated travel books. The series covered cathedrals and towns across Europe, town by town and church by church. Gallichan had written The Story of Seville and books on Spain and Cheshire. His plate of Rouen in 1822, showing a street under the cathedral tower, sets the book's tone: old streets, old stones, and the life among them.

Volumes of this kind served the growing class of independent travellers. Readers could plan a tour of French, Belgian, or German towns with a companion that explained what they were seeing. Gallichan mixes history with practical observation, giving each town its character in a short compass. The book belongs to the shelf of pre-war guide literature that taught English readers to wander the continent before the motor tour changed travel for good.
46275-redmanship-in-kentucky-for-fifty-g:
Frank Smith, Past Sachem and Great Chief of Records, wrote and published Redmanship in Kentucky for Fifty Great Suns at Lexington. The book is dedicated to Miantonomo Tribe Number 1, the mother tribe of the Great Council of Kentucky. A note explains the order's dating, by Great Suns of Discovery counted from 1492.

Chapters trace the Improved Order of Red Men from its fore-history of 1765 to 1833, its national establishment and its planting in Kentucky in 1852. Kentucky's years under the Ohio council and under a deputy follow, down to the Great Council record of 1895 to 1908. Rosters of tribes, councils and chiefs and biographies of Past Great Sachems fill the later chapters.
46394-birds-of-the-plains:
Birds of the Plains, by Douglas Dewar, treats the common birds of India in short essays, and it was issued at London in 1909. Sixteen pictures from photographs of living birds go with the text. Captain Fayrer took those photographs in the field. A grey pelican fronts the volume in full dignity.

British birds in the plains of India open the chapters of the book. The bird in blue and sparrows in the nursery follow in the list. The care of young birds after they leave the nest gets a chapter. The adjutant bird and the sarus crane stand among the larger subjects. Dewar writes with wit about crows, tailor birds, and honey suckers. His essays made Indian birds familiar to readers at home.
46421-coyotes-in-their-economic-relation:
