David Lantz wrote Coyotes in Their Economic Relations, bulletin number twenty of the federal Biological Survey, printed at Washington in 1905. Lantz was an assistant in the survey under its chief, Merriam. The letter of transmittal states the stakes. The subject mattered at once to the sheep industry of the West, where wasteful open herding prevailed. If sheep could be fenced against coyotes at moderate cost, herding might end and the range carry far more stock.

The bulletin surveys the animal whole. Chapters treat the abundance and habits of coyotes, their food, and their good and bad deeds: game destroyed, farm animals taken, and the relation to sheep. Means of destruction follow, by poison, trap, and hunt, with bounties. A last section reports tests of coyote-proof fencing.
46432-hanging-in-chains:
Albert Hartshorne, a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries, wrote this grim study of an old English punishment. Cassell printed Hanging in Chains at New York in 1893. A pirate's chains, fished from the Thames, head the plates.

Hartshorne opens with the twelve ways of English criminal courts. Of them all, he treats the last alone: execution, and the hanging of the dead body in chains. A scarlet thread is his name for that record through English history. Other modes of death cross his path as he goes. A line from The Pilgrim's Progress heads the book: let them hang, and their names rot, and their crimes live for ever.
46472-inventors-inventions:
Henry Robinson, an engineer and inventor writing from New York, published this handbook of advice for inventors in nineteen eleven. Fleming drew the illustrations. The early chapters stay practical. They cover successful invention, machine designing, financing a new invention, marketing it, setting its selling price, and running the office behind it.

The longer second half turns angry. Robinson warns readers about the many ways inventors are cheated and robbed. He compares the legal protection given to mental property with that given to physical property. He argues that a poor inventor can hardly get justice under the system as it stands. He even charges the government with taxing inventions while paying bounties for sugar beets. The book is a period piece from the great age of the independent inventor, part manual and part protest.
465-the-mountains:
Stewart Edward White recounts a horseback trip into the California mountains in this outdoor book. Six trails lead to the main ridge, and White takes the Cold Spring Trail with friends, horses, and a tenderfoot who stands for many greenhorns he knew. Ridge trails, coast ranges, canyons, and giant forests fill the chapters.

White writes on gear, horses, camp cookery, trout, and cowboys with practical humor. The tenderfoot's blunders supply much of the fun, while the lure of the trail supplies the theme. The book charms as a classic of western camp life, best read by anyone who loves high country.
46634-life-of-richard-trevithick-with-an:
Life of Richard Trevithick, volume 2, is a biography by Francis Trevithick, the engineer's son, published in London in 1872 with wood engravings by W J Welch. This volume gives an account of the inventions of Richard Trevithick, builder of early high-pressure steam engines and locomotives.

Contents of its later chapters list stone-crushing mills, portable engines, engines for South America, and mine engines on wheels from 1804. The West India Dock locomotive, a thrashing engine, and work for Sir Christopher Hawkins and the Board of Agriculture all appear. Comparisons with Watt's engine run through the notes. Francis wrote to secure his father's place in steam history, and the dense contents show how many fields the elder Trevithick's engines touched.
46711-secrets-of-wise-men-chemists-and-g:
Secrets of Wise Men, Chemists and Great Physicians is a storehouse of trade secrets and recipes, with copyright in 1889. Its author is shown in a signed sketch as William David. The opening pages note how many great trades and fortunes rest on a few simple secrets, guarded with jealous care against rivals who would pay much to learn them.

The book sets out to pry such secrets loose for plain buyers: the formulas and methods by which goods are made and work is done. Its pages mix workshop practice, household hints, and the cures of famed doctors. In an age of guarded craft knowledge, such a book sold the promise of level ground.
46884-the-origin-of-man-and-of-his-super:
Carveth Read wrote The Origin of Man and of His Superstitions, issued by Cambridge University Press in nineteen twenty. Read lectured on comparative psychology at University College, London, and had been Grote Professor of Philosophy. The book was printed in Great Britain in July nineteen twenty. Chapter one treats how man split from the anthropoid stock. Sections and subsections structure the argument closely.

Man split from the anthropoids by becoming a hunter, perhaps in the Oligocene period, Read holds. The theory explains world wide range, the erect gait, and why the first known men were hunters. Hands grew special, arms and teeth shrank, and the skull changed shape, he argues. Social cooperation, rudiments of speech, intelligence, and control of fire follow. Minor results include the food canal, loss of seasonal marriage, naked skin, cannibalism, and division into races. Students of human origins get a full evolutionary argument.
4709-brewster-s-millions:
George Barr McCutcheon, author of Graustark, opens Brewster's Millions with a birthday dinner, where the Little Sons of the Rich gather around a long table in Pettingill's studio. Nine of them sit there, and from that dinner grows the famous bargain: Monty Brewster must spend a million dollars, and spend it in a set time, to inherit far more. Chapters trace shades of Aladdin, Mrs. and Miss Gray, a second will, and a message from Jones.

Monty Cristo, a lesson in tact, the forelock of time, love and a prize-fight, and the Napoleon of finance follow. Coals of fire, Christmas despair, a friend in need, a cut direct, and the sunny south lead to a prodigal at sea, a rescue of Peggy, a mutiny, and a catastrophe. Readers get a light, clever American comedy of money, love, and reckless spending, with a race against the clock at its heart.
4731-seven-little-australians:
Ethel Turner tells Seven Little Australians, opening with a warning to readers. If you imagine model children, with one naughtily inclined child to point a moral, she says, lay the book down and take up Sandford and Merton. Not one of the seven is really good, Turner admits, and that fact sets the tone.

Chapters run from chiefly descriptive, through fowl for dinner and virtue not always rewarded. The general seeing active service and next Monday morning follow. Sweet sixteen, falling in love, a catapult and a catastrophe, and consequences follow. Bunty in the light of a hero, a truant, and uninvited guests lead to a squatter's invitation and three hundred miles in the train. Yarrahappini, cattle-drafting, a picnic, a pale-blue hair ribbon, and little Judy follow, before a last chapter at sundown. Readers get a lively Australian children's classic, full of mischief and affection.
4734-the-grim-smile-of-the-five-towns:
Arnold Bennett gathers stories of the Five Towns in The Grim Smile of the Five Towns. He dedicates the book to Joseph Dawson, a student profoundly versed in Five Towns human nature. Its contents include The Lion's Share, Baby's Bath, and The Silent Brothers. The Nineteenth Hat follows. Vera's Christmas adventures, the murder of the Mandarin, and the burglary follow, with news of an engagement, and the death of Simon Fuge.

The Lion's Share opens as a history told in the Five Towns as side-splittingly funny, one of the best jokes in a district devoted to jokes. Bennett, writing it down, finds it a pretty grim tragedy instead, and leaves readers to laugh or cry as they please. It begins in Mrs. Carpole's house at Bleakridge, on the hill between Bursley and Hanbridge. Readers get Bennett at his best: pottery towns, sharp humour, and sadness close beneath the joke.
4738-three-prayers-and-sermons:
Jonathan Swift's Three Prayers and Sermons appears here from the 1889 Routledge edition of The Tale of a Tub and Other Works. Its contents list three prayers used by the Dean for Stella in her last sickness in 1727. Sermons follow, on mutual subjection, on sleeping in church, and on the wisdom of this world. The first prayer opens with a plea for pity toward a languishing servant.

Swift asks God to teach Stella to place hope and confidence entirely in him, to sense the emptiness of earthly things, and to feel true repentance for infirmities of life past. He prays for a sound mind during visitation, kept from presumption and despair, and for grace to remember mercy if health returns. Readers get Swift as clergyman and friend, not only as satirist, in short, moving devotional prose from his Dublin years.
47405-short-sixes-stories-to-be-read-whi:
H C Bunner wrote a set of short tales meant, as the subtitle says, to be read while the candle burns. Keppler and Schwarzmann brought the book out at New York in 1891, with art by three hands. Thirteen tales fill the set, each short enough for one sitting by lamplight.

First comes The Tenor, set in a dim, quiet room of an old New York house with a garden in winter dress. Two girls enter, one in hat and furs, fresh from outdoors and fearing she is late. Other tales tell of love letters, two churches in one town, a round up, and a girl named Zozo.
47446-ceremonies-of-the-pomo-indians:
S A Barrett reports on the rites of the Pomo Indians of California in a university study. The University of California Press issued it at Berkeley on July 6, 1917. It fills pages 397 to 441 of volume twelve in the series on American archaeology and ethnology.

Barrett worked among the Pomo at a time when their old ways were fading fast. He records the forms of their ceremonies in close detail. Eight text figures support the account. The paper stands in a long line of California studies from that department. It was sent in exchange to museums and journals abroad. Such reports saved facts that memory alone would have lost. Students of Native California still cite this series as a base record of practice and belief.
47484-america-s-black-and-white-book-one:
America Black and White Book: One Hundred Pictured Reasons Why We Are at War, by Rogers, was published in New York in 1917, copyright by the New York Herald Company. Rogers was the Herald cartoonist, and the book is a list of his war cartoons, one hundred in number.

Early titles set the tone. A verdict of carelessness on the part of the deceased opens. The first great German U boat victory, and modern German Gothic art, follow. The announcement, and a silent company whose voice is heard above the roar of cannon, come next. Those cannon on the forward deck, and here are the facts, follow. The crushing of Belgium follows. Readers get American entry into the Great War argued in cartoons.
4755-california-and-the-californians:
David Starr Jordan, president of Stanford University, wrote California and the Californians, opening with the Californian's love for his state. The Californian loves his state because his state loves him, Jordan says, returning her love with affection that surprises strangers to California. Hence he grows impatient of outside criticism, since strangers to California cannot understand her.

In discussion the Californian may admit hard charges himself, yet he does not find them acceptable from outsiders. Jordan lists them plainly: California commercially asleep, her industries gambling ventures, and local politics in professional pickpockets' hands. Small towns, he says, are the shabbiest in Christendom, saloons control more constituents than churches, and the state is a slave to corporations, with no public opinion. Nor has she learned, critics say, to tell enterprise from highway robbery, or reform from blackmail. Readers get Jordan's sympathetic portrait of a proud state and its people.
47762-records-of-steam-boiler-explosions:
Edward Bindon Marten collects Records of Steam Boiler Explosions in a London book of 1872. Marten was chief engineer to the Midland Steam Boiler Inspection and Assurance Company. His preface says plain facts on blasts must help all who work steam boilers in safety.

The pages hold brief abstracts of records got for that company, now reprinted in compact form. Two papers of his lead the book. One, read at Manchester in 1866, treats blasts and their records. One, read at Nottingham in 1870, draws the lessons of late blasts. He argues that inspection is the way to stop them. Names of works and firms are left out.
47831-railroads-rates-and-regulations:
Railroads: Rates and Regulation is an economics treatise by Ripley, professor of economics at Harvard, first published in 1912 and reprinted here in 1916 with forty-one maps and diagrams. A companion volume covers railroad finance and organization. This one moves from the history of American transport to the theory of rates, valuation, security issues, combinations and pooling.

The first chapter traces transport from toll roads and the National Pike through the canal age to the railroads. It follows the slow growth before 1848, the rapid expansion of the fifties, the effect of the Civil War, the trunk line rate wars and the end of canal and river traffic. Later chapters take up stock-watering, state regulation of securities, the anthracite coal arrangement and dissolution under the anti-trust law. The book is a Progressive-era summing up of the railroad problem: how a network built by speculation should be priced and policed.
47935-fathers-and-sons:
Ivan Turgenev wrote a novel of two ages in clash in Russia. Hogarth turned the book into English. This form came out in London in 1921. Its first scene is set on May 20, 1859, at a post house. A land lord of forty waits, hatless, in a dusty coat.

His man Peter, with a dyed lock and a ring in his ear, scans the road. The young in Peter show the new age on the rise. Sons who mock the old ways will soon stride in. Fathers hold to farm, rank, and calm old rules. The clash of those two worlds drives the whole tale. World tale fans rank this book with the great ones.
48408-letters-from-the-alleghany-mountai:
Charles Lanman wrote letters from the Alleghany Mountains, printed in New York in 1849. Lanman had written A Tour to the River Saguenay and Essays for Summer Hours. The letters first ran in the National Intelligencer. He gives the volume to Joseph Gales, his counsellor and friend in all matters of his pen for many years, in love and gratitude.

Letter one starts at Dahlonega in Georgia gold country. A trip to Track Rock, the valley of the Nacoochee, the cascade of Tuccoah, and the falls of Tallulah follow. A hunter of Tallulah, Trail Mountain, a run down the Owassa, Hickory Nut Gap, the French Broad, Black Mountain, and the Catawba country fill the road. Lanman sketches mountain folk and wild southern scenery for northern readers.
48420-three-little-kittens:
Three Little Kittens is a picture story book written and illustrated by Katharine Pyle, published in New York. The kittens are named on the first picture page as Jazbury, Fluffy, and Yowler. Pyle was also the author of Six Little Ducklings and Two Little Mice, as the title page notes. Copyright was taken in nineteen twenty, with many printings after.

Printing followed printing through the nineteen twenties, up to a sixth in nineteen thirty one, its own record shows. Such demand marks a nursery favourite that parents kept buying. Pyle's soft pictures and simple tales of animal children fill the pages. The famous kitten rhyme's spirit, loss and recovery, stands behind the title.
48678-dutch-bulbs-and-gardens:
Dutch Bulbs and Gardens, published in London in 1909, pairs paintings by Mima Nixon with description by Una Silberrad. Nixon dedicated the book to a friend in memory of happy days spent seeing Holland together for the first time. The volume thanks the great Haarlem growers and the head gardener at Het Loo.

Silberrad's six chapters begin with getting there, then follow the bulb year: crocus and early spring flowers, and hyacinth weighed against iris. Old favourites and new kinds follow, and the tulip stands as the aristocrat of the bulb gardens. A closing chapter enters the bulb barns and meets the growers by name. Sophie Lyall adds appendices on hyacinth culture at Haarlem in the 1700s and on the old tulip trade from town histories. Color plates show Het Loo and the crocus fields. Readers get a painter's Holland at flowering time.
48808-top-of-the-ladder-marine-operation:
Captain John C Chapin wrote Top of the Ladder, on Marine operations in the Northern Solomons in World War II. The pamphlet belongs to a Marines in World War II commemorative series. Contents cover planning, diversionary landings, and a battle at sea. Sidebars treat the 3d Marine Division, coastwatchers, war dogs, and Navajo code talkers.

Landings began in darkness on 1 November 1943, with the 3d Marine Division woken before 0400. Destroyers shelled the target areas as aircraft spotters adjusted the fire. At 0710 the first landing craft set out on a 5,000-yard run to Bougainville. Almost 7,500 Marines landed on twelve colour-coded beaches near Cape Torokina. Later parts treat the Piva Trail, Coconut Grove, and Hellzapoppin Ridge.
48826-the-art-of-home-candy-making-with-:
The Art of Home Candy Making is a kitchen manual issued at Canton, Ohio, in 1913 by the Home Candy Makers. This third revised edition is dedicated to the ladies of the country. It speaks to women who love good candy and wish to learn to make it. Pictures show the steps and the sweets.

The general instructions stress who the book is for at the start. It is not written for the professional candy maker at all. It is written for those who make candy at home. Full detail is thus given on every small step of the work. Length follows from that care, the makers admit. Home cooks of that age made fudge, taffy, and creams for gifts and sales. This book taught the craft from the sugar pan up.
48848-frank-armstrong-at-queens:
Matthew Colton wrote a school tale of Frank Armstrong at Queens school. The book's rights date to 1911. Frank had starred in tales of college, rest days, and the nine. A front plate shows a race start: a shot, then legs like pistons. Frank meets a bully in the first part of the tale.

An afternoon of football and Jimmy's first game come next. Frank gets a new name, is seized by the foe, and is hazed. A water cure and school pride fill the mid parts. Queens meets Barrows at football in a key game. A fall, a shock play, and track tries close the list. School boys get sport in bulk.
48858-the-expositor-s-bible-the-epistle-:
Handley C G Moule, head of Ridley Hall at Cambridge, wrote a verse by verse study of the Epistle of Paul to the Romans for the Expositor Bible series. The London book was edited by W Robertson Nicoll. It prints the date in Roman numerals as MDCCCXCIV. Moule gives his own rendering of the Epistle in bold type. Side notes mark where each verse starts.

Chapters move through the letter in order, from time and place to the last parts of the text. Early chapters treat the writer, his readers, and the good report of the church at Rome. Later chapters treat sin, faith, Abraham, and peace for those who are made right with God. Readers get a close, plain guide to one long New Testament letter.
48924-joseph-pennell-s-pictures-of-the-p:
Joseph Pennell's Pictures of the Panama Canal is an album of lithographs with notes. Lippincott issued the fourth edition in 1913. Pennell made the drawings on the isthmus in early 1912. The book is dedicated to Bishop of the Canal Commission. Bishop made the drawing trip possible. He also read and corrected the proofs. An introduction tells how the scheme began.

Pennell proposed the trip himself, he says. The Century and the Illustrated London News agreed to print drawings. He feared he had come too late in 1912. Photos had shown the locks nearly finished a year before. He found instead a vast work still in full swing. His lithographs catch steam shovels, locks, and cuts. The album is a visual record of the canal's building. Text and plates together fix that moment.
48936-up-the-slot-marines-in-the-central:
Up the Slot: Marines in the Central Solomons, by Major Charles Melson of the Marine Corps, retired, is a pamphlet in the Marines in World War II Commemorative Series. It tells how American forces moved up the Solomon Islands chain toward the Japanese stronghold at Rabaul. The drive began with the Guadalcanal landings on 7 August 1942, under Operation Watchtower.

Patrol flights late in 1942 found the Japanese building a hidden airfield at Munda, on New Georgia, and that field had to be taken. The pamphlet follows the Munda drive and the Fighting Ninth, with sidebars on landing ships, long guns, field medicine, and flight gear. A second part treats air supply, and a closing part draws the joint pattern of the campaign. Sources and notes on the author and the series end the work.
49023-tennessee-at-the-battle-of-new-orl:
Tennessee at the Battle of New Orleans is a short history booklet by Elbert Watson. The Battle of New Orleans 150th Anniversary Committee of Louisiana published it in 1965. It is number five in a set of sesquicentennial booklets sold at fifty cents each. Sister volumes treat the city as it was in 1814, sea power in the battle, and the British commander Pakenham.

Watson's subject is the Tennessee men who marched with Andrew Jackson to meet the British below New Orleans in January 1815. The battle's fruits, the series notes, reached far beyond the field. On the national scene there emerged, in Jackson, a leader destined for future greatness. At the same time the disunion talk of dissident Federalists fell quiet. The booklet tells how Tennessee riflemen helped win the republic's most famous victory of the War of 1812, in plain, brief chapters for the anniversary crowd.
49060-the-walcott-twins:
Lucile Lovell wrote a tale printed at Philadelphia in 1900, with drawings by Ida Waugh. Twenty seven chapters carry the book. Gay and May, the twins, open it. A first parting and jokes follow, then a strange household and more muddles.

Being a boy and being a girl take a chapter each. Training begins, a plan fails, and the boy in Gay comes to the fore. Dark days, the event of the season, and the belle of Hazelnook fill the middle. The tale opens in a sick room, where a father frowns at his new born son and bids the nurse take him away. The nurse, a proud English import, bears the crown prince baby out at her own slow pace.
49075-alice-lorraine-a-tale-of-the-south:
Alice Lorraine is a novel by Richard Doddridge Blackmore, subtitled A Tale of the South Downs. This new and cheaper edition was published in London in 1893. Blackmore also wrote Lorna Doone and The Maid of Sker. He dedicated the book to Professor Owen in gratitude for encouragement and kindness, dating the dedication April 1875.

The contents open All in the Downs, then reach Coombe Lorraine and its lineage. A legend of an astrologer runs through three chapters, followed by his forecast and his legacy. A boy and a donkey, chamber practice, and costermongers vary the scene. Blackmore sets a family romance among the Sussex downs and cherry orchards.
49125-stories-from-dickens:
Stories from Dickens is a retelling for children by McSpadden. Crowell issued it in New York in 1906. David Copperfield and little Emily front the book. The preface calls Dickens a king of story-tellers. The tales are drawn from his most famous boys and girls. They are lifted out of the big crowded novels. Dickens's own words are kept wherever they serve.

Smiles are favoured over tears in the choosing. Only two deathbed scenes are allowed a place. The book is no substitute for the novels, McSpadden says. It is an invitation to the fat volumes themselves. Big books can frighten young readers by their size. This one opens the door to them gently. McSpadden also wrote of Robin Hood and stage tales.
49126-the-duty-of-a-christian-people-und:
Newton Smart, of University College, Oxford, wrote this sermon-like treatise, printed in London in 1832. Its title is The Duty of a Christian People Under Divine Visitations. Smart opens with a verse from Isaiah asking what folk will do in the day of visitation. The book is inscribed to the memory of his mother, with deep thanks.

Smart surveys the times with concern for the safety of the empire. He notes unrest across Europe and hearts failing for fear. A fatal pestilence that spread through Asia and Europe was now drawing near British shores. Against that dread, he urges the lessons that such judgments should teach the people of the land.
49140-studies-on-slavery-in-easy-lessons:
John Fletcher of Louisiana compiled these studies on slavery and had them printed at Natchez in 1852. The title page calls the book eight studies cut into short lessons for the ease of readers. It reached a fifth thousand, a sign of wide sale in its day.

Fletcher writes from the slave-holding South, and his lessons take up bondage as his world knew it. The text draws on old tongues, since the notes treat Arabic, Greek, Coptic, Hebrew, and Syriac words. Short, plain lessons let a common reader work through the case step by step. The book now stands as a record of how men of that place and time argued about slavery.
49229-yule-tide-yarns:
G A Henty edited Yule-Tide Yarns for Longmans, Green at London in 1899, with forty-five illustrations. Nine tales of adventure fill the volume, opening with Henty's own Château and Ship, drawn by Gordon Browne. A front plate shows a quartermaster firing two pistols as a man falls.

John Bloundelle-Burton tells of an adventure of a night, and W C Whistler of an outlaw's fortunes. Percy Groves gives a flight from justice, Robert Leighton a tale of longitude ten degrees. David Ker, Fred Whishaw, Harry Collingwood, E F Pollard, and George Manville Fenn complete the set. Sea fights, dacoits, and jungle drama suit the Christmas market for boys.
49353-lives-of-distinguished-north-carol:
Peele's Lives of Distinguished North Carolinians was published at Raleigh in 1898 by the North Carolina Publishing Society. Peele, a member of the Raleigh bar, collected and compiled the sketches and speeches. The subjects are fifteen: Davie, Macon, Murphy, Gaston, Badger, Swain, Ruffin, Bragg, Graham, Moore, Pettigrew, Pender, Ramseur, Grimes, and Hill. Each life comes from a different hand: Walter Clark writes Davie, Vance writes Swain, and Graham writes three of the lives.

Speeches and addresses fill out the portraits: Macon on the Missouri Compromise, Badger on slavery and the Union, Grimes on the surrender at Appomattox. The preface argues that printing the state's best sketches lays a foundation for a distinctive literature. Character, it says, comes first; art will follow in due season. The dedication addresses the subjects' descendants and all North Carolinians who would copy the virtues recorded.
49527-ethnobotany-of-the-ojibwe-indians:
Huron Smith's Ethnobotany of the Ojibwe Indians was issued on May 2, 1932, as a bulletin of the Public Museum of the City of Milwaukee. It runs from page 327 to 525, with plates 46 to 77. A note at the front says the spellings of Ojibwe words have been left as found. The study sorts every plant use it records by kind.

Medicines come first and take the longest room, with a short list of cures drawn from other than plants. Food plants follow, then fiber plants for baskets, mats, and canoe work, and dye plants after them. A last part gathers mixed uses, and a conclusion sums the whole. The plates show the world the text names: gardens, wigwams, birch bark work, and the building of a canoe step by step.
49559-modern-design-in-jewellery-and-fan:
Charles Holme edited a plate book on new design in jewellery and fans, put out from the offices of The Studio in 1902. A first note quotes John Ruskin's broad rules. Never back the making of a thing not truly needed, Ruskin says, where invention has no share. Never back mere copying, save to keep a record of great works.

On those rules Holme chose fresh work by British and mainland hands. Essays treat French, British, Austrian, German, Belgian and Danish work in turn. Lists name the craftsmen plate by plate, from Boucheron and Fouquet to lesser shops. The editor holds that good taste in buyers is the true spur to good work.
49662-the-cure-of-rupture-by-paraffin-in:
The Cure of Rupture by Paraffin Injections, by Charles C Miller, a Chicago physician, was printed by the Oak Printing Company at Chicago in 1908. Miller presents his method as one destined to occupy an important place, owing to the extreme simplicity of the technic and its economic advantages.

His foreword answers surgeons who censured the treatment without experience of it, judging from a few mishaps. Paraffin, he argues, does more than plug a hernial opening. It promotes the formation of connective tissue, occludes the hernial sac, and glues together the walls of the hernial canal.
49960-irish-historical-allusions-curious:
Corkaguiny is a local history of a Kerry district by Patrick Foley, printed in the United States in 1916. Its full title promises Irish historical allusions, curious customs, and superstitions. Foley published the book himself. It is the fourth of a series meant to give all essential history of the county.

He dedicates the volume to his son Michael. The preface tells a wartime tale: while the manuscript lay with Dublin printers, the Irish rising of 1916 broke out. Fighting between British troops and Irish forces touched the very print shop. The text proper goes far back, holding with the old historians that Ireland was fairly well peopled close on three thousand years ago. Tribes, customs, and tales fill the record of one storied barony.
50042-the-forgery-or-best-intentions:
James wrote The Forgery, or Best Intentions, printed in London in 1853. The first chapter is an introduction. One of the finest characters in the world, it opens, was the old English merchant. A different spirit reigns in trade now, and not a better one. We are more the shopkeeper now, and less the merchant.

Trade is wider, the chapter holds, but its single deals are smaller, and small dealings breed small minds. The old sort is not gone, though its men are fewer. Among them, not very long ago, was Humphrey Scriven. He was a gifted man of the untitled country gentry, first meant for the church. By chance he met the only daughter of a rich merchant, loved her, and won her love. Her father consented to the match on one term: that Scriven give up the church and become a merchant like himself.
50049-king-rene-d-anjou-and-his-seven-qu:
Edgcumbe Staley's King Rene d'Anjou and His Seven Queens was published in London by John Long in 1912. The book carries a coloured frontispiece and thirty-five other illustrations, including the ceremonial entry at the Saumur tournament of 1446 from Rene's own Livre des Tournois. A first chapter sketches Rene himself: prince, artist, craftsman and troubadour king.

Staley lists Rene's paintings, his books of hours, his poems and plays and his treatise on tournaments. The queens then follow in turn, beginning with his mother Yolanda of Aragon. Her chapter runs from her troubadour court and the Academy of the Floral Games to her years as lieutenant-general of Anjou against the English invasion.
50245-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Philippine Islands, fourteen ninety three to eighteen ninety eight, is a series of documents in many volumes. The hosted text is volume forty five, for the year seventeen thirty six. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited and annotated the set. Edward Gaylord Bourne added an introduction and notes. The Cleveland edition is dated nineteen oh six.

Contents of this volume open with a document on the commerce of the Philippines with New Spain. That paper, by Antonio Alvarez de Abreu, runs from sixteen forty to seventeen thirty six. An appendix on education in the Philippines follows. Letters and histories there treat colleges at Manila across two centuries. A royal decree on native schools of sixteen eighty six stands among them. Bibliographical data close the main document's account.
50270-the-delectable-mountains:
Arthur Colton's Delectable Mountains was published by Scribner in 1901 and dedicated to the memory of his sister Mabel. A long epigraph from The Pilgrim's Progress gives the book its name: the shepherds on the mountain tops show the pilgrims the gates of the Celestial City through a perspective glass. Twelve stories follow. The first, The Place of Abandoned Gods, opens at a boys' secret shrine on Cattle Ridge.

The hut of sodded poles stands by a cliff full of caves, with slim white birches around it. In the caves the boys keep idols, Baal the most energetic, and sacrifice corn, peas, turnips, or a shot chipmunk on a mossy altar stone. Other titles name the Leather Hermit, Black Pond Clearing, Joppa, and Tobin's Monument. Sanderson of Back Meadows and Two Roads That Meet in Salem fill the middle.
50332-the-diamond-lens:
Fitz-James O'Brien wrote The Diamond Lens, first printed in the Atlantic Monthly in 1858. A note calls it the first of the great weird-scientific stories. It won O'Brien quick fame, which held until his death in the Civil War. The tale here is taken from Weird Tales of April 1929.

The narrator tells how, from age ten, his whole bent ran to the microscope. A relative made him a crude tool from a copper disk and a drop of water. It magnified some fifty diameters and fired his imagination. He smashed panes of glass and stole his Aunt Agatha's spectacles in vain hunts for lenses. At last a proper Field's simple microscope arrived, costing about fifteen dollars, and a new world opened.
50540-a-turkish-woman-s-european-impress:
Zeyneb Hanoum wrote A Turkish Woman's European Impressions, edited by Grace Ellison and issued at Philadelphia and London in 1913. Zeyneb was the heroine of Pierre Loti's novel Les Desenchantees. Twenty three pictures from photos aid the text. One drawing is by Auguste Rodin. A front print shows Zeyneb in her Paris drawing room.

Twenty chapters trace a dash for freedom and a girlhood in Turkey. Europe at first bewilders her, she tells. The Alps, art, and smart women seen through the veil get chapters. Freedom's charm is doubted more than once. The Empress Eugenie is called a star from the West. A clash of creeds and the end of the dream close the tale of two worlds.
50668-the-secret-martians:
Jack Sharkey wrote this tale of secret Martians and a master spy. Ace Books printed it in New York in the year 1960. Jery Delvin can spot the flaw in any scheme at sight. World Security chief picks him to crack a solar mystery alone.

Fifteen boys vanished from a spaceship in mid space without trace. On Mars Jery finds himself turned into a walking bomb device. When he sets himself off, the puzzle ends with him first. Sharkey taught Chicago high school English before New York writing life. A two year Army hitch and a year in ads fill the author note.
50706-the-social-life-of-the-blackfoot-i:
Clark Wissler wrote The Social Life of the Blackfoot Indians for the American Museum of Natural History in nineteen eleven. The study forms part one of volume seven of the museum papers. Wissler thanks D C Duvall, who helped gather the facts on a museum trip in nineteen hundred and six.

Most facts came from the Piegan group in Montana, and Blackfoot readers checked the draft. Wissler argues that bands are social and work units that split, join, and shift over time. Their loose link to marriage rules looks, to him, like chance. Plates show tipis, war marks, tops, and games such as shinny.
50739-our-monthly-devotions:
Dean A A Lings arranges a year of Catholic prayer in a devotional book issued by Benziger Brothers in 1899. The firm kept houses in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago. Lings had written Our Favorite Devotions before it.

Each month takes a theme and gives matter for every day. January belongs to the Holy Infancy. Thirty-one days of considerations and prayers fill it. A mass in commemoration, two litanies, and communion prayers close the month. February turns to the Holy Family. March belongs to St Joseph. The catalogue pages list kindred matter: a thirty days' prayer, meditations on the Passion for every day of Lent, and prayers to the Five Wounds. Such manuals structured the prayer life of parish homes.
50944-salmonia-or-days-of-fly-fishing-in:
Salmonia is a book of talks on fly fishing, in its first form for the United States from 1832. The copy came from the second London form of the work. The writer calls himself an angler, and no more. He gave the book to William Babington, his friend of a full score and five years.

The talks grew from months of grave ill health, when hard study was out of reach. They mix sport with an account of the ways of fish of the salmon kind. Talk, not rule, is the form, as in the famed Complete Angler of old. The writer hopes the book will please folk who love plain sports of the field. He also aims at those who watch and think on the life of streams.
50975-motor-matt-s-prize-or-the-pluck-th:
Motor Matt's Prize, or The Pluck That Wins, filled number 23 of Motor Stories, Street and Smith's weekly of thrilling adventure motor fiction. The number is dated July 31, 1909, and sold for five cents. The tale is by the author of Motor Matt. Matt King, king of the motor boys, heads the cast. His chum Joe McGlory is a young cowboy of worth and humor. Ping Pong, a Chinese boy, insists on working for Matt.

George Lorry, befriended by Matt at a hard moment, stands among the friends. Pickerel Pete works a grievance against Matt into a plot. The chapters run from a clash in black and yellow to firebugs at work. Saving the Sprite from a blazing furnace comes midway. The race, its start and its finish, closes the tale.
51034-the-invention-of-printing-a-collec:
The Invention of Printing, a history by Theo L De Vinne, gathers facts and views on how printing began. De Vinne was a leading American printer, and the book bears his trade knowledge on every page. Facsimiles of early types and wood cuts run through the volume.

The subjects start with early prints and playing cards. They move to the block books of the fifteenth century. A long section weighs the legend of Lourens Janszoon Coster of Haarlem, whom Dutch tradition credits with the first movable type. The rest treats the work of John Gutenberg and his partners. Printers and book historians still cite the study.
51211-a-rebel-s-recollections:
George Cary Eggleston wrote A Rebel's Recollections, here in a fourth edition printed at New York in 1905. The book was first entered for copyright in 1874. Eggleston gives it to his brother Edward Eggleston, the novelist.

An added chapter treats the old regime in the old Dominion. The recollections come from a Confederate veteran looking back at the South he served. Putnam's list at the front praises the sketches as models of characterization, and quotes a Philadelphia paper: the author deserves the thanks of all true Americans. Eggleston had written Dorothy South and A Captain in the Ranks.
51233-the-marching-morons:
The Marching Morons is a science fiction story by C M Kornbluth, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in April 1951, with illustrations by Don Sibley. Its blurb asks a sharp question. In the country of the blind the one eyed man is king, but what of a live wire in a civilisation of pure chumps?

The future world of the tale has bred intelligence nearly out of mankind. Some things, the opening notes, had not changed. A potter's wheel is still a potter's wheel, and clay is still clay. Efim Hawkins fires his bottle nosed kilns by Goose Lake, hiding from their sight while they cool. Open one too soon, in impatience, and the new glaze cracks to the shard pile. Kornbluth's satire of a dumbed future became one of the most reprinted stories in the field. Its title passed into the language.
51350-no-substitutions:
Jim Harmon wrote No Substitutions, a short science fiction tale in Galaxy Magazine in November nineteen hundred fifty eight. Drawings by Johnson go with the text. Warden Walker runs Dreamland, a place that puts men to sleep without pain. His job keeps him awake at night, he says.

Councilman Coleman, one of his chiefs, calls one tense morning. Walker chews pills to calm and brace himself for work. He calls Dreamland the next step in how men hold law breakers. Some men, he argues, can not be cured or freed. Sleep vaults hold them apart with no pain at all. Coleman probes if the place is the most kind form of jail. Doubt creeps in as they talk.
51655-the-historical-jesus-a-survey-of-p:
John Robertson wrote a survey of views on the historical Jesus, issued in London in 1916 for a press group that backed free thought. Chapter heads in the contents map the ground he covers, starting with a warning on set views held before proof is weighed. Copernicus, Galileo, Harvey, and Darwin serve as cases of new truth met with scorn.

Later chapters fault safe, church minded writers for clinging to each lost post with the same heat. Gospel morals, the worth of the book of Mark, and a scholar named Schmiedel and his use of scornful tales all get a close look. Mill and Newman are set side by side as guides who fail the test.
51660-the-girls-book-of-famous-queens:
Lydia Hoyt Farmer writes lives for girls in The Girls' Book of Famous Queens, printed in New York with copyright in 1887. Crowell made the book, here in its twelfth thousand. Farmer had writ The Boys' Book of Famous Rulers and a life of La Fayette. A portrait of Queen Victoria fronts the volume. She gives the book to her daughter.

Women have played an important part in history, her preface holds. Among famous sovereigns, queens, as well as kings, have made their names illustrious by heroic deeds and great enterprises. The contents run from Semiramis, queen of Assyria, dated back before Christ. Dido of Carthage, Cleopatra of Egypt, and Zenobia of Palmyra follow. Matilda of Flanders, Margaret of Anjou, Catharine of Aragon, and Queen Elizabeth with Mary, Queen of Scots, fill the mid run. Marie Antoinette, Josephine, Eugenie, and Victoria close the line.
51804-plague-of-pythons:
Plague of Pythons is a science fiction novel by Frederik Pohl. Galaxy Magazine printed it in October and December 1962, with illustrations by Ritter. Its premise is possession: the pythons had entered into mankind. No man knew at what moment he might be possessed. The story opens at a trial. Chandler faces his judges in the all-purpose room of a high school.

Chandler's court-appointed lawyer does his job without liking his client. The police who arrested Chandler beat him senseless after he stopped resisting. He remembers the nightstick and the kick clearly. The bruises on his ribs he does not remember getting. Judge Ellithorp presides over six hundred spectators. The judge himself, while possessed the previous December, smashed his own radio station's transmitter. The fire he set killed his son-in-law. Chandler expects destruction, not fairness, from such a court.
51890-browere-s-life-masks-of-great-amer:
Browere's Life Masks of Great Americans is a book of art lore by Charles Henry Hart. It was print at a famed press of New York in eighteen ninety nine. A note at the front tells of a small run on fine hand made stock. The front plate shows a great chief of the land at the age of eighty two. The masks of the name were made from the live face.

The book is sworn to the fame of a small plate art man. That man first woke the taste for art in the hand, Hart says. His first words tell how the book grew from a small seed. There was once a man named Browere, Hart had heard. That man had a gift for the make of masks from the live face.
52014-sir-william-johnson-and-the-six-na:
William Elliot Griffis wrote a life of Sir William Johnson in the Mohawk Vale. The book came out in New York in 1891. It sits in the Makers of America set of brief lives. Griffis gave it to the folk of that vale with a low bow. Their kin fought at Oriskany, the blood war's most dire fight, he says.

Johnson dwelt in that vale from 1738 to 1774 as a grown man. Trade, land, and talk with the Six Nations filled his days. Griffis calls that vale the most fair part of their realm. His bow to its dead shows the book's warm aim. Past fans get a chief of two worlds in brief. Clear prose suits school and home.
52142-the-war-stories-of-private-thomas-:
Private Thomas Atkins tells his war stories in letters from the front. Newnes published the set for the Daily Chronicle at London. The price was one shilling net, the title page says. His tales are a selection of the best things in his letters. Great deeds are done for a great cause in them, it promises.

Simple duty and gallant gaiety mark the spirit of the telling. His war cry asks if we are downhearted, and answers no. The marching song of Private Atkins is the Tipperary song. Contents open with bugles blowing, then marching to war. Things by the way and the friendly French follow the march. Battles in being and what the soldier sees fill the middle. How it feels under fire and hit and missed close the heads. The book gives the Tommy of the Great War in his own voice.
5220-the-satyricon-volume-03-encolpius-a:
This third volume of Petronius's Satyricon, in W. C. Firebaugh's translation, carries the further adventures of Encolpius and his companions from chapter seventy-nine onward. The volume opens at midnight, with the travellers drunk, torchless, and lost in an unfamiliar district, and follows their wanderings, quarrels, and encounters through the chapters that follow.

The volume holds only this stretch of the novel, between Trimalchio's dinner and the escape by sea. Its bracket code marks forgeries and additions woven into the text, and readers following the story in order will find here its restless middle passage, full of low comedy and sharp satire.
52216-glacie-res-or-freezing-caverns:
Edwin Swift Balch wrote Glacieres, or Freezing Caverns, at Philadelphia in 1900. Allen, Lane and Scott published the book, with rights held by Balch. He was a member of the Franklin Institute and the Philosophical Society. A plate shows an ice slope and basin in an Austrian cave. Balch gives the book affectionately to his mother.

Her deep interest in his work has helped him greatly, he writes. A preliminary note thanks helpers in many countries for facts. Librarians in Paris and London supplied him from great collections. The note is dated at Philadelphia on February 10, 1900. His subject is caverns where ice abides through the summer heat. How such freezing caves form, and where they lie, fills the study. Balch gives a strange corner of the earth in a scholar's survey.
52516-san-antonio-city-of-missions:
San Antonio, City of Missions, by Claude Aniol, was published in 1942. Hastings House issued the city history at New York. Photographs of Mission San Jose and the Alamo front the book. Aniol begins with a village of Tejas Indians. Skyscrapers now mark a prosperous city, he writes. Yet old buildings and customs survive off its busy streets. Spain feared French entry into Texas in the late sixteen hundreds. Teran de los Rios was named governor of the new dominion in 1691. Father Massanet travelled with him. Mass was said on this site, salutes fired, and the place named San Antonio.

No lasting settlement followed then. Saint Dennis, a French trader, praised the spot in 1714. Spain answered in 1718 with a presidio and a mission. That mission, San Antonio de Valero, is the Alamo.
52768-memorials-of-francis-storr-sermons:
Memorials of Francis Storr gathers sermons preached at his funeral. Rice printed the pamphlet in London in the year 1888. Canon Hoare and Reverend May preached in Brenchley Church February 26. Notes of Storr last sermon, preached February 12, join them.

Storr was vicar of Brenchley parish for thirty four years there. Snow lay thick at his burial, the Guardian account says. Sun shone bright as mourners felt sorrow and rejoicing mixed. The parish was his sphere, home, and one life object. The Bishop of Dover praises his clear Christian character, humility, and genial ways here.
53105-london-signs-and-inscriptions:
Philip Norman's London Signs and Inscriptions, published by Elliot Stock in London in 1893, belongs to the Camden Library, edited by G Laurence Gomme and T Fairman Ordish. Henry B Wheatley introduces the volume, praising Norman's years of patient labour hunting sculptured signs in out-of-the-way corners of London.

Wheatley notes that Norman is an accomplished artist as well as an antiquary, doubly fitted for the work. The introduction hopes that attention to signs lately disappeared may bring some of them to light again. It recalls a curious sculptured sign over the entrance to Bull Head Court in Newgate Street, showing William Evans of the time of Charles I.
53480-the-leardo-map-of-the-world-1452-o:
John Kirtland Wright, librarian of the American Geographical Society, wrote this study of the Society's Leardo map, number 4 in its Library Series, published at New York in 1928. The map is a great disk of the world as the Venetian Giovanni Leardo drew it in 1452 or 1453, one of three signed Leardo maps, the largest of them. Archer Huntington had presented it to the Society in 1906.

Wright reads the map piece by piece: its calendar and inscription, its sources, and the known world as Leardo laid it out, region by region from northern Asia to the far north. An appendix comments in detail on twenty-four sections, and Hoen adds a note on how the map was reproduced. Key maps at the end let the reader find every name on the disk.
53481-printing-telegraphy-a-new-era-begi:
Printing Telegraphy, a New Era Begins, by Edward Kleinschmidt, recounts the rise of the teletype art. An autograph page dated 1967 signs the front of the book. Chapter one opens with work at the Western Union Telegraph Company. Barclay of that firm designed printing gear and punched tape gear for the system there.

After limited use of a high and low voltage plan, he changed the design. Long and short pulses with relays that could tell them apart took its place. Later gains put the system into service on many Western Union message circuits. A note looks ahead to methods of the 1960s in the same field. Frequency division and electronics could send three line states from four tones, it observes. The maker of the machines tells how printing by wire was born.
53666-george-in-camp-or-life-on-the-plai:
George in Camp, or Life on the Plains, published at Philadelphia in 1879, is Harry Castlemon's boys' novel in the Roughing It series. Castlemon had already filled shelf after shelf, with his Gunboat, Frank Nelson and Boy Trapper series. The book opens on a Texas ranche where trouble has walked in. A sturdy boy complains that two newcomers have turned the place upside down.

Chapters bring a neighborhood row, a clerk's ruse and a frontier hotel. Raiders visit the camp, and a narrow escape follows. News good and bad arrives from home. The plot ends with what happened at the rancho and a capture at last, in the brisk outdoor manner Castlemon sold by the thousands.
53833-american-unitarian-hymn-writers-an:
Henry Wilder Foote compiled American Unitarian Hymn Writers and Hymns for the Hymn Society of America. The work was made in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in January nineteen hundred fifty nine. It was meant for a planned Dictionary of American Hymnology. Ruth and Orlo McCormack helped Foote build the large file.

Five parts sort the whole mass of fact and name. A sketch of Unitarian hymn song leads, at eleven pages. A list of hymn books made for those churches comes next. Near fifty such books mark one hundred fifty years of song. Short lives of the writers fill the great bulk of the work. Those lives run from page forty to page two hundred forty seven. An index of first lines closes the thick reference book.
53890-some-of-our-east-coast-towns:
J Ewing Ritchie, who wrote as Christopher Crayon, set down Some of Our East Coast Towns, issued at Chelmsford in 1893. Most of the pieces had first run in the Christian World. Ritchie had also written East Anglia. His eleven chapters visit Chelmsford, Colchester, Hadleigh, Bury Saint Edmunds, Ipswich, Norwich, King's Lynn, Framlingham and its castle, Sudbury, Haverhill, and Maldon.

The first chapter calls Chelmsford one of the youngest of the Essex boroughs, almost a suburb of greater London by the Great Eastern Railway. Ritchie recalls when it was a county town whose leading folk counted a second post from London a nuisance. He notes the Quakers' chapel, the big brewery, the Shire Hall, and the statue of Chief Justice Tindal. The book gives a newsman's plain sketches of East Anglian town life at the close of the nineteenth century.
53931-the-gathering-of-the-nations:
The Gathering of the Nations is a religious tract, Number Two Hundred Seventy Two, transcribed from a John Stabb edition of about eighteen sixty two. A tract cover picture heads it. The text opens on the sight of great multitudes. There is a peculiar sublimity in the description in Revelation, it says. A great multitude which no man could number stood before the throne and the Lamb.

The solitary traveller excites no attention, the tract notes. The ordinary concourse of crowded cities soon grows familiar. But when large masses of humanity gather for one common object, no one can be an unconcerned spectator, it holds. These emotions were powerfully excited at the Exhibition of eighteen fifty one, when vast numbers visited the metropolis, it adds. Church readers get a short tract on prophecy, crowds, and the end of days.
53986-right-half-hollins:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote a school football novel about Bert Hollins. The book came out in 1925 as one of the Football Eleven Books. Each book in the set takes one place on the team. Bert plays right half at Alton Academy. Leslie Crump drew the pictures.

The tale opens in rain, with Alton tied in a hard first game. Bert sits on the bench while Chick drops pass after pass. Later parts bring a shake-up, a lost ball, and a night-before talk. Tommy Parish jokes from the stands and stirs the plot. Young fans get a full season in short, brisk scenes.
54160-the-lushei-kuki-clans:
The Lushei Kuki Clans is an ethnographic study by Lieutenant-Colonel Shakespear. Macmillan published it in London in 1912. It appeared under the orders of the government of Eastern Bengal and Assam. Maps and illustrations support the text. Shakespear dedicated the book to an earlier officer remembered fondly by the people.

The contents map a full account of the clans. A first chapter covers habitat, dress, and weapons. Later chapters treat domestic life and farming. Laws and customs fill another chapter. It covers marriage, inheritance, and war. A religion chapter treats the creator Pathian and the spirits. Funerals, festivals, and folk tales follow. A glossary aids the reader.
54348-the-slav-nations:
Advertisements for Daily Telegraph war books fill the front of this study of the Slav nations. The contents reach from Russians and Cossacks to the people of the sunflower, in its chapter phrases. Russian national characteristics form chapter three, with the mir, stress and famine among its topics.

The Duma, Russian literature and the Russian soul appear in that chapter's summary. Gogol, Tolstoi and Dostoievski stand for the nation's letters there. Poland and Bohemia follow, then the southern Slavs, with Bulgaria and Serbia treated in turn, in a wartime survey of peoples suddenly central to European politics.
55164-the-picaroons:
The Picaroons, by Gelett Burgess and Will Irwin, was published at New York in 1904. McClure, Phillips and Company issued it in April of that year. Parts first ran in Pearson pages in 1903 and 1904, the copyright notes show. A dedication names the book to the Red Cyclone in playful style.

Chapter one is called a miracle at Coffee John place in the contents. Linked tales follow of a syndicate, a Harvard freshman, and a stage professor. The story of the ex medium, the hero of Pago Bridge, and Big Becky fill the set. Coffee John dimes and forty cigars carry later chapters of the romp. Rogue heroes in the picaresque line give the book its title and its fun. San Francisco colour fills these yarns of sharp practice and luck.
55176-cartoons-and-caricatures-of-seattl:
Cartoons and Caricatures of Seattle Citizens is a picture book of pen and ink sketches, issued at Seattle in 1906. Eight local artists are named on the title pages, and two photo studios supplied the likenesses behind the drawings. An engraving company made the plates. The press work was done by a Seattle printing firm.

An opening piece, called A Word About the Wise, sets the tone with a line from Charles Lamb. A laugh, Lamb wrote, is worth a hundred groans in any market. The writer says hard headed business men have seized that truth and set out to supply the world's need of laughter. The man who laughs, they argued, is the man who buys. Portraits of the city's leading men follow in that joking spirit.
55402-our-fellows-or-skirmishes-with-the:
Harry Castlemon wrote a boys' tale of twins and swamp fights, issued at Philadelphia. The John C Winston Company brought out Our Fellows, with first rights from 1872. Castlemon had written the Gunboat and Boy Trapper sets for young readers. A plate shows the capture of Luke Redman at the front.

Joseph Coleman tells the tale, twin to Mark and near his double in face and dress. The boys are sixteen as hunts, rides, and picket duty begin. Mix-ups over which twin did what bring laughs and whippings near alike. Twenty chapters of stratagems and escapes close a brisk frontier tale.
55431-old-man-savarin-stories-tales-of-c:
Old Man Savarin Stories: Tales of Canada and Canadians, by Edward William Thomson, was copyrighted in 1917 and published at Toronto, with pictures by Charles Jefferys. Thomson dedicates the book to Quiller-Couch, who gave him the good word in season. Several stories had first appeared in other Thomson books and magazines.

Contents open with the Canadian abroad, then privilege of the limits, and the Waterloo veteran. John Bedell, a United Empire Loyalist, and Old Man Savarin himself follow. Great Godfrey lament, McGrath bad night, and the shining cross of Rigaud come next. Dour Davie drive, Petherick peril, Little Baptiste, and a red headed windego fill the middle. A ride by night, a turkey apiece, and the Swartz diamond close the list. Readers get Canadian short tales of settlers, loyalists, and the backwoods.
55442-german-war-practices-part-1-treatm:
German War Practices, Part One treats the treatment of civilians. Dana C Munro of Princeton edited the papers. George C Sellery and August C Krey aided him. The Committee on Public Information issued the book. Its date is November 15, 1917. George Creel chaired that committee.

President Woodrow Wilson's order creating the committee leads the text. The secretaries of state, war, and navy sat on it. The intro turns to the laws of war. Geneva and Hague meetings tried to soften war's brute force. Geneva's 1864 pact guarded the sick and wounded. It set up the Red Cross as well. Hague rules of 1899 and 1907 came later. A wartime brief, the book charges Germany with breaking pledges she herself had signed.
55584-the-manufacture-of-chocolate-and-o:
The Manufacture of Chocolate and Other Cacao Preparations is a technical handbook by Paul Zipperer, in a third edition rearranged and largely rewritten. Schaeffer, a food chemist and works director, edited it. Spon published it at London and New York in 1915, from the Berlin original. It holds one hundred and thirty two pictures, twenty one tables, and three plates.

A plate of the cacao tree, Theobroma cacao, fronts the book. In his preface the editor notes that a decade had passed since the last edition, and the book had long been out of print. Delays came from his wish to take in the newest rules and decrees of the trade and the law. Help came from fellow workers and from the association of German chocolate makers. The handbook covers beans, roasting, grinding, and the making of chocolate and cocoa for the factory.
55720-the-wolf-hunters-a-story-of-the-bu:
George Bird Grinnell edited and arranged this story of the buffalo plains from the manuscript account of Robert Peck. Scribner published it at New York in 1914. In the days of the buffalo, wolfing was a recognized industry. Small parties went out with team, saddle-horses, and camp outfit, and wintered on the range. They killed buffalo and poisoned the carcasses with strychnine. The wolves that fed died about them, and their pelts were stretched and dried in camp.

Peck and two companions, all lately discharged soldiers, wolfed in the winter of 1861 and 1862. Peck had been born in Mason County, Kentucky, in 1839 and had served in the First Cavalry from boyhood. The contents take the party to the Big Bend of the Arkansas, Fort Larned, and Walnut Creek. Satank, Satanta, Jayhawkers, and Wild Bill all cross the trail. Grinnell vouches for the man and the winter.
55792-greeks-barbarians:
Thomson wrote essays on the Greeks and their others, first published in 1921 at London and New York. A line of Heine stands at the front, promising that mankind's host will always divide into two parties, Barbarians and Hellenes. The front matter reprints the reviews of his earlier Greek Tradition, and they set the tone: scholarship with a bright and eager face.

The Scotsman found profit in him for any reader wishing to understand ancient Greek life; the Times called him a classicist who forms his own theories. The contents begin with The Awakening and Keeping the Pass, pass to The Adventurers, and reach Eleutheria, freedom itself. Heine's division, tested against the texts, is the argument.
55819-the-story-of-lutheran-missions:
The Story of Lutheran Missions, by Elsie Singmaster, was published in 1917 by the missionary societies of the Lutheran Church. A portrait of Francke, a pioneer of missions, fronts the book. The first chapter treats the beginnings of the work. The second takes up pioneers and their methods in the field.

Later chapters follow the Lutheran Church into India and other lands. Singmaster wrote for the women of the church who funded the missions. Her book is both a history and a call to support the work. It tells who went, where they laboured, and what churches grew from their work. Church mission books of this kind shaped how members at home saw the wider world. The story runs from the first sendings to a global field.
5601-jan-of-the-windmill-a-story-of-the-:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote Jan of the Windmill as a story of the plains, in a fifth edition illustrated by Mrs. W. Allingham. The book is dedicated to Ewing's dear sister Margaret, and its cover picture shows even a sandy kitten neglected when a slate pencil's moving point tempts a child to play. Jan grows up around a windmill, among plain folk and country work.

The story follows a boy's childhood, friendships, and lessons on the plains, told with Ewing's warmth and attention to rural detail. Readers get a classic Victorian children's tale, gentle, observant, and full of country life.
56247-catty-atkins:
Catty Atkins, by Clarence Budington Kelland, was first printed in 1919. Harper issued it at New York and London, out in January 1920. Kelland had written the Mark Tidd books for boys. The tale is told by Catty himself. His father gave him a rifle for his birthday. At once he set a bottle on a box by the barn. He aimed at the neck and fired, sure of a hit. The bottle stood untouched. Six shots brought him so close he could have knocked it over with the barrel.

A voice behind him praises the middling shooting. The front picture shows Catty felling Skoodles with two quick blows. Catty writes in a boy's plain speech, full of slang and pride. The book opens a set of small-town adventures.
56376-the-americans:
Hugo Münsterberg, who held the chair of psychology at Harvard, wrote this study of the American people. Edwin Holt, also of Harvard, turned it into English. McClure, Phillips printed The Americans at New York in November 1904.

Political life fills the first great part. The spirit of self-direction, parties, the President, and Congress come in order. Justice, city and state, public opinion, and the sore points of numbers follow. Economic life takes the second part, starting with the spirit of self-starting. Münsterberg, a German who had made America his home, reads her ways with a friend's eye and a scholar's frame.
56449-snowed-up-or-the-sportman-s-club-i:
Snowed Up, or the Sportsman's Club in the Mountains, is a boys' tale by Harry Castlemon, one of the Frank Nelson set of three. Its first plate shows a band of robbers foiled at their work. The print host holds the year nineteen hundred and four. The title leaf lists the long line of the same hand's sets for boys: gun boat tales, rock mount tales, and club tales in the main.

The club of the name is a band of boys who hunt, fish, and camp as one corps. In this tale the club is in the high hills when snow shuts them in. The front list of the print house shows how wide the Castlemon world ran for the boys of that age.
56601-a-text-book-of-tanning-a-treatise-:
Henry Procter wrote A Text-Book of Tanning, a treatise on the conversion of skins into leather, both practical and theoretical. It was published at London and New York in 1885 with eight plates. Procter worked at Low Lights Tannery and examined in tanning for the City and Guilds Technical Institute. A frontispiece shows lime pits and rinsing tanks.

The preface states a two-fold aim. It gives, in compact form, the scientific knowledge a practical tanner can use. It also sketches manufacturing processes so the chemist can apply his knowledge to improve them. Each reader, Procter warns, will find some matter superfluous to him. Readers get the founding textbook of leather chemistry, written from inside the trade.
56628-an-essay-on-colophons-with-specime:
Alfred Pollard wrote this essay on colophons, with specimens and translations, printed at Chicago by the Caxton Club in 1905. Richard Garnett adds an introduction. The edition ran to two hundred and fifty-two copies on French hand-made paper, plus three on imperial Japanese paper. A colophon is the note a printer set at the end of an old book.

Chapters ask why colophons exist, then work through them town by town. Mainz comes first, with the Latin Bible of Fust and Schoeffer from 1462 and the Catholicon tied to Gutenberg from 1460. Venice follows, with John of Speier, Jenson, and Valdarfer in the early 1470s. Each specimen lets readers see how the first printers signed their work.
5677-jimmie-higgins:
Upton Sinclair's novel follows Jimmie Higgins, a working man and socialist agitator, through the years when war and politics test his beliefs and his marriage. It opens at home, where his wife Lizzie asks to see the pictures. Jimmie, three and a half years married, holds back words he knows better than to say. From that small domestic scene the story widens to meetings, campaigns, and the hard choices of a propagandist with a family to feed.

Sinclair uses Jimmie to show how large causes land in a small household. Meetings compete with wages, and ideals compete with loyalty. Lizzie learns that a propagandist husband is not the worst fate a wife can meet. Readers get a vivid, partisan portrait of American labor politics, told with sympathy for ordinary people caught between conviction and daily need.
5687-the-water-of-life-and-other-sermons:
Charles Kingsley gathers sermons on faith, duty, and daily conduct in The Water of Life and Other Sermons. The volume, first issued in 1867 and reprinted through the 1870s and 1880s, draws its texts and images from Scripture, including Isaiah, and speaks to ordinary listeners rather than scholars alone. Kingsley preaches in plain, earnest English, with nature and home life close at hand.

Readers will find encouragement to live honestly, to care for neighbors, and to trust a faith that works in weekday life. The sermons avoid abstract debate and return again and again to conduct: how to bear trouble, how to treat others, and how to keep hope. For readers of Victorian religion, this is a warm, direct sample of a popular preacher at work.
56923-turner-s-golden-visions:
C Lewis Hind wrote Turner's Golden Visions for T C and E C Jack at London in 1907, with fifty paintings and drawings by Turner reproduced in colour. A quote from John Constable on the 1828 Royal Academy show heads the book: Turner has golden visions, glorious and beautiful.

Part one tells of a boy who loved Turner's View of Orvieto and wondered at his art and his life. Part two runs from 1775 to 1803, from Folly Bridge to Calais Pier. Hind thanks A J Finberg for the inventory of the Turner bequest drawings. He also leans on Walter Armstrong, W G Rawlinson, Ruskin, and Thornbury, whose life of Turner he calls inaccurate but indispensable.
56959-the-fern-bulletin-october-1903-a-q:
The Fern Bulletin for October 1903 is volume eleven, number four, of a quarterly devoted to ferns. The Fern Bulletin Company of Binghamton, New York, published it at 20 cents a copy and 75 cents a year. Willard N Clute edited the journal, which had taken a grand prize at the Paris Exposition.

The number leads with the fern flora of New York, worked family by family from the adder's-tongues to the club mosses. Fernwort notes, a Canadian scolopendrium, and a study of the genus Equisetum in North America follow. Around the science sits the machinery of a hobby. The Linnaean Fern Chapter invites new members, and ferns are offered for sale. A wants and exchanges column trades California plants for United States ferns. It is a small journal binding scattered fern hunters into one society.
57091-astronomy-for-young-australians:
James Bonwick wrote a star book for young Australians, issued at Melbourne in 1866. Samuel Mullen brought out the second form from Collins Street East. Bonwick had written a geography of Australia for schools. A note from St Kilda, dated November 1, 1866, frames the cheap school form.

A fine ship rides high seas under bright stars as the book opens. Families leave England's white cliffs for gum forests and a new home. A boy named James clings to his mother and vows to be a comfort. Through the voyage tale, Bonwick teaches the sky to colonial children.
57142-how-does-a-tree-grow-or-botany-for:
James Bonwick wrote How Does a Tree Grow, or Botany for Young Australians. Blundell at Melbourne and Sands and Kenny at Sydney sold it in 1857. Bonwick was a sub-inspector of schools in Victoria then. Several teachers asked him to begin a shilling series of school books. Colonial history and popular science filled that series.

The form of dialogue is adopted for the botany in this volume. A juvenile questioner keeps young friends' interest alive. A dialogue on astronomy is to follow in the same series. Willie, a fine rosy-faced boy of the southern colony, opens the tale. Not eight years old, he climbs gum trees and picks up manna. He rides in a bullock dray like a true young colonist. His hero later holds a piece of land of his own. Bonwick gives plant life in the talk of home.
57280-the-fern-bulletin-april-1912-a-qua:
The Fern Bulletin, a quarterly devoted to ferns, is shown here in its April 1912 issue, volume twenty, number two. Willard Clute edited it, and his company published it at Joliet, Illinois. A copy cost twenty five cents, or a dollar a year. The journal had earlier won a grand prize at the Paris Exposition, its cover notes.

The issue mixes journal business with the world of plant study. Notices cover subscriptions, back volumes, and indexes offered to readers. Advertisements for patents and for Scientific American sit beside the fern matter, as was common in such journals. The Bulletin served fern lovers and botanists who traded notes on finds, names, and growing. Small specialist journals like this one knit together scattered collectors long before the internet. This number preserves the look and business of American fern study in 1912.
57359-the-logic-of-chance-3rd-edition-an:
The Logic of Chance, by John Venn, is an essay on the foundations of the theory of probability. This third edition, rewritten and enlarged, was printed by Macmillan in London in 1888. The first edition had come out in 1866 and the second in 1876.

Venn was a fellow and lecturer in the moral sciences at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. His title page adds the book's reach: probability applied to moral and social science and to statistics. In his notes he claims originality only in working out one view in full. That is the material view of logic, applied to chance, with its odd results set out in the tenth chapter. The first part treats the physical foundations of the science, starting with the series of probability.
57507-the-hopi-indians:
The Hopi Indians is an ethnological handbook by Walter Hough. The Torch Press published it at Cedar Rapids, Iowa, in 1915. Hough was curator of ethnology at the United States National Museum. It is number four in the Little Histories of North American Indians. The Navaho, the Iowa, and the Indians of Greater New York precede it. A photograph shows a Madonna among the Moki, an older name for the Hopi. The contents begin with the country, towns, and peoples.

Social life, food and rearing, and the workers follow in the contents. Amusements and the round of birth, marriage, and death come next. Religious life fills a long section after those chapters. Myths, traditions and history, and brief biographies follow. The Ancient People closes the text before the index. Hough writes a compact survey of a mesa people.
57581-the-evolution-of-the-idea-of-god-a:
Grant Allen's The Evolution of the Idea of God, an inquiry into the origins of religions, was published by Grant Richards in 1897. Allen had written on aesthetics and botany before it. The preface sets the book between two schools of religious thinking, the humanists and the animists, and offers it as, in part, a reconciliation of the two.

The work is, he claims, the first extended effort to trace the genesis of the belief in a god. It follows the idea from its earliest origin in the mind of primitive man to its fullest development in advanced Christian theology. The method is constructive, not destructive: the question is by what successive steps men came to frame the conception of a deity. The inquiry divides three ways: how men came to believe in many gods, how some races came to one supreme god, and what followed that arrival.
57864-dictionary-of-historical-allusions:
Thomas Benfield Harbottle compiled this Dictionary of Historical Allusions, published at London in 1903. It stands in a uniform series with dictionaries of English, classical, French, and Italian quotations, some by Harbottle himself. An errata leaf corrects dates: read 1780, not 1870, for the Armed Neutrality.

Further corrections fix Bar, Bobbing John, and Cyprus. The dictionary exists so that a reader meeting a phrase like Bobbing John in a history or newspaper can learn, in a line or two, which event or person it names. Readers get a Edwardian desk reference for the allusive shorthand of older books, arranged for quick rescue.
57903-soldiers-and-sailors-or-anecdotes-:
Soldiers and Sailors collects anecdotes of naval and military life for young readers. An unnamed old officer relates them to his nephews. John Harris published the book in London in 1842. More than fifty wood engravings illustrate it. Gilbert designed the pictures. A portrait of Tippoo Saib fronts the volume.

The contents promise a full course in service life. A first chapter weighs red-coat against blue-jacket. Recruiting sergeants and Jack-tars appear. The oldest regiment and the life-guards earn notice. Discipline fills a later chapter. Great captains parade through another. Alexander, Frederick, and Charles of Sweden stand there. Marlborough and Buonaparte join them. Famous battlefields from Marathon to Culloden are listed. Uniforms and sea fights follow in their turn.
58089-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Wilkie Collins lists his tales. David Widger compiled the index of Collins books in that free library. The Moonstone, No Name, and Man and Wife head the contents list. The Black Robe, A Rogue Life, and Miss or Mrs follow in order.

Law and the Lady, The New Magdalen, and The Two Destinies stand there. The Frozen Deep, After Dark, and The Evil Genius swell the catalogue. Armadale, The Queen of Hearts, and The Legacy of Cain are included too. The Woman in White and The Haunted Hotel anchor the famous titles. Tables of contents for each volume follow the master list here.
58157-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Charles Dickens is a finding aid compiled by David Widger. It lists Dickens's books as issued in the Gutenberg collection and prints their tables of contents. The shelf it surveys is the whole range of England's most popular novelist.

A Christmas Carol and A Tale of Two Cities lead the contents. David Copperfield, Bleak House, Great Expectations, and Little Dorrit follow among the novels. Oliver Twist, Nicholas Nickleby, Martin Chuzzlewit, and Dombey and Son stand with them. Pictures from Italy, American Notes, and A Child's History of England cover the nonfiction. Sketches by Boz and the Christmas stories round out the list. The index notes that the remaining files, like The Mystery of Edwin Drood, carry no tables of contents. It is a plain reader's key to a very large digital shelf.
58166-the-art-of-tying-the-cravat-demons:
The Art of Tying the Cravat teaches gentlemen to dress their necks with elegance. Le Blanc wrote the pocket manual. Wilson published the third edition in London in 1828. Sixteen lessons demonstrate thirty-two different styles. Plates explain each knot. A portrait of the author fronts the book.

An introduction argues the cravat's importance at length. It preserves health, the author claims. It marks the wearer's rank at a glance. It serves as a letter of introduction. A history of the cravat precedes the lessons. The Romans wore a chin cloth much like it, he proves. Persian and Greek collars began the modern stock. Black silk cravats won fame around 1800. Form and colour are described for every style.
58168-the-puering-bating-drenching-of-sk:
A trade manual treats three wet steps used to get skins ready in leather work, the steps named in its title as puering, bating, and drenching. The book is a science based work, packed with tables, sums, and chemical forms that a plain text copy can only partly show. Its title page takes a Latin line from Bacon on knowledge and power.

Workers in tanneries used such steps to clean and soften skins before the main tanning work could start. Exact mixes, strengths, and times matter in this trade, since a wrong bath can spoil a skin. Readers get a close, hands on guide to the craft as it stood when such handbooks were the mainstay of the shop floor.
58181-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Robert Louis Stevenson lists Stevenson's books in that library. David Widger compiled the index from the texts held by the project.
