It opens with contents lists for the best known works in the set. Jekyll and Hyde, Treasure Island, and the Vailima Letters head the gatherings.

Ballads, Kidnapped, Tales and Fantasies, and Underwoods follow in the front list. Child's Garden of Verses appears four times over in differing forms and copies. Some listed books lack tables of contents in their electronic form at all. Memories and Portraits, Father Damien, and Saint Ives stand in that bare list. Full contents for Treasure Island are printed chapter by chapter in the index. The Vailima Letters to Sidney Colvin run from eighteen ninety to eighteen ninety four.
58193-villars-and-its-environs:
G Flemwell painted and described Villars and its country in a book on fair Switzerland, printed in 1914. Flemwell had earlier done books on Lucerne, Chamonix, and Lausanne in the same set. Colour views show the Grand and Petit Muveran, Bex, Les Plans, Leysin, and Champery, each tied to a page in the text.

No district in the Rhone valley, Flemwell opens, holds more charm or more range in so small a space. Broad river plain, old castle towns, a famed health resort at Leysin, and high pleasure villages all sit close. Mont Blanc shows from Bretaye, and the Dent du Midi rises over village roofs in view after view.
58218-old-english-mansions:
Old English Mansions was edited by Charles Holme and published in London, Paris, and New York in 1915, by The Studio. The houses are depicted by Richardson, Harding, Joseph Nash, Shaw, and others. A front plate in colours shows Hampton Court Palace, the entrance gateway to the first court, by Nash.

Plates then move house by house. Aston Hall in Warwickshire gets both its front and its entrance hall. Audley End in Essex gives a staircase and a plaster ceiling portion. Barrington Court, Benthall Hall, and Blickling Hall follow, with a chimney piece in a dining room. Boughton Malherbe, Burton Agnes, Charlecote great hall, Charlton House, and Coombe Abbey Elizabethan room are all pictured. Text pages sit beside some plates. Readers get a plate book of great English houses, room by room.
58245-the-jews-among-the-greeks-and-roma:
The Jews Among the Greeks and Romans, by Max Radin, is a study of Jewish life in the ancient world. The Jewish Publication Society of America published it at Philadelphia in 1915. A picture of the Arch of Titus at Rome stands early in the book. Radin dedicates the little work to his mother, in Latin, as a token of piety.

The contents begin with Greek religious concepts, then Roman ones. Greek and Roman ideas of race follow, and a sketch of Jewish history from Nebuchadnezzar onward. Radin notes that Greek and Latin writers who spoke of the Jews have mostly come down to us in fragments. Later writers quoted brief pieces of them, and the rest is lost. His book gathers what the classical world said and thought of the Jews in its midst. It served general readers as a clear guide to a meeting of cultures.
58509-brave-belgians:
Brave Belgians reached English readers in nineteen eighteen from Putnam's Sons in New York and London, translated by Alys Hallard from the French of Baron Buffin. Buffin had been Belgium's minister of war, and the French Academy of Moral and Political Science awarded the book its Audiffred Prize. The chapters are built from named men's own accounts of the invasion's first fights.

Staff officer Collyns of the Twelfth Line Regiment reports the defence of Visé and the taking of the first German flag. Generals, captains, an adjutant, and a private describe the attack on the Third Division's offices. An army chaplain and a major report the Sart-Tilman combat. Later chapters rest on army doctors and a quartermaster of the gendarmerie, so the record stays close to the men who fought.
58541-pioneer-colored-christians:
Pioneer Colored Christians is a set of lives by Harriet Parks Miller, out in nineteen eleven. A quote at the front mourns the mute banjo and the lost songs of the old farm rows. Miller writes to keep the worth of plain folk past their death, when their good shines most clear. Her thoughts center on one house, the Carrs, with grace notes on more.

The first part is a talk with an old wife of that house, who tells of her birth in the east in eighteen fifteen. She was free born, yet men sought to rob her of that right, and kind white friends helped her prove it in law. Her spouse, a church man born a slave, takes the next part. White friends of the race in its first fight for free faith are named with thanks.
58625-hours-in-a-library-volume-3-new-ed:
Hours in a Library is a set of literary essays by Leslie Stephen. Smith, Elder and Company published this third volume in London in 1892. It is a new edition with additions.

The essays treat Charlotte Brontë, Charles Kingsley, Godwin and Shelley, and George Eliot. Others cover Sterne, Carlyle, Coleridge, and the State Trials. The Brontë essay opens by weighing praise given by Swinburne. Stephen argues that criticism should rest on calm, rational ground. He still admits that love of an author begins in sympathy. Stephen helped define Victorian literary criticism. These essays show his method at work on major writers.
58878-donahey-s-cartoons:
Donahey, cartoonist of The Cleveland Plain Dealer, gathered his daily panels in this book. The Korner and Wood Company printed it at Cleveland, by the paper's leave. Why she didn't get her new hat Easter morning heads the named plates.

The cartoons in this volume, the artist writes, show in simple fashion the little joys and little troubles that make up the sum of life. Beneath their whims and stretches he hopes for an appeal to the touch of nature that makes us kin. Moving day's last load, every Sunday morning, and wouldn't it make you mad fill the set. Bruder ain't saving nothing for me, one small boy wails. Donahey drew the American kitchen and street with a kind, sharp pencil.
59022-myself-when-young-confessions:
Alec Waugh wrote these confessions, Myself When Young, printed in London in 1923. Waugh had written The Loom of Youth in fiction and The Prisoners of Mainz and Public School Life as studies. He gives the book to his mother, to whom he first spoke of it. The tale opens in the world of London parties and late trains.

Waugh weighs where a man should live if his friends sit in Kensington and Bloomsbury. Golders Green, his own end of the line, spoils an evening with the thought of the last tube home. At twenty-five minutes past twelve he rises, makes his excuses, and is begged to stay a little longer. Vanity and thrift fight it out over the price of a taxi.
59177-the-lone-wolf-returns:
The Lone Wolf Returns, by Louis Joseph Vance, was held under a 1923 copyright and printed in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Plates from the Columbia photoplay fill the book. Vance gives the book to Frank Edwin Verney, because he asked for more.

A note states that this is the fifth and last of the Lone Wolf stories, as Vance meant it. It stands alone like the rest, from The Lone Wolf to Alias the Lone Wolf. The hero is Michael Lanyard, the famed jewel thief turned fighter of crime. Nine printings ran from August to December 1923 alone, which shows the heat of the series. Crime tale fans get the last bow of a suave hero of his day.
59267-the-laboratorians:
A research center on the Moon is the setting for Edward Peattie's story from the May 1955 issue of Worlds of If. Whitemarsh runs the laboratory with the help of his assistant Rocco, and the work of the laboratorians mixes daily routine with the strain of living off the Earth. Sally Chester's arrival stirs the small crew, and the closed world of the station turns small frictions into large ones.

Peattie keeps the science close to the people: the experiments matter less than the tempers, hopes, and rivalries of the staff who run them. Life in the station is rendered in ordinary detail, meals, shifts, and quarrels, against the strange fact of the Moon outside the walls. The story is a quiet piece of fifties science fiction about work and isolation.
59272-the-use-and-abuse-of-church-bells-:
The Use and Abuse of Church Bells, with practical suggestions concerning them, is a treatise by Walter Blunt, a priest of the English Church. Masters published it at London in 1846. Blunt says it has fallen to his lot to be entrusted with the care, or joint care, of very many parishes in various parts of England. No outward matter common to them all has caused him more pain.

The pain is the ordinary use of the church bells, and their almost utter neglect for their own proper purposes. So lost is their true use, he writes, that among all the new churches built in recent years scarcely any have more than one bell. A greater number is thought a vain superfluity, a kind of church luxury. His book argues for ringing them as meant.
59282-buster-bear-s-twins:
Buster Bear's Twins, by Thornton W Burgess, was published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York. The copyright runs nineteen twenty-one and nineteen twenty-three. Harrison Cady illustrated the story. Burgess dedicated the book to childhood: little human folk and all children of Old Mother Nature.

Mother Bear has a secret, and Peter Rabbit burns to learn it. The twins are named Boxer and Woof-Woof in chapter four. Out in the great world they climb trees, meet their father, and get even with Peter. Boxer is spanked, turns sulky, and spends a dreadful night alone and lost. Peter scares the twins, gloats, and lands in a tight place himself. Burgess's Green Meadow tales taught natural history through exactly such small prides and falls.
59313-jack-s-two-sovereigns:
Annie S Fenn wrote Jack's Two Sovereigns, issued by Blackie and Son in London, Glasgow, and Bombay. Fenn also wrote Little Dolly Forbes and A Year with Nellie. The tale opens at eight in the evening at 15 Buxton Street, Denham Green. The Kayll family crowds a small sitting-room, and talk flies in all directions.

Madge darns eight pairs of stockings while Edie rests and Bessie is excused as younger. Mr Kayll, a small, bald, pleasant man, cleans a clock he has taken to pieces at the table. Mrs Kayll patches a small pair of tweed trousers. Jack, fourteen, with dark curly hair, earns five shillings a week. Contents promise money matters, a cry of Stop Thief, a storm, and a reunion.
59440-rake-knitting-patterns:
Bertha Thompson wrote Rake Knitting Patterns, published by the Bruce Publishing Company in Milwaukee in 1923. Thompson directed occupational therapy and ran a summer school in the subject at Woodstock, New York. She dedicated the book to the happiness of the sick and convalescent. A photograph shows twins wearing sweaters made by a patient at Kenilworth Hospital in North Carolina.

Her preface recalls the spool knitter of childhood: an empty spool with four brads, making an endless rope of yarn. Wounded soldiers in army and public health hospitals had enlarged the toy into rakes of many sizes. On them they knitted neckties, shawls, caps, sweaters, and capes. A patient flat on his back in a plaster cast, with the use of one hand, could make garments as good as any man's. Thompson's book collects the patterns, turning a hospital pastime into a small industry of recovery.
59447-the-barbarians:
Tom Godwin wrote The Barbarians, a tale first printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in December 1955. Tal-Karanth, Supreme Executive of Tharnar, signs a paper that sets a final hearing for a Terran man and woman. The headnote warns that their execution would break the basic laws of Tharnar. Still, the danger is judged too great for them to live.

Tharnar has known peace for fifty thousand years, centred on one great City of gardens and parks. Tal-Karanth's desk of eternalloy has stood unmarked for more than thirty thousand years. Terrans, by contrast, are a young race, only three hundred years from their last war. He calls them barbarians in spaceships, too immature to trust.
59571-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled a guide to the works of Robert Burns as Project Gutenberg holds them, listing the contents of each volume. The collections covered are the Poems and Songs of Robert Burns and the Complete Works, with Tam O'Shanter and A Day with the Poet Burns besides. A glossary stands at the head of the poems.

The poems are then listed year by year, from 1780 onward, so a reader can find any piece and the volume that holds it. The early years give The Ploughman's Life, songs such as Mary Morison, and the dirge Winter. By 1785 the list holds Holy Willie's Prayer, To a Mouse, The Cotter's Saturday Night, and The Jolly Beggars. Like Widger's other Gutenberg indexes, the file is a map of the set rather than a text to read straight through.
59599-farmhouse-plans:
Farmhouse Plans is Farmers' Bulletin number 1738 of the United States Department of Agriculture. The plans grew out of a Farm Housing Survey made in the spring of 1934 with agricultural colleges in forty-six states, funded by the Civil Works Administration. More than a hundred plans were prepared, and this bulletin selects from them.

Cooperating agencies include the Bureau of Agricultural Engineering and the Bureau of Home Economics, with engineers and professors named state by state, from Alabama to California and Georgia to Illinois. Readers get New Deal rural housing on paper: government-drawn farmhouse designs meant to raise the standard of farm family living during the Depression.
59845-the-able-mclaughlins:
Margaret Wilson wrote this novel, The Able McLaughlins, printed in New York in 1923. The tale opens on a prairie afternoon in September, still as an ocean in small ripples. For centuries the land had lain so, silent under high white clouds. Scarlet swamp-lily seeds fall, goldfinches start up, and young prairie chickens scratch in the short grass.

In that vastness sits a house where little David and the fatter little Sarah play. Their father halted his ox team there ten years before, at the end of a journey from Ayrshire. His eight boys and girls fell on the wild strawberries with shrieks that broke the silence of centuries. The railroad ended sixty miles away, and no buffalo had called there for fifteen years.
5995-chapters-of-opera-being-historical-:
Henry Edward Krehbiel chronicles the lyric drama in New York from its earliest days to the present time. The Metropolitan Opera House completed twenty-five years with the season of 1907-08. From his seat, stall D-15, Krehbiel watched each season as music editor of the New York Tribune.

Krehbiel witnessed the institution's ups and downs across a quarter century and recorded its significant turns. The book mixes history with critical judgment, naming managers, singers, and fashions that shaped the house. It serves as both memoir and record of opera in America's largest city.
59959-english-surnames-their-sources-and:
Charles Wareing Bardsley wrote English Surnames, here in a second edition of 1875. Chatto and Windus published the revised and enlarged book in London. Its subtitle promises the sources and significations of names. Bardsley dedicates the work to his father.

The new preface reads the quick demand for a reprint modestly. It shows growing interest in a neglected subject, Bardsley says. Reviewers in the Times and the Athenæum advised a new plan. He has rearranged the chapters on patronymics and nicknames. Names that belong together now stand close under clear heads. Criticism, kind and harsh, gets his thanks. One journal, he adds, has not quite grasped the nature of his work. The study treats surnames as records of language and life.
60074-the-mysterious-stranger-and-other-:
John McCutcheon bound his best news cartoons on the great days of his age. The book came out in New York in October 1905. His plates first ran in the Chicago Tribune and Record-Herald. A first note hopes they keep worth for the years to come. The last years had moved fast past their wont, it says.

A war that was a war in truth had marked that span, it holds. Dire wrecks and world shocks crowd those same short years. The title tale, a strange guest, leads the drawn set in name. Each plate turns a news day into one bold, clear joke. Town readers kept such books as a past in pictures. Wit and fact mix.
60134-lumber-legal-opinions:
Lumber Legal Opinions was issued in 1910 by the National Wholesale Lumber Dealers Association, at 66 Broadway in New York. Robert Higbie heads the officer list as president for 1910 and 1911. Trustees are named by the year their terms expire, from towns across the country. The front pages explain the work of the association's bureaus.

The Bureau of Information held 28000 reports on the standing of lumber buyers, each rated for credit. Members rated those reports above any other mercantile agency. A legal and collection department handles past due accounts and holds court decisions for members on request. A railroad and transportation bureau serves members on freight matters as well.
60245-fort-robinson-outpost-on-the-plain:
Fort Robinson, Outpost on the Plains, by Roger Grange, is a history reprinted from Nebraska History, volume thirty nine, September 1958, by the Nebraska State Historical Society. Grange had served as the society's museum director. A photograph of a Ninth Cavalry lieutenant of 1897 faces the title.

The tale begins in March 1874, when the Sioux Expedition marched from Fort Laramie toward the Red Cloud Agency in bitter cold. Some nine hundred fifty men went to overawe the Sioux and guard the agency where thousands drew treaty rations. Crazy Horse rides at the edge of these pages. The fort born of that march guarded the plains for decades.
60348-professor-w-g-elmslie-d-d-memoir-a:
W Robertson Nicoll and A N Macnicoll edited this memorial book for Professor W G Elmslie, printed by Hodder and Stoughton of London in 1890. The second edition joins a brief life to a set of his sermons. Nicoll wrote the life, save for the pages on Regent Square and Willesden, which Macnicoll supplied. Friends added their memories, and Principal Dykes read the proofs.

The editors had matter enough for a larger life but chose a book at a fair price. Sermons are printed as they were spoken, from shorthand notes where they had them. Two Sunday readings come from Good Words, and a paper on Genesis from the Contemporary Review. The volume keeps a loved teacher's voice on the page.
60447-the-twins-of-emu-plains:
Mary Grant Bruce's The Twins of Emu Plains was published by Ward, Lock in London and Melbourne. A frontispiece shows Jean reassuring a hidden someone that no one knows he is there. Eighteen chapters run from the pleasant madness of the twins through midnight, the last days of term, and a letter from home, to Emu Plains itself.

The story opens on a school tennis final. Merriwa and Kooringal schools are locked in the last struggle of their match, the air about the court alive with noise. Kooringal's backers mass under their green and mauve flag on the western side, screaming as one at their champions' strokes. The Merriwiggians face them in dark-blue favours. Later chapters promise a surprise-packet, a jersey bull, and gentlemen adventurers.
60683-baker-s-dozens:
Baker Dozens is a science fiction story by Jim Harmon, taken from Worlds of If for July 1959. A blurb says catching him was no problem, for they caught him everywhere, and practically all at once. Baker is a famed space criminal with many deaths on record.

Mr Street, the foremost xenologist on Earth, faces the director of Extraterrestrial Investigations. The director asks what he knows about the infamous criminal Baker, the so called Robin Hood who is actually a scarlet fiend. Street says he knows everything. Surely not how he died, the director asks. Everything but that, Street answers. The agency has received many accounts of his death, or deaths, on various worlds. It needs absolute proof, since Baker has supporters even on Earth. Space tale fans get a puzzle of a man with too many deaths.
61021-some-war-impressions: War impressions by Jeffery Farnol fill this volume, from the writer known for romances such as The Broad Highway, The Money Moon, and The Amateur Gentleman. The opening pages of the hosted copy are mostly publisher notices for those earlier novels, with press praise quoted for Beltane the Smith and The Honourable Mr. Tawnish, before the title page of Some War Impressions appears in full.
61143-some-reflections-upon-marriage-wit:
Some Reflections Upon Marriage reached a fourth edition in London, printed for William Parker at Saint Paul's Church-Yard. The title page notes that the new issue carries added matter. A list of the author's other books stands in front.

Those books include A Serious Proposal to the Ladies and letters on the love of God. The preface asks readers to excuse faults where the book that sparked these thoughts came late to hand. The aim, it says, is to correct abuses in marriage. Power and long custom, the author argues, do not make a wrong right. The tone is firm and devout.
61187-all-that-earthly-remains:
C C MacApp wrote All That Earthly Remains, a short tale first printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in July nineteen sixty two. The head note says the tale came from that magazine. Rumour said devils lived in a cave, but the truth was even more appalling, the blurb warns. Dr Luis Craig is flown south in haste by jet bomber. Thin Andean air leaves him breathing hard.

A strong helicopter waits to take Craig on the last leg of his trip. Lieutenant Rabar, in the uniform of a Latin American air force, will fly him and speaks with smooth care. Shouts break out at the field edge, and a rifle cracks near Craig ear. He hits the dirt as sidearms and automatic weapons answer. Craig had disliked Rabar from the first, and now trusts him even less. Danger and mistrust drive the tale from its first pages.
61360-witch-of-the-glens:
Witch of the Glens, by Sally Watson, was first published in New York in 1962, with drawings by Barbara Werner. Watson gives the book to her favourite witch, and to Jean and Don and their two small kelpies, Kathy and Mark. A list of Gaelic terms at the back explains words for fool and witch.

The tale opens with gypsies and a waif, then moves to Glenfern and the daft folk. Chapters name bewitchery, a picture in a loch, and a task for Kelpie. Inveraray Castle, Argyll dungeon, and the hexing of Alex follow. Later come a witch hunt, snow footprints, vengeance, and a last word. Readers get a Highland tale of witchcraft, castles, and clan lands for young readers.
61553-rootabaga-pigeons:
Rootabaga Pigeons, by Carl Sandburg, copyright 1923, is a second book of his tall tales for children, following Rootabaga Stories. Maud and Miska Petersham drew the pictures and decorations. The book is dedicated to three Illinois pigeons, and its storyteller is the Potato Face Blind Man with his accordion.

Six groups of tales fill the volume: a skyscraper built to the moon, Hatrack the Horse and his six pigeons, three wild Babylonian baboons, and boys with monkey wrenches for Christmas. Sandburg writes plain prairie speech turned into pure play. Grown readers steal these stories as often as children hear them.
61612-the-temples-and-ritual-of-asklepio:
The Temples and Ritual of Asklepios at Epidauros and Athens prints two lectures delivered at the Royal Institution of Great Britain by Richard Caton. Caton was honorary physician to the Liverpool Royal Infirmary and an emeritus professor of physiology. This second edition came from the University Press of Liverpool in 1900, with thirty four illustrations.

Lecture one opens on the great age of excavation: Schliemann's light on Greece, German sums spent at Olympia and Pergamos, and French work at Delphi. Against that backdrop, Caton calls the shrines of Asklepios, the god of healing, an important field still comparatively unknown in England. His lectures report what digging at Epidauros and Athens had lately shown.
61616-lichens:
Annie Lorrain Smith's Lichens was published by the Cambridge University Press in 1921 in the Cambridge Botanical Handbooks. Smith was acting assistant in the botanical department of the British Museum. Her first chapter gives the history of lichen study in seven periods, from before 1694 down to 1867 and after.

The second chapter takes up the parts of the lichen thallus. It treats the gonidia, the hyphae and the algae, and weighs how alga and fungus live together, whether as partners or as parasite and host. Culture tests with the thallus alone and with its parts apart are described. A chapter on form follows, with a glossary at the front of the book.
61752-exiles-of-the-three-red-moons:
Exiles of the Three Red Moons is a science fiction story by Carl Selwyn, taken from Planet Stories for the summer of 1940. Its hero is Rusty Carter, a Tele-news reporter who has lived for months in the penal colony on Pluto. Under the green light of Pluto's three moons, men die of the Emerald Death in that Devil's Island.

Carter's presence there is a plant. His editor, Skipper Russell, had him stage a bank robbery with a harmless ray gun and hired actors, so police would trap him and a court send him to Pluto for life. The point was a first-hand story worth millions, since the Interplanetary Control bars reporters from the colony. Now the job is done, and the monthly ship is due in twenty revs. This time it will land, and Carter means to be on it going home.
61758-irish-impressions:
Chesterton wrote Irish Impressions, first printed by Collins at London in November 1919. Nine essays record a visit to Ireland. The first takes its title, Two Stones in a Square, from a statue half seen on St Stephen's Green in Dublin.

Chesterton jokes that St George's Channel might better be St Patrick's, and that statues in frock coats might kill a Christian at sight. Later chapters treat the root of reality, the family and the feud, and the paradox of labour. The Englishman in Ireland, the mistake of England, and the mistake of Ireland build the argument. Belfast and the religious problem end the book.
61902-how-salvator-won-and-other-recitat:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox gathered How Salvator Won and Other Recitations at New York in 1891, from the press of Edgar Werner. She had also written Maurine, Poems of Passion, and Poems of Pleasure. Her preface says readers and speakers kept urging her to furnish verses for recitation, and that she chose the poems with the best dramatic scope for the platform. Some are among her earliest efforts, and some were written for this book.

Meg's Curse, never before in print, stands among them. Wilcox owns that in it she set aside all rules of art to give the public reader a chance to use his powers of speech. The list runs to dozens of pieces: Gossips, Grandpa's Christmas, The Giddy Girl, Gethsemane, and the title poem of the race horse Salvator. Such books fed the great age of elocution.
61969-prince-dusty-a-story-of-the-oil-re:
Kirk Munroe tells an oil country tale in Prince Dusty, a story of the oil regions, printed in New York and London in 1891. Putnam made the book, in the Rail and Water series of books for boys. Munroe had writ Under Orders and Derrick Sterling. A plate shows a great oil tank struck by lightning, a roaring mass of flame.

A prince and princess go in search of adventures to open the tale. A present from a fairy godmother and Brace Barlow the moonlighter follow. A torpedo man's peril, Arthur and his cousins, and a gallant rescue build the run. Uncle Phin's plan, a hurried flight, and life on board the ark raise the stakes. A torrent of flame and the saving of the ark form the peak.
62025-positions:
Richard Mulcaster, first head master of Merchant Taylors' School from 1561 to 1586, wrote this treatise on the training of children, first printed at London in 1581. Longmans reprinted it in 1888. The reprint carries an appendix on Mulcaster's life and writings by Robert Hebert Quick, Cambridge's first lecturer on the history of education.

Mulcaster's full title promises an examination of the primitive circumstances needed for training children up, either for skill in their book or health in their body. He dedicated the work to Queen Elizabeth, arguing that his book pretends to a common good, since it concerns the general bringing up of youth. Learning for the mind and health for the body are its twin aims, and the old spelling of 1581 is kept throughout the reprint.
62413-downright-fighting-the-story-of-co:
Downright Fighting, the story of Cowpens, is a handbook for Cowpens National Battlefield in South Carolina, written by Thomas Fleming. It was produced by the National Park Service at Washington in 1988, as Handbook 135. Fleming, a biographer, military historian, and novelist, had written lives of Jefferson and Franklin and an account of the Pilgrims' first year.

The opening pages call Cowpens the patriot's best fought battle of the Revolutionary War, and Fleming a master storyteller. The handbook is made, like its fellows, to inform visitors and guide them through the park's features. More than a hundred such titles were in print, sold at parks and by mail, covering the nation's natural and cultural inheritance.
62497-goose-creek-folks-a-story-of-the-k:
Goose Creek Folks, subtitled A Story of the Kentucky Mountains, is a work of fiction by Isabel Graham Bush and Florence Lilian Bush. It was published in 1912 by the Fleming Revell Company in New York, Chicago, and Toronto. The book is dedicated to a teacher of Berea College whose zeal for learning inspired many mountain boys and girls.

The chapter list gives the shape of the tale. It opens with a discovery by Dan Gooch, follows a surprise brought by Martin, and shows a girl named Talitha solving a puzzle. A storm, an unexpected rival, and a hunt for a varmint fill the early chapters. Later come a jam social, a baptizing, and a secret revealed. One chapter title shows the creek folk plotting against the schoolmaster, a hint that the mountain school stands at the heart of the story.
62544-technique-of-eye-dissections:
Frederic Woll wrote a small handbook on the cutting open of the eye, in a second edition from New York in 1924. The first edition came in July 1914. Woll taught hygiene at the City College of New York and eye work at Columbia. He gave the book to his first teacher in optics, Andrew Jay Cross.

The aim, as the opening states, is to give set methods for the work. Eye specialists, teachers, and students of the build and working of the eye are all addressed. Chapters treat the taking out of the clear membrane with its contents whole, the canal of Petit, and the inside of the eye. The iris, cornea, lens, choroid, and retina each take a chapter in turn. Pictures show the glassware and tools, the first cut, and each stage of the work.
62844-the-fair-dominion-a-record-of-cana:
The Fair Dominion is a travel book of views on Canada by R Vernede. Twelve colour prints from drawings dress the text of the tour. The book came out in London in the year nineteen eleven. Its author had past form as a teller of tales in print.

The route runs from a Liverpool ship berth to lakes high in the Rockies. Steerage life, Quebec days, and a habitant village earn full parts. Montreal, Toronto, the great falls, and prairie towns pass in review. Farm belts made to order and the pull of Yank ways draw long thought. A lone close at the lakes among clouds ends the long north tour.
62847-beautiful-beautiful-afghans:
Beautiful Afghans is a crochet pattern booklet, Star Book number 82, issued by the American Thread Company in 1951. It sold for ten cents. The cover promise is homely: one afghan in the set can be made while watching television. The softest afghans, the booklet says, are made of the company's Dawn wool.

The design studio gathered easy patterns, old favourites among them. The Granny and the Chevron are included because readers had asked for them. The Square Dance, shown in gay bright colours, also comes in a shorter version that makes a handsome shawl. The flower afghan on the cover calls for black yarn and twenty-one assorted colours. Its 672 small motifs, each about two inches across, join into a blanket of forty-seven by seventy inches.
62920-sketches-and-cartoons:
Charles Dana Gibson draws society in Sketches and Cartoons, from R H Russell of New York in 1900. Russell's note calls it the third book in the regular series of Gibson's published drawings, after Drawings and Pictures of People. Each book holds eighty-four of his best cartoons, drawn from the magazines by permission.

The plates speak in captions: Is a Caddie Always Necessary?, One of the Hazards of Golf, and a Christmas fantasy. A mock civil-service father consults his clerk on whether Maud is engaged yet before listing a baron among her suitors. Courtship, sport, and folly fill the pages in pen and ink.
63090-everyday-americans:
Everyday Americans is a set of essays on American character by Henry Seidel Canby, published by the Century Company. Canby copyrighted the book in 1919 and 1920. He had earlier written College Sons and College Fathers and Our House.

Seven chapters sort the nation by temper. They treat the American mind, conservative America, radical America, and American idealism. Religion and literature in America follow, and a portrait of the bourgeois American closes the book. The first chapter begins in England, with the figure of the radical-conservative. Such a man, Canby says, agrees with radical principles but dislikes radicals for their manners. The type frames his study of how Americans hold their politics. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
63205-a-boy-s-trip-across-the-plains:
Laura Preston wrote a boy's adventure published at New York and San Francisco in 1868, dedicated to her nephews and nieces. In a village in western Missouri lived a widow, Mrs Loring, and her son Guy, a little boy about ten years old. They were very poor, for the debts of the dead father had eaten the estate.

The widow, delicate and never trained to work, opened a little school, then took in sewing, and lost her scholars for doing two things at once. Early winter found them needing money more than at any other season. Guy's trip across the plains, the title's promise, grows out of that straitened home. A juvenile emigrant tale of the overland years is the ware.
63234-dirigible-balloons:
Charles Hayward prepared this instruction paper on dirigible balloons for students. The American School of Correspondence issued it at Chicago, copyright 1918. Hayward served the Society of Automobile Engineers as secretary once. Early attempts open the paper with Leonardo da Vinci flight studies.

Da Vinci sketches show batlike wings folding on the upward stroke. Francisco de Lana planned a flying ship with emptied metal spheres. Water filled, then drained, the spheres were to hold vacuum lift. He never built it, holding God would not permit such change. A figure shows De Lana airboat as the first picture in the instruction paper.
63268-the-happy-go-lucky-morgans:
Edward Thomas wrote The Happy-Go-Lucky Morgans, published at London by Duckworth and dedicated to his father and mother. A title motto, Thomas Hardy's Julie-Jane, hangs over the book. Twenty chapters open on Abercorran Street.

My story is of Balham, the narrator begins, and of a family. The Morgans of Abercorran House, wild swans, and Hob-y-deri-dando follow. Aurelius the superfluous man, Lydiard Constantine, Mr Torrance the cheerful man, and Mr Stodham the respectable man people the middle. The castle of leaves, Philip and the outlaws of the island, and the poet's spring close it. Readers get a Welsh-London family chronicle in Thomas's lyrical, digressing prose.
63283-new-mexico-magazine-s-a-taste-of-n:
A Taste of New Mexico Kitchens is a cook book from a state magazine. Its lists run from bean pots and rolled corn cakes to sweet pies. Named inns and home cooks lend their best known dishes to the set. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

Main plates lean on beans, corn, and the hot pods of the land. Red and green sauces get a full part of rules in their own right. Breads run from flat wheat cakes to blue corn loaves and fried puffs. Sweet ends hold small pies, spice snaps, and nut sweets of the place. Drinks from a famed ranch inn close the gay home cook set.
63344-paper-shell-pecans:
Paper Shell Pecans is a promotional book for the Hess Brand pecan orchards of southwest Georgia. Every photograph in it was taken on the company's own plantations, more than 7000 acres in all. One plate shows sixteen nuts on a single small branch. Another shows the rows of a bearing orchard in Calhoun County, where single trees have borne over two hundred pounds in a season.

The argument is food and profit together. Chapters set nut meat against beefsteak, call the pecan the ideal fat food, and claim twenty times as much food per acre. A cooperative, profit sharing system then offers acre units to investors, with letters from owners and a tour of the company's officers and references.
63516-the-vanishing-venusians:
Vanishing Venusians is a science fiction tale by Leigh Brackett of Venus seas. The story ran in Planet Stories for Spring nineteen forty five. For years a people wandered the eternal seas of Venus seeking home. Death walked in their wake as they sought their birthright land again.

Three of them now make a final bid toward the promised land shore. Matt Harker lies by the tiller of a weed grown hull at night. Twelve ships carry thirty eight hundred exiles, going no place at all. Venus thick clouds make the sun a half remembered legend to them. The Sea of Morning Opals lies black and streaked with phosphor light.
63673-narrative-of-my-captivity-among-th:
Narrative of My Captivity Among the Sioux Indians is a memoir by Fanny Kelly. Wilstach, Baldwin of Cincinnati printed the book in the year 1871. Kelly entered the rights herself in that same year at Washington. She gives the book to the officers of two cavalry regiments. Their daring efforts aided her husband in effecting her rescue, she writes.

A brief account of General Sully's Indian expedition of 1864 stands added. That expedition bore upon events occurring in her captivity, she notes. The summer of 1864 marked unusual peril for western pioneers seeking homes. Massacres in Minnesota in 1862 still cast their shadow over the trails. Her small emigrant company was attacked by an overwhelming Sioux force. She promises a plain, unvarnished narrative of habits and treatment of prisoners. Facts, not fine-wrought sentences, guide her telling of the captivity.
63993-lord-of-a-thousand-suns:
Lord of a Thousand Suns is a science fiction tale by Poul Anderson. The Project Gutenberg text was taken from Planet Stories for September 1951. Its headnote tells of Daryesh, a man a million years old, once lord of a thousand suns. He is condemned to rove the spaceways in an alien shape, in search of the great lost Vwyrdda.

The tale opens in talk between spacemen. One holds that any tall story ever told has its match somewhere in the galaxy. He has seen fire-breathing dragons and witches with real powers. Laird, a gaunt man of the Galactic Survey, answers in a slow, soft voice. He once let a genie out of a bottle, he says. It killed him. The look behind his eyes stops the laugh before it starts.
64020-the-pit-of-nympthons:
The Pit of Nymphons is a science fiction story by Stanley Mullen, taken from Planet Stories for November 1951. Its teaser locks the horror-secrets of the universe in the mutant jungle of Venus. Into those thousand deaths goes luxury-soft Kial Nasron, led by a convict. Kial is the daughter of a Martian politician and a great shareholder in Venusian Exports.

Hailard, the director of Venusian Exports, is a man of few words. He reflects that after two hundred years Venus still holds problems and eerie mysteries for the earth colonists. He tells Kial that a man without deviltry has little capacity for wisdom. The convict Craig Alston must guide her into the jungle. The copyright was never renewed.
64364-sword-of-the-seven-suns:
Gardner Fox wrote this planet tale for Planet Stories' spring 1947 issue. Its world was dark, its machine-god dead, and wild hordes pressed to overrun its folk. What was Flane doing out in the desert, alone with a wrecked spaceship and a strangely wrought sword?

The ship flees like a silver bullet across black nothing, the tale opens. Round windows stare from her curved sides. Dust clouds whirl past, and chunks of rock bounce off her hull. To one side shine triple stars strange to the crew. Hercules hangs changed on the other hand. Ahead lies great Deneb, with its ring of giant worlds. The ship sweeps closer, trailing billows of space dust, toward a planet near kin to the voyagers' own.
64385-why-authors-go-wrong-and-other-exp:
Why Authors Go Wrong, and Other Explanations is a book about the writing trade by Grant Overton, author of The Women Who Make Our Novels. Moffat, Yard and Company published it at New York in 1919. The title piece opens by owning that its subject could fill a book by itself. Overton takes up Arnold Bennett's The Truth About an Author, doubting that it tells truth about authors in general rather than about Bennett.

The chapters move through a barbaric yawp and the critical court. Book reviewing, literary editors by one of them, and what every publisher knows follow. The secret of the best seller and a chapter on writing a novel close the book. Overton holds the question to be moral and human, not merely literary.
64394-sweet-hampstead-and-its-associatio:
Caroline White's local history of Hampstead, the hill village above London, was published by Elliot Stock in nineteen hundred. Its title borrows the village's pet name. Its epigraphs quote Leigh Hunt, who called Hampstead a village revelling in varieties. The painter Constable asked when he would see sweet Hampstead again.

White explains in her preface that the idea came to her more than thirty years before publication, and that the first draft waited while a busy life intervened. Writing at the perspective of eighty nine years, she says the task brought back sunny days through a mist of tears. The book gathers Hampstead's houses, heath, and residents into one mosaic, dedicated to the conservators of the heath and to all who love the place for its own sake. It is amateur history in the best sense, written from a lifetime of knowledge.
64460-the-armenians:
Dixon-Johnson wrote The Armenians, printed at Blackburn in 1916. A saying from the Koran heads the title page, and the author dates his preface from Croft-on-Tees in February of that year. Eight chapters argue a case.

The first chapters give the Armenians' early history and the land they share with Kurds and Turks. The Armenian Question follows, with the Treaty of Berlin and foreign missionaries named as disturbing factors. Dixon-Johnson then weighs Armenian character through quoted opinions, and past risings at Zeitun and elsewhere. Recent troubles and victim figures close the argument: he holds the reports one-sided and the numbers inflated.
64472-christian-literature-a-sermon-deli:
J Stoughton gave Christian Literature as a sermon on May 8, 1870, in Kensington Chapel at the seventy first anniversary of the Religious Tract Society. The sermon was printed at London that year by request. A verse from John chapter twenty one heads the talk. It says the world could not hold the books of all Christ did.

Stoughton calls that chapter a supplement to the main history. John had closed his Gospel sure it was far from full, he says. The added chapter tells the draught of fishes in minute detail. John then pledges the truth of the whole tale. Fullness of facts and lessons in Christ's life defies all record, Stoughton holds. The sermon then turns to the work of Christian print in spreading that tale. Tracts and books are its theme.
64553-the-cameroons:
Albert Calvert's study of the Cameroons, published in London by Werner Laurie in nineteen seventeen, tells the rise and fall of a German colony as a lesson for British readers. Calvert had written on the German African empire, South West Africa, and Nigeria, and he treats German colonial policy as one design.

The preface argues that the Cameroons chapter shows that design completely, from acquisition to collapse. Calvert describes how Germany assured England in eighteen eighty four that it wanted no possessions in Britain's sphere. Germany then built protectorates in Africa anyway. Bismarck disowned, and used, the agents who did the work on the ground. The book appeared while British and French forces were taking the German colonies one by one. It is part history and part warning, written to prove that the German empire had aimed at Britain's place in Africa.
6458-air-service-boys-in-the-big-battle-:
Charles Amory Beach sends air service boys Tom Raymond and Jack Parmly into the big battle to silence the big guns. Bad news from the air opens it, with Tom in French aviator uniform on a cot in a tent near Paris airdromes. Jack teases him about his head and calls him cabbage, a pet name picked up from French flying comrades. Such odd, endearing terms, cucumber or rose, cabbage or cart wheel, matter less than the meaning behind them.

Chapters promise a girl's appeal, anxious waiting, transfer, resolve, Paris, the American front, a battle in the air, a falling glove, stunts, and a daring scheme. A mid passage reaches General Pershing's headquarters with the cry that the American front is here at last, though strictly no American front yet existed, troops being brigaded with French and British. Beach writes war flying adventure for boys, with chums, machines, and battle.
64628-narratives-of-colored-americans:
Narratives of Colored Americans is a set of Black life stories printed at New York in 1875. William Wood published the book by order of the Lindley Murray estate trustees. A verse from Acts heads the title, that God made all nations of one blood. Murray, the famed grammarian, left funds for books promoting piety and virtue.

Trustees in America used his bequest for free distribution of such improving books. Short lives of pious Black men and women make up the narrative contents here. Conversion, industry, and patient suffering under slavery mark the chosen examples. Abolition era biography for the young survives in this trustee printed volume.
64654-harvesting-ants-and-trap-door-spid:
Traherne Moggridge wrote this work of natural history, published in London in 1873. Its full title promises notes and observations on the habits and dwellings of two small creatures. Part one deals with harvesting ants, and part two, starting much later in the book, deals with trap-door spiders.

For the ants, Moggridge describes nests of Atta barbara and Atta structor, with trains of workers bearing seeds. He shows the mounds of refuse at the nest mouths and the stored seeds in their granaries. Long plate notes follow each figure in close detail, down to jaws and wings shown enlarged. The book rewards readers who like field study done slowly and at close range.
65290-among-the-lindens:
Evelyn Raymond wrote this novel for young readers, printed in Boston in 1898 with pictures by Victor Searles. Raymond had earlier books listed on the opening pages, among them The Little Lady of the Horse and The Mushroom Cave. Chapter one opens with a schoolgirl calling out a sharp warning to a man in danger.

The chapter list sketches a warm story of home, school, and kindness. Titles point to a chrysanthemum dinner, a stay in a new home, Miss Joanna, bits of natural history, and a modern King Arthur. Later chapters move three years ahead to show the result. Readers get a gentle period story told in short, lively chapters.
65431-the-maid-of-orleans:
Frederick Henning wrote this life of the Maid of Orleans in German, and George Upton turned it into English for young readers. The Chicago firm of McClurg brought it out in 1904 in the Life Stories for Young People line. Its subject is Joan, the village girl of Domremy who rose to lead French arms.

Seven chapters trace her course from the Fairy Tree at Domremy to the stake. The Dauphin and La Hire, a plot, camp and court, the crowning and capture, and the death scene fill the middle of the book. A short last chapter tells of a rescue, and an appendix closes the tale for its young audience.
65454-the-trail-of-the-swinging-lanterns:
John Morison Copeland wrote this railway miscellany, The Trail of the Swinging Lanterns, printed at Toronto in 1918. Its title page calls it a racy railroading review of transportation matters, methods, and men. A long contents page mixes line histories with portraits of railway men, poems, and tall tales of the road.

A deceased Canadian railway stands near the front, then a sister line, the Grand Trunk; pieces follow on named locomotives, a Milton celebration, and a crusade of American railway interests in Canada. Thomas Edison gets a piece, and a great railway is called a gigantic human hive. The book opens with a poem, Navigators of the Blue, about carrier pigeons as pioneers of the air. They wheel above dormant farms and winter brooks, each a spark of life on the wing.
65618-practical-farm-buildings-plans-and:
Hunter edited Practical Farm Buildings, a book of plans and suggestions published by Bird and Son of East Walpole, Massachusetts, with a 1905 copyright. The firm, founded in 1817, sold building materials from offices in New York, Chicago, and Washington. A warm welcome for the first edition led the firm to make this larger and fuller one.

The foreword states the rule of the book: only plans that had proved their worth in constant farm use were admitted. A special aim was poultry housing. The newer plans open the houses to sunshine and fresh air, a turn tied to healthier and more profitable flocks. Hunter thanks the Cornell Reading Course for Farmers for help from its bulletin on building. Farmers get tested barn and henhouse plans from a firm that sold the boards to build them.
65668-revolt-of-the-brains:
Thames wrote this science fiction tale for Imagination, where it ran in December 1956. Its tag line warns that Earth faced its darkest hour. Men stood ready to fight any foe from space, except the one foe they had made themselves.

Harry Taylor is called in by the Chief, a three-star Air Force general. Every guided missile in the free world's store has vanished, and radar tracked them as they blasted off on their own. Maps of the West line the wall, with White Sands, the Everglades, and the Mojave marked in red. Taylor hears that Earth may now be unable to strike back if an enemy learns the truth.
6581-a-treatise-on-the-six-nation-indian:
J. B. Mackenzie first gave this short work as a lecture on the Six Nation Indians, and later set it in print with a frank correction. He takes back a harsh phrase he had laid on a Native writer, Peter Jones, and admits the faults he named belong to many whites as well. That honest note opens a study meant to be fair, not flattering.

The treatise sketches the history, ways, and standing of the Six Nations in Canada, in plain, direct prose. Mackenzie writes as a man of his time, with limits his own correction hints at, yet keen to set the record right. Readers get a brief, early Canadian view of a proud confederacy and its place in a changing land.
65992-portraits-and-speculations:
Arthur Ransome gathered his essays as Portraits and Speculations in nineteen thirteen, giving the book to John Masefield. Ransome had written studies of Edgar Allan Poe and Oscar Wilde. Several essays had first run in leading reviews.

The lead essay, Art for Life's Sake, attacks the doctrine of art for art's sake. That creed, Ransome says, came from French artists and a German thinker. Portraits follow of Aloysius Bertrand, Alphonse Daudet, and François Coppée. Long pieces treat Nietzsche, Walter Pater, and Remy de Gourmont. The poetry of Yone Noguchi and a study of speech in motion and at rest close the book.
66103-lambkin-s-remains:
H B wrote Lambkin Remains, a book of light verse and prose put out at Oxford in 1900. The writer had made a name with The Bad Child Book of Beasts. Most of the pieces first ran in The J C R, a college sheet. One piece, on sleep, first ran in The Isis.

A mock grand gift page gives the book to a club of a set frame of mind. A long ode in jest then states the plan of the book. The poet sings of his own dear friends, not of fame or of the crowd. A new boy at Oxford walks the High and sniffs the west wind with joy. He asks if this can be the place his sire called a shame. Tales of an uncle lost to drink, debt, and a drug fill the fun. The tone stays light, fond, and full of school wit.
66111-afghans:
The Spool Cotton Company issued Afghans as Afghan Book Number 289 in July 1952, priced at ten cents. The booklet pushes Chadwick's Red Heart yarns and J and P Coats threads. A headnote urges readers to add an afghan to the family possessions.

The cover pattern, Persian Print C-117, makes a throw of about forty-six by sixty-two inches. It calls for twenty-one skeins of bittersweet and twenty-five of navy worsted, with a plastic crochet hook number five. Each motif works four inches square, starting with a ring of chain stitches. Full stitch-by-stitch rounds follow. More patterns fill the booklet, all built for home crochet with the firm's yarns.
66146-the-cream-of-the-jest-a-comedy-of-:
James Cabell wrote the Cream of the Jest, in 1917. A comedy of evasions is the book's own subtitle. McBride at New York put it out in September that year. Cabell's other novels fill a page of its front matter. The Soul of Melicent and the Rivet in Grandfather's Neck stand there.

Tales, verses, and genealogies of his stand in the same list. A French sentence stands as the book's epigraph in front. You led me in a dream to the land I wanted, it runs. I have loved only your shadow, the French continues there. A clerk appraises a fair country in an early chapter's head. The double-dealer's traffic with a knave fills another contents line. How the double-dealer was dealt with follows in that list. Cabell gives longing a jest for its cream.
66195-south-sea-yarns:
South Sea Yarns, by Basil Thomson, with illustrations, was published by William Blackwood and Sons at Edinburgh and London in 1894 and dedicated to the author's wife. The introduction sets a story-telling scene in the great bure, or house, of Raiyawa.

Lying-places of mats fill three sides of the house, with smouldering logs between them and blue smoke curling to the blackened thatch. Elders dive head-foremost through the rush-screen doorway, beating the reed walls to stir the mosquitoes into the smoke. The foreign visitor, footsore from the mountains, takes the solitary couch of honour by the door.
66242-one-hundred-cartoons:
A cartoon collection by Cesare, published at Boston in 1916. Small, Maynard and Company issued the volume. Cesare drew for the New York Sun and Harper's Weekly. The editors of both receive grateful acknowledgement here. A self-sketch of the artist forms the frontispiece. One hundred numbered cartoons follow it.

The list of illustrations reads as a war diary. The Kaiser bleeds for Antwerp in one early plate. The Lusitania crisis, Tirpitz, and the hyphen debate all appear. Belgium restored and dividends on a scrap of paper close the argument. Christmas morning and dropping the pilot borrow older cartoon symbols. Cesare drew with a fine, nervous line for American papers. The book preserves editorial cartooning from the neutral years before America entered the war.
66290-the-scandalized-martians:
The Scandalized Martians, by Arnold Marmor, was produced from Imagination, a science fiction and fantasy magazine, for June 1954. A head note gives the premise: David Fry wanted to make an epic movie in the realistic school, but his ideas would not pass the censors, here or anyplace else.

David Fry was a realist, the narrator Ronnie says, and also slightly crazy. I want her nude, Fry screams; naked, he insists. Impossible, Ronnie answers. The Breen office will not allow it, and Fry knows it. Fry defies them: it will be his most realistic picture, a milestone in film making. It will not get the seal of approval, Ronnie warns. Every state will ban it. Nevada will not, Fry answers. Harriet Desmond, he is told, would never agree either. Readers get a Hollywood satire that heads, by title, for Mars.
66334-aunt-lydia-s-designs:
Aunt Lydia's Designs is Star Book number 236, a pattern booklet from the American Thread company of Stamford, Connecticut, priced at thirty five cents. It teaches three crafts in one set of pages: knitting, crochet, and macrame. Short lists of abbreviations open the book, giving the code letters each craft uses.

General instructions come first, with the tools a knotter needs: T-pins, scissors, a tape measure, and a knotting board marked in one inch squares. Five knots are taught step by step with figures, from the reversed double half hitch to the overhand knot. The book warns learners to practice every knot on a sample piece first, to get the tension right.
66380-the-incredible-aliens:
The Incredible Aliens is a science fiction story by William Bender, printed in a magazine of science and fantasy in July 1954. A head note frames its hero, a man named Narant. His personal problem seemed of more weight than his mission as an interstellar investigator. The two combine, the note says, when he meets the aliens of the title.

The tale opens as a tiny dot on a view screen is picked out as an alien spaceship. A lookout on an armed cruiser sounds the general alert. Narant, the ship's chief mind doctor, studies the approach with a rebellious hope. They were the first men to visit this system of planets. Why could they not meet a truly superior race for a change, he asks himself, watching the stranger's course.
66717-a-life-unveiled-by-a-child-of-the-:
An unnamed writer looks back in A Life Unveiled, by a child of the drumlins, printed at Garden City, New York, in 1922. Doubleday Page made the book, first edition. John Burroughs writes an introduction. A French line of De Musset stands as motto: this book is all my youth; I made it almost without thinking.

Contents walk a life in twelve chapters. To the reader leads, then the family tree and the roof tree. A child went forth, in the old paths, as twig is bent, and bred in the bone fill the youth. School days follow. Three chapters named the Medic carry the training of a doctor. Through the gate of dreams closes the book. Have you ever reached a time in your life, the reader is asked, when all that had gone before seemed cut off from the present?
6675-the-loss-of-the-s-s-titanic-its-sto:
Lawrence Beesley, a survivor of the Titanic and a scholar of Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, wrote his account five weeks after landing in New York. At a Boston lunch, he told fellow guests how survivors left the ship and reached the Carpathia. An editor of the Boston Herald then urged him to write a correct history for the public good. That lunch gave the book its start.

Beesley tells the sinking as he lived it, with care for fact over thrill, and draws lessons from the loss. His voice is calm, clear, and first-hand. The Loss of the S. S. Titanic is a key survivor's record, still read for its sober, human detail.
66785-the-poems-of-felicia-hemans:
It calls itself the complete copyright edition. The book opens with her juvenile poems, pieces written from the age of eight to fourteen. Among them are verses on her mother's birthday, a prayer, a sonnet to her mother, and England and Spain, written at fourteen.

The next great part is The Domestic Affections, with poems to her mother and brothers and a Christmas carol. A large part of the book is given to translations from Camoens and other poets, above all sonnets. The whole shows the range of a poet who began as a child prodigy of verse. She wrote on home and family, on Greece and Italy, and on tales and songs of many lands. The edition gathers that life's work between two covers.
66792-great-leaders-historic-portraits-f:
Ferris's Great Leaders: Historic Portraits from the Great Historians was published by Appleton at New York in 1889. Ferris selected the passages, adding notes and brief biographical sketches. The preface says Hume's portrait of Alfred the Great suggested the compilation. Historians, he argues, concentrate their powers on these pen-portraits until they stand out from the narrative. Passages from different pages are sometimes joined to complete a portrait, but no other liberty is taken.

The contents open with Grote on Themistocles and Aristides, from the History of Greece. Curtius supplies the Pericles that fronts the volume as an illustration. The selections end at Waterloo, Ferris holding that later leaders lack the perspective a sound judgment needs. He aims the book at readers new to the historians and at school reading classes. Its double purpose is introduction to the writers and a spur to studying history itself.
66798-secret-of-the-martians:
Paul Fairman wrote this science fiction story, printed in Imagination in February 1956. Few colonists had ever seen a Martian, yet a man named Spencer has been killed, and Rex Tate is trapped by whatever secret the Martians hold.

The story opens in the office of Gordon Malloy, Chief of Interplanetary Security, who teases Tate about seven dull months on Pluto. Mars, he warns, could be nasty. Tate volunteers to go and find out what is happening there. Readers get a brisk 1950s space-detective tale, with a security agent sent to a colony world where the natives stay unseen and the danger stays unexplained.
66822-fifty-great-cartoons:
Fifty Great Cartoons gathers drawings by Frank Beard, printed at Chicago by The Ram's Horn Press. The pictures were copied from the artist's own drawings by a new process. A note at the front quotes Charles Wesley: there is no reason why the devil should have all the best tunes, and, the writer adds, all the best pictures.

The opening essay says the cartoonist's pen long served the worldly and comic press, where it did good work for reform. Beard, it claims, was the first great artist to give that pen to Christian living and reform. His cartoons ran in The Ram's Horn, a weekly paper of wide fame in its day.
67044-ten-kittens:
Ten Kittens, by Puckett, is a book of cat tales for children. The Burton company printed it at Kansas City in 1919, with pictures by Helen Walley. The book is given to children who care for the welfare of their pets.

The preface is plain: every tale is true to life. They were gathered across the country, and each kitten lived its part. The aim is to stir love for kittens in boys and girls. If the tales make a reader kinder to kittens, the purpose is met. The first cat, Mack, was a tiger Persian born at a rescue league in Albany. His sick mother came there with mange, and the litter caught it. At six weeks, mother and litter were chloroformed for their awful state, all but Mack. A kind lady chose the orphan and took him home.
67221-pueblo-pottery-making-a-study-at-t:
Pueblo Pottery Making is a study of the craft at the village of San Ildefonso, by Carl E. Guthe. It came out in 1925 from the Yale University Press, for the Department of Archaeology of Phillips Academy at Andover. It is number two of the Papers of the Southwestern Expedition. A plate at its front shows Maria Martinez, called the most skillful potter of San Ildefonso.

The contents set out the steps of the craft in order. An opening part stands first, then raw materials and their gathering and making ready. Red clay, white clay, and temper are treated in turn. Cooking vessel clay and slips and paints stand in the list, with native slip and Santo Domingo slip named. The work is a close record of how the pots of that village were made.
67386-a-preliminary-dissertation-on-the-:
A Preliminary Dissertation on the Mechanism of the Heavens is a work of star lore by Somerville. It was put out at a great port town of the east in eighteen thirty two. A few first words set out its aim. Those words sort the kinds of lore men hold of the world. They show how facts, set side by side, yield laws.

All lore of things past us, the work holds, rests on what we have seen and felt. From like facts men draw the faith that like causes give like fruits. By that path the fall of a stone at the earth's face was shown one with the force that holds the moon. That same force, drawn wide, holds the far worlds in their rounds past the sun.
67566-war-52-carey-cartoons:
War, a set of fifty two Carey cartoons in colour, grew out of a window display scheme of the Carey Fountain Pen Stores. For about eight years the stores had shown cartoons of current events in their windows, drawing crowds in the chief cities. Other merchants took up the plan, in the United States and abroad. This book spreads the war series wider, with an account of how it was made.

The European war was a hard subject, since many readers had kin in the fighting lands. The President had asked all citizens to keep neutral in word and deed. The makers say they kept strict neutrality, no easy task. The cartoons aim to lift the gloom of the man in the street while picturing the monarchs and peoples of the war.
67585-the-psychology-of-the-emotions:
Ribot wrote The Psychology of the Emotions, a work in the Contemporary Science Series edited by Havelock Ellis. Walter Scott put it out at London in 1897. Ribot taught at the College of France and edited the Revue Philosophique. His preface says the study of feelings is still in a muddled and backward state. Other fields of mind, such as memory and sight, drew far more hands. Less than one part in twenty of new books each year touched on feelings at all.

That gap is odd, Ribot says, since feelings rule so much of life. The book sets out to put the field on a firm base. It weighs states of feeling, passions, and their ties to acts. Readers get a sober survey of a field that science had left thin and scattered.
67603-the-man-who-liked-lions:
John Bernard Daley spins a tale of a zoo and a stranger in a story from Infinity Science Fiction for October 1956. Mr Kemper leans on the rail at the lion cage, watching the beasts sleep in the August sun. Beside him a mother scolds her small girl and threatens that a lion will eat her.

Kemper corrects her, noting that only old lions turn to human flesh, Tsavo aside. The mother hurries away, as mothers with children often do near him, and Kemper wonders if they sense what dogs sense in him. A tanned man with a long, narrow face then trades a mind-probe with him across the walk. Readers get a quiet, cold tale in which the hunters at the zoo may not be human at all.
67626-twenty-years-residence-among-the-p:
Twenty Years' Residence Among the People of Turkey reports life in the Ottoman lands. The author signs herself a consul's daughter and wife in the book. Stanley Lane Poole shaped her text as its editor for print. Harper brought it out in New York in the year 1878. Bulgarians, Greeks, Albanians, Turks, and Armenians fill its view of peoples.

The preface takes aim at the fog round the Eastern Question then. Party papers had fed the public a bent stream of news reports. No book of weight had yet told what those folk were like. Long years of life among them ground each claim in the text. What a consul's house sees in twenty years fills the chapters. Manners, faith, and home life of five peoples are set down plain.
67685-rocks-and-their-origins:
Rocks and Their Origins is a geology primer by Grenville Cole, professor of geology in the Royal College of Science for Ireland. Cambridge University Press issued it in 1912 in the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature. The preface is dated from Dublin in February 1912.

Six chapters cover the ground. Rocks in general come first, with a list of the common minerals that form them. Limestones, sandstones, and clays, shales, and slates follow. Igneous and metamorphic rocks close the survey. References, a table of the rock systems in order, and an index end the book. Illustrations show cliffs, quarries, and waterworn limestone. The manual gave general readers a compact, exact start in geology. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
67699-adair-s-history-of-the-american-in:
James Adair wrote a history of the American Indians from his long years as a trader among them, here in a careful reprint form. The editor of this form kept Adair's own page marks, set as bracketed numbers in the text. Adair's fifty six notes are signed with his initial. The editor's added notes are signed with his own.

The editor, Williams, had made like reprints of early Tennessee country texts, such as the memoirs of Henry Timberlake. His front notes list those works and set out the rules of this print. Adair's book is prized as a first hand record of the lives, wars, faith, and speech of the southeastern tribes. Its author lived and traded in their towns for years.
67702-crashing-suns:
Edmond Hamilton wrote this space tale for Weird Tales, where it ran in the August and September 1928 issues. Jan Tor stands at the levers of a ship diving through space. A meteor's near miss sets the tale's pitch in the first lines.

The ship spins like a top after the graze, dials and windows whirling round the conning tower. Jan swings the levers back and rights her by main force. Big Hal Kur pops up through the trap-door, eyes wide. An inch nearer, he swears, and the ship was done. Jan laughs it off with an old saw: a miss is as good as a mile. The suns of the title wait ahead, on a crash course.
67742-the-arch-ology-of-the-cuneiform-in:
The Reverend A H Sayce wrote The Archaeology of the Cuneiform Inscriptions for lay readers. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge issued this revised form in nineteen hundred eight. Sayce held the chair of Assyriology at Oxford in those years. A Hittite tablet from Boghaz Keui fronts the wide survey.

The reading of the wedge script was the age’s great romance of lore. No Rosetta stone gave a key to those lost kings and gods. Wedges, not pictures, made the script a hard sealed book at first. A Greek trained scholar who knew no east tongues guessed the start. Susa digs and the birth of bronze fill the next long part. Sumerians, first lords of the plain, take their own full span. Babylon and Egypt, then Palestine, are weighed side by side. Canaan in the age just before the Exodus closes the tale.
67825-views-and-opinions:
Ouida gathered her essays as Views and Opinions in eighteen ninety-five, giving the book to W H Mallock. Ouida was known for Under Two Flags and Santa Barbara. All but two essays had run in the Fortnightly Review or the North American Review.

The Sins of Society opens the set, with a line from Pascal at its head. Essays treat conscription, gardens, and the cities of Italy. The Failure of Christianity and The New Woman show her bold range. Female suffrage, vulgarity, and the penalties of a famed name follow. Ouida writes with heat and polish, praising taste and leisure. She calls the butterfly a creature of perfect taste.
67874-some-english-gardens:
Some English Gardens pairs drawings by George Elgood with notes by Gertrude Jekyll, published in London, New York, and Bombay in 1904. The contents list more than forty gardens, from Brockenhurst and Great Tangley Manor to Berkeley Castle, Penshurst, and Levens. Plates are lent from the owners' own picture collections.

Notes treat hollyhocks at Blyborough, the yew alley at Rockingham, garden roses, and autumn flowers. Jekyll, a leading garden writer, reads each place for its planting, form, and mood. Elgood's plates show terraces, gates, pools, and pergolas in soft color. The book is both a tour of great grounds and a lesson in how to plant in the English style Jekyll helped define.
67965-aniwee-or-the-warrior-queen-a-tale:
Lady Florence Dixie wrote a tale of the Araucanian Indians and the mythical Trauco people, printed at London in 1890. Dixie had written Redeemed in Blood, Gloriana, and The Young Castaways. Aniwee leading the charge stands as frontispiece. The book is given, by leave of the Duchess of Albany, to the memory of Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany.

God gave thee life, a life of noble aims, the dedication verses run. Brief, yet inspired by loftiness of thought. To know thee was to love thee, they add. Dixie, who had travelled in Patagonia and written across the continent, sets her warrior queen among the Araucanians of Chile. Romance, war, and a lost mythical people fill a tale by one of the boldest women writers of her day.
68004-pandora-s-millions:
George Smith imagines a rich world gone broke in Pandora's Millions, from the June 1945 issue of Astounding Science Fiction. Orban draws the plates. A framed quote warns of luxury amid bankruptcy, a new twist on starving amid plenty.

Keg Johnson is chief of Interplanet Transport, a man of guts, good judgment, and bold gambles that pay. He knows science pays in the long run and loves a new find from the lab. In a Buffalo court hall he meets Don Channing. Johnson dangles an exact copy of the judge's watch. Such a watch was once a rare prize for collectors. It is rare no more, which hints at the flood to come.
68011-etching-in-england-with-50-illustr:
Frederick Wedmore wrote a survey of fine etching done in England. George Bell and Sons issued Etching in England in London in 1895. Fifty plates show works from Turner onward. Wedmore skips craft talk, pointing readers to Hamerton and Haden for method.

His aim, he writes, is the finer and truer work only, not all popular etching. Many fine etchers were poor sellers, and some prized hands were bad etchers, he notes. Much of the best English work came after Hamerton wrote, Wedmore adds. Art readers gain a shaped, candid history of a quiet, exacting craft.
68075-the-lenni-lenape-or-delaware-india:
The Lenni Lenape or Delaware Indians is an address by Edwin Robert Walker, Chancellor of New Jersey. He gave it before the New Jersey Historical Society at Newark on 31 October 1917. One hundred copies were reprinted from the October 1917 number of the Society's Proceedings, printed at Somerville, New Jersey.

Walker opens by borrowing the start of Scott's Ivanhoe, turning it to the old forest between the Atlantic and the Delaware river. There the bands known to themselves as the Lenni Lenape once lived. He notes that the name Delaware is not Indian at all, but comes from De La Warr, an old English family name. The address traces the people who gave the state much of its early story.
68145-use-of-tobacco-among-north-america:
Use of Tobacco among North American Indians is an anthropology leaflet by Ralph Linton, issued by the Field Museum of Natural History at Chicago in 1924. It is Leaflet 15 of the museum's anthropology series. Linton was the museum's assistant curator of North American ethnology. A plate shows Pawnee priests making a smoke offering.

Tobacco, Linton argues, was a gift from the New World to the Old. Smoking was established across the Americas long before Columbus. Pipes fill the pre-Columbian mounds of the eastern United States. The Basket Makers of the Southwest smoked at a very early date. Coca replaced tobacco in the Andean highlands. Tribes of the northwest coast mixed tobacco with shell lime and let pellets dissolve in the mouth. Europeans took both the custom and the pipes from the Indians.
68172-the-man-in-grey-being-episodes-of-:
Man in Grey is a set of episodes by Baroness Orczy of Chouan plots. Burt published it in New York with rights held in 1918. Orczy also wrote Lord Tony's Wife, Leatherface, and The Bronze Eagle. The episodes treat the Chouan conspiracies in Normandy under the first Empire. A proem opens on the hard task of piecing his story together.

Fragmentary documents alone throw a dim, flickering light on the man in grey. Age, looks, home life, even his name, stay matters of conjecture there. Contents run from Silver Leg and The Spaniard to Marie Vaillant's mystery. Emeralds, a Bourbon prince, and a league of knaves fill later episodes. Arrow poison and a last adventure close the shadowy record in print.
68473-war-cartoons:
John Knott, cartoonist for the Dallas News, collected these war cartoons under a 1918 copyright, with grateful acknowledgment to the Belo company, publishers of the News, for leave to reprint them. A sketch of the artist by himself stands at the front. The cartoons are printed one to a page with their titles and the dates they ran in the paper.

The series begins before American entry, with The Pioneer of January 26, 1917, and John Bull declaring there is no such animal as a harmless submarine, from July 1916. Lincoln's shade tells a storm-tossed president that he too had a stormy voyage. Through 1917 come The Mad King of Prussia, the German pitfall, meatless days, Oliver Twist Hoover rationing food, and a drafted man at Christmas. Early 1918 brings the original ground hog and an unsinkable ship.
68694-roger-the-ranger-a-story-of-border:
E F Pollard wrote Roger the Ranger, a tale of border life. Partridge of London published the story. Pollard had written The Green Mountain Boys before. Thirty-four chapters carry Roger's road. Esau opens the action. Parted and Bad News follow fast.

Roger tells Father Nat he will not farm in New England. Other reasons push him forth as well, he says. Marcus, near manhood, will serve his mother better, he claims. Lois clings to him in the parting scene. Chapters run through storm, diplomacy, and disaster. Nadjii and an attack fill the middle. The Plains of Abraham host a late chapter. A long journey and a conclusion close the tale. Border adventure fiction sent its hero from a New England farm to the wars that made Canada.
68804-three-generations:
Maud Howe Elliott wrote Three Generations, a memoir printed at Boston in 1923. Her father was Dr. Samuel Gridley Howe, and her mother was Julia Ward Howe. The book opens in 1916 with the death of Henry James, an old family friend.

Chapters move through schools, a stay at the White House, Newport, Rome, and Egypt. Elliott recalls painters, poets, and her uncle Sam Ward, and ends with Theodore Roosevelt and the Progressive Party. She calls the book an honest accounting of a life rich in love and friendship. Portraits of her parents and friends fill the plates.
68847-the-hollow-lens:
The Hollow Lens is a crime novel by Henry Leverage, billed as another adventure of Chester Fay. Leverage had written Beyond the Wall and Whispering Wires before this tale. The front matter calls the story a tale of underworld life at the author's best. Fay is a cracksman who works under a second name, Edward Letchmere.

The story opens at a golf club in Short Hills, California. Fay has fled there and sits at rest after a game. A young woman in a picture hat crosses from the clubhouse and takes the chair at his table. She names herself as the only daughter of Charlie Laurie. Laurie is serving fifty years for breaking a national bank and fleeing with its vault contents. The girl looks nothing like her scarred, rough voiced father. Yet she knows Fay's true name and his old ties to Laurie.
68876-unparliamentary-papers-and-other-d:
Unparliamentary Papers and Other Diversions is a book of comic pieces by Reginald Berkeley, printed in nineteen twenty four. Squire supplies an introduction, and Bohun Lynch draws the pictures for it. Berkeley had written plays called French Leave and Eight O'Clock before this volume. Many pieces first ran in journals such as the Outlook and provincial papers.

Four groups divide the contents of the book for the reader's ease. The papers proper mock parliament, the Derby, hats, and the personal column.
