Latter day dramas burlesque Wilson, King David, and an enchanted island play. Impolitics treats members, whips, and front benches with a light hand throughout. Irreverent interviews with Balfour, Briand, and Lloyd George close the set. A front plate shows alleged meddling with the Heavenly Twins in fun.
68981-through-a-pocket-lens:
Henry Scherren, a fellow of the Zoological Society, wrote this guide to small life seen through a hand lens. The Religious Tract Society printed it in 1897 with ninety plates. Scherren had written Ponds and Rock Pools and a famed history of animals.

The pocket lens, the cutting scope, and plain home tools open the book. Then come the beasts: water beetles great and small, cockroaches, earwigs, and the great green grasshopper. Water scorpions and boatmen share the third chapter. Spiders, mites, and thousand-legs follow, then prawns, shrimps, and crabs. Young water insects close the list. Enlarged photos of flies, bred by Scherren himself, head the plates.
69054-the-rambler-club-in-the-mountains:
Crispin Sheppard wrote this boys' adventure, published by the Penn Publishing Company at Philadelphia in 1910, as a companion to The Rambler Club Afloat and The Rambler Club's Winter Camp. Twenty-eight chapters carry the club from a lake camp up cliffs, down a gorge, and above the clouds. Illustrations show the boys around a camp fire and their boat, the Dauntless, in the gorge.

Chapter one lands Bob Somers and his friends at a small railroad station in Oregon, in a rich valley under snow-crowned mountains. Stout Dave Brandon, the club's artist in chief, promises great sketches, while Dick Travers claims the office of photographer and Sam Randall wants only hunting and fishing. Talk of grizzly and cinnamon bears sets the trip's tone, and the contents promise an island camp, a storm, a moose for Dick, and a brush with Old Ephraim, the grizzly.
69284-essay-on-burns:
Essay on Burns is a critical essay by Thomas Carlyle, here edited by George Noyes. Houghton, Mifflin and Company issued it in the Riverside Literature Series in 1896. Noyes supplied an introduction and notes for student readers. The essay had a famous first life in a great review.

Carlyle's piece first appeared in the Edinburgh Review for December 1828. In form it reviewed Lockhart's new Life of Robert Burns. In substance, the introduction says, it is an independent work of its own. The Edinburgh Review had begun in 1802 under Jeffrey and his circle. It changed reviewing from a hack's summary into serious literature. Men of learning and original thought wrote its long critical essays. Carlyle's Burns took its place among the reviews that outlived their occasion. The school edition presents it as a classic of English criticism.
69570-friends-and-cousins:
Friends and Cousins, by Abbie Farwell Brown with drawings by Ethel Brown, was published in Boston and New York in September 1907. Brown also wrote Brothers and Sisters, The Flower Princess, and In the Days of Giants. Twelve chapters follow a group of children through a summer of play, quests, and small perils.

The tales start with a wigwam and mock Indians, then move to an ants' fire escape and a beech house. Later chapters bring a pirate cave, a buried hoard, a box of candy, and a rescue at Gull Rock. Plates show Tom as an outlaw and children digging for treasure. The book keeps a warm, safe tone, with mischief that ends in friendship.
6983-missionary-work-among-the-ojebway-i:
Edward Wilson, a missionary, tells his work among the Ojebway Indians in Canada, from his first call to the opening of the Shingwauk Home. His contents trace how he came to Canada, first missionary trials, arrival at Sarnia, Kettle Point, and Indian names given. Christmas on the reserve, mission work at Sarnia, the bishop's visit, and the baptism of pagan Indians follow, with a Red River expedition and changes in prospect.

Later chapters rough it through a first winter in Algoma, meet Chief Little Pine and Chief Buhkwujjenene, and carry an Indian chief to England. A trial of faith, a wedding and a death, fire and rebuilding, and the laying of a foundation stone close the arc. Wilson writes to help readers know his people, not merely to count converts.
69987-mood-fashions:
Star Book Number 234 of the American Thread Company, printed at Stamford, Connecticut, teaches a wardrobe of knitted and crocheted fashions. Tables of knitting and crochet abbreviations open the book, down to the pass slip stitch over and the treble treble. The patterns are photographed as contents: a ribbed sweater and helmet, knitted gaucho pants, a moss stitch dress, plain pants, a poncho and hat, and a skirt.

A sleeveless maxi coat, a cable sweater, and a short vest complete the set. The first pattern gives its sizes as 10, 12, and 14, and its yarn as Dawn knitting worsted, seven to eight skeins in wood brown. Directions run in the compressed code of the craft, row by row, with gauges in stitches to the inch. Such booklets sold yarn by selling the clothes a woman could make from it.
70040-practical-recitations:
Practical Recitations is a book of selections for speaking, gathered by Caroline Lerow. Lerow taught elocution at the Central School in Brooklyn, and earlier at Vassar and Smith colleges. Clark and Maynard published it at New York. The pieces serve reception days, holidays, poets' birthdays, and like occasions, with concert and musical recitations and dialogues from popular authors, arranged for this work.

A companion practical reader by Lerow is described within. It teaches reading aloud with exercises in vocal culture. All students, it says, are expected to read ordinary prose and poetry well, and the book exists to help them and their teachers do it. Physical development and correct voice use must come before all good reading. Exercises for the body and chest, breathing drills, whispering, and articulation fill its method. Such books trained the school recitations that were once a staple of American public life.
70052-ancient-calendars-and-constellatio:
Emmeline Plunket wrote a study of old calendars and star groups, printed at London in 1903 with many plates. Part one opens with the Accadian calendar. It then takes up Aries, and Gu, the eleventh sign of the zodiac. A chapter on the Median calendar follows, with Taurus.

Later chapters treat star lore in the Rig Veda and old Indian sky study. A last chapter sets the Chinese calendar beside that of the Chaldeans. Plates at the back show carved stones, the bull Apis, parts of a tomb roof at Thebes, and Pegasus. The book binds the reckoning of time to the shapes men saw in the stars.
7010-graded-lessons-in-english-an-elemen:
This elementary English grammar, built as graded lessons, teaches sentence structure with diagrams drawn in plain text. A transcriber's note explains the marks: underscores for italics, plus signs for boldface, slashes for underlining, and tildes for wavy underlines. Heavy horizontal lines for main clauses appear as equals signs, verticals as minus signs, diagonals as backslashes, and dotted lines as periods or apostrophes.

Words on broken lines or bending around a diagonal are shown with matching breaks, so a pupil can follow the diagram in type. The lessons rise step by step, from simple sentences to fuller constructions, in the graded manner of the schoolroom. The book serves teachers and learners who want grammar made visible, rule by rule.
70254-bedouins:
James Huneker gathered essays on music and art in a book called Bedouins, printed in New York in 1920. A list at the front runs from Chopin in 1900 to Unicorns in 1917. Portraits show Mary Garden in operatic costume. The subtitle names his themes, Mary Garden, Debussy, Chopin or the circus, Botticelli, and Poe among them.

Caruso on wheels, calico cats, idols and ambergris, and a masque of music fill the table. The vision malefic gives the set a dark closing piece. Huneker writes as a gay wanderer among arts, a bedouin of culture. His wit, learning, and love of strong art make each short essay a performance of its own.
70264-women-as-army-surgeons:
Women as Army Surgeons is the history of the Women's Hospital Corps in the First World War, written by Flora Murray and published by Hodder and Stoughton of London. Murray, a doctor of medicine, commanded the corps. The book covers Paris, Wimereux, and the Endell Street hospital in London from September 1914 to October 1919.

Murray dedicates the work to Louisa Garrett Anderson, her fellow founder. Her letter to the corps says their work was too good to go unrecorded. A frontispiece shows the Endell Street staff in August 1916. The corps proved that women could run military hospitals at scale. The War Office had doubted it, and Endell Street answered with wards, surgery, and order. Murray writes with little praise, she warns, but with affection and pride between every line.
70346-the-alo-saka-cult-of-the-hopi-indi:
The Alósaka Cult of the Hopi Indians is an ethnological study by Walter Fewkes, reprinted from the American Anthropologist of July 1899 and published by Putnam's Sons. Its subject is a masked personage of Hopi ceremony and the men who personate him. In the Flute and New-fire ceremonies the personators of Alósaka act as escorts. They lead the columns of dancers and the processions of priests.

At Walpi the personation was by a member of the Asa clan. On the fifth day he drew a line of ground corn and made rain-cloud symbols along the path of the altar objects. He drew a line of meal across the trail into Walpi, closing it to visitors on the seventh day.
70357-the-jumano-indians:
Frederick Webb Hodge's paper on the Jumano Indians was reprinted from the Proceedings of the American Antiquarian Society, from its semi-annual meeting in April 1910. Hodge sets out a puzzle: a populous tribe that played a prominent part in the early exploration of the Southwest has suddenly and almost completely disappeared.

The Jumano were first visited by Cabeza de Vaca and his three companions of the Narvaez expedition in 1535, as they crossed Texas and Chihuahua. The name is not given there; they are called merely the Cow Nation. Hodge places them on the Rio Grande about the junction of the Rio Conchos, living on beans and squashes in houses of real structure.
7042-discipline-and-other-sermons:
Charles Kingsley preaches discipline and other sermons in this 1881 Macmillan collection of twenty four discourses. The contents run from Discipline, preached at the Volunteer Camp at Wimbledon on July 14, 1867, through the Temple of Wisdom, Prayer and Science, and God's Training. Good Friday, False Civilization, the Name of God, and the End of Religion follow, with the Humanity of God and God's World.

Later sermons treat the Armour of God, Paul and Felix, the Good Samaritan, and Consider the Lilies of the Field. Jewish rebellions, terror by night, the son of thunder, humility, and a Whitsun sermon lead to self help, endurance, toleration, and the kingdom of Christ. The first sermon opens on Numbers, with a lion couched and laid down.
70447-the-nantucket-indians:
Douglas-Lithgow wrote this history of the Nantucket Indians, printed on the island by the Inquirer and Mirror Press in 1911. He begins with the settlement and the natives, and says the tale of the island's transfer has been told so often that a summary will do. That summary keeps the thread of his own account clear.

Nantucket lay in a royal grant to the Plymouth Company in 1621, he writes. Lord Stirling and Gorges were charged with planting the territory, including islands south of Cape Cod. Stirling's agent sold Nantucket in 1641 to Thomas Mayhew, who had come to New England in 1631 and settled at Watertown.
70465-opinions:
Claude Washburn wrote this book of essays, Opinions, first published in 1926 and printed at New York. A list at the front names Washburn's other books, among them Pages from the Book of Paris and The Lonely Warrior. A note thanks two periodicals for leave to reprint four of the essays, and the book is dedicated to a friend named in full on the dedication page.

Contents give the range: on living abroad, zenith, disillusionment, sophistication, meditations about women, legend, truth and fiction in Italy, an essay on Pirandello, the French, pornography, success, and black-and-white. The first essay denies being a defence of living abroad. It explains, coolly, why many Americans who are neither loafers nor dreamers prefer it, and takes up the objection that the exile is cut off from the life he belongs to.
70555-the-feather-symbol-in-ancient-hopi:
J Walter Fewkes examines one design found on old Hopi pottery from Tusayan, the feather. The people of old Tusayan left no books or codices. Their picture writing survives on pottery dug from ruins and cemeteries across the Southwest, and much of it is symbolic rather than a plain record of things seen.

Fewkes traces the feather through its many changed forms, forms that can make it hard to recognize at first sight. He draws chiefly on the old yellow ware of Sikyatki, with cases from other Tusayan ruins. He also links the designs on pottery to the feather's large place in Hopi ritual, on altars and ceremonial gear.
70639-the-life-and-adventures-of-alexand:
The Life and Adventures of Alexander Selkirk, billed as the real Robinson Crusoe and a narrative founded on facts, was published in New York in 1841. Day and Company of Pearl Street shared the edition with Baker, Crane and Company. Pictures show Selkirk on his island with his cat, and a caption mourns the sound of parting oars.

Selkirk was born in 1676 in Largo, Scotland, the seventh son of a shoemaker and tanner. A wild youth, he went to sea at 19 and shipped as sailing master on the Cinque Ports, in company with Captain Dampier, bound for the South Sea. After a quarrel with his captain, he asked to be set ashore on the uninhabited island of Juan Fernandez. He repented as the boat pulled away. Readers get the true castaway behind Defoe's famous tale, in the plain dress of an 1841 chapbook life.
70853-old-and-rare-scottish-tartans:
Donald William Stewart gathered old and rare Scottish tartans in a limited book printed at Edinburgh in 1893. Only three hundred copies were made, most on Dutch hand made paper, and this copy is number one hundred sixty two. Two main objects guided the work, Stewart says. The first was to make accessible fine old tartans known only from family portraits, miniatures, and relics.

Family collections of tartan are drawn on as well. Identifying and verifying the setts took years of preliminary work, he notes. In no case where permission to reproduce a tartan was asked was it refused. Historical introduction and descriptive notices frame the plates. Clan members and cloth historians get a careful record of patterns that might otherwise have been lost.
71094-re-creations:
Re-Creations is a novel by Grace Livingston Hill, published by Lippincott of Philadelphia. Golden Rule held the copyright in 1921 and 1922; Lippincott took it in 1924. Hill had written Marcia Schuyler and The City of Fire. Cornelia Copley, the heroine, opens the tale on a train. She presses her face to the window as college mates wave her off. They shout reminders to write and to come back for commencement.

Cornelia watches the gray college buildings slip away behind her. The good times within those walls are over forever, she thinks. She will never be able to graduate now. Tears gather as the flag on Dwight Hall vanishes from sight. She settles back in her seat like a melting candle. Hill's Christian romances often begin with such a break from the past.
71266-the-boke-of-saint-albans:
The Boke of Saint Albans is a facsimile of a book printed at Saint Albans in 1486. Dame Juliana Berners is named as its author on the title. It contains treatises on hawking, hunting, and coat armour. The schoolmaster printer of Saint Albans printed the original. William Blades wrote the introduction to this facsimile. Elliot Stock published it in London at Paternoster Row. A verse from Thomas More's poems fronts the book. It praises delight in hunting, hawking, and good horses.

Blades says several printing presses worked in England before 1500. Their books throw light on the nation's social habits, he writes. Not one exceeds this work in interest, he holds. The book has always been a favourite with readers, he adds. Its feelings are appealed to in its lady author as well. The facsimile preserves an early printed book page for page.
71282-criminality-and-economic-condition:
Criminality and Economic Conditions is a study by William Adrian Bonger of Amsterdam, rendered into English by Henry Horton of Ithaca. It belongs to the Modern Criminal Science Series, issued under the American Institute of Criminal Law and Criminology. Heinemann published it at London. A judge of the Nevada high court supplied the preface matter at the front.

The first part weighs all earlier writing on the tie between crime and wealth or want. It starts with the forerunners, from Thomas More and Rousseau to Beccaria, Godwin, Owen, and Engels. Then come the counters of figures, the Italian school, and the French school of the milieu. Bonger's own findings rest on that wide survey.
71392-a-bunch-of-rope-yarns:
Stanton King gathered these sea sketches under the title A Bunch of Rope Yarns, copyrighted in 1902 and printed in Boston in 1903. King also wrote Dog Watches at Sea. The book opens with a tribute to Mary Bennett Holden, who spent two years in kind work among seamen at the Sailors' Haven.

The contents range across a sailor's whole world. Chapters treat how King was educated, mission work among seamen, the forecastle, and the superstitions of seamen. Others cover pets aboard ship, how sailors wash their clothes, the lead line, weather rhymes, rules of the road at sea, and signalling at sea. Readers get plain, first-hand talk about ship life and the men who lived it.
71437-the-chickamauga-dam-and-its-enviro:
Robert Sparks Walker wrote this guide to the Chickamauga Dam and its environs, printed in Chattanooga, Tennessee, in 1949. The Andrews Printing Company issued it at 50 cents, as a companion to his This Is Chattanooga at 75 cents. Walker writes as a host standing on the dam with the reader.

The book opens on top of the great pile of concrete, 129 feet above the ground floor and about seven miles from the center of Chattanooga. The lake spreads east, and Walker praises its shoreline of peninsulas, capes, inlets, and tiny bays. He does the math of a walk: at 20 miles a day, the whole shore would take 40 days. Fifty-nine miles up the river stands Watts Bar Dam. Local readers got their new lake, made by the dam, walked in print mile by mile.
71439-temptations:
Temptations is a book of short stories by David Pinski, turned from Yiddish into English by Dr Isaac Goldberg. Brentano held the American rights in 1919, and the first British printing came in 1921. Pinski mixes tales of old Bible folk with tales of work and want.

The list holds Beruriah, The Temptations of Rabbi Akiba, and Johanan the High Priest. Later tales name Zerubbabel, a black cat, and a hungry man. One long tale, Drabkin, treats the life of poor workers. Pinski gave Beruriah to the memory of his young son Gabri, who died as the tale was begun. Readers meet faith, grief, and hunger in tales that join old lore to new pain.
71566-cousin-becky-s-champions:
Cousin Becky's Champions is a children's story by Eleanora H. Stooke, issued in London in 1909 with two full-page pictures by Isabel Watkin. The contents list twenty-five chapters. They run from the home in Princess Street through a snowstorm, a visit to the Rookery, and Cousin Becky's arrival at Beaworthy.

Chapter titles hint at the plot's turns: a secret told, a lost item found by Mr. Marsh, a boy named Edgar under a cloud, and a strange figure called the Calais Noble who returns late in the tale. The story is told in the plain moral manner of its day, with family trouble, kindness, and young champions standing up for their cousin. The spelling is kept as printed, odd forms and all.
71670-royal-fruit-gelatin-suggestions:
Royal Fruit Gelatin Suggestions is a recipe booklet issued by the Royal Baking Powder Company in 1926. Its cover boasts that 189,000 women asked for it in seven weeks. The booklet promotes a new fruit-flavoured gelatin dessert sold under the Royal name.

Testimonials fill the first pages. Women from Oklahoma, Massachusetts, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New York praise the real fruit flavour. One writes that the orange gelatin smelled exactly like the fresh fruit. The recipes then show how to use the crystals, plain and with added fruit. Brand booklets like this one taught home cooks to build desserts around a packaged product. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
71679-a-friend-of-marie-antoinette-lady-:
Frederic Barbey wrote this life, A Friend of Marie-Antoinette, the story of Lady Atkyns. It was rendered from the French and printed in London in 1906. A preface by Victorien Sardou of the French Academy stands at the front. A miniature of Charlotte Atkyns forms the frontispiece. Eight chapters and an epilogue carry her story through the Revolution.

The Chevalier de Frotte opens the book, and London follows. A Breton magistrate's wanderings and the mystery of the Temple take two chapters each in weight, and the friends of Lady Atkyns and the little baron come after. Chapter one begins in noise: at dawn on April 7, 1790, the streets of Lille filled with soldiers firing on soldiers, regiment against regiment, with no order in the fight.
71710-three-little-kittens-who-lost-thei:
Laura Rountree Smith wrote Three Little Kittens Who Lost Their Mittens, with pictures by F R Morgan, issued by Whitman Publishing Company at Racine, Wisconsin, with copyright in nineteen nineteen. Five chapters fill the picture book. A front plate shows Whisk bound into the Sandman bag. Chapter one is Losing Their Mittens. Dot, Tot, and Trot are the kittens.

Once upon a time three little kittens went out to slide upon the ice. Old Mother Kit Cat called after them that they had forgotten their mittens. They came back pitter patter as fast as their furry little feet would carry them. She gave Dot a pair of red mittens and Tot a pair of blue. Old Mother Catastrophe, The Three Little Foxes, and Grandpa Growler and the Three Bears follow. The Surprise Party closes the book. Small children get the old rhyme grown into a full story.
71713-great-captains:
Great Captains is a course of six lectures by Theodore Ayrault Dodge, a retired brevet lieutenant-colonel of the United States Army, published by Houghton Mifflin. The lectures show the influence on the art of war of six commanders: Alexander, Hannibal, Caesar, Gustavus Adolphus, Frederick and Napoleon.

The front matter advertises Dodge's larger project, a multi-volume history of the art of war built around the same captains. Each volume pairs a history of war in its age with a detailed account of the great man's campaigns, hundreds of charts and battle plans included. The Alexander volume runs to the battle of Ipsus; the Hannibal to Pydna and the Second Punic War; the Gustavus volume ends with Marlborough. The lectures distill that life's work into a single course on how genius remakes warfare.
7172-early-plays-catiline-the-warrior-s-:
Henrik Ibsen's three early plays stand together here: Catiline, The Warrior's Barrow, and Olaf Liljekrans, translated from Norwegian by Anders Orbeck. The volume belongs to the Scandinavian Classics series, which sought to bring the chief literary monuments of the North to American readers and to build sympathy between peoples through books.

These are young works, written before the great prose dramas that made Ibsen famous, and they show a poet-dramatist still testing history, legend, and heroic speech. Orbeck's translation keeps their verse and stage shape plain enough for English readers to follow. Read together, the three plays trace the first steps of a major playwright.
71741-the-english-of-military-communicat:
Ganoe, a major of infantry and assistant professor of English at the United States Military Academy, wrote this textbook on the writing of orders. The George Banta Publishing Company issued it at Menasha, Wisconsin, in 1918, while the country was at war. His first principle is stark: all military language should be of the utmost brevity and clarity. Death and disaster, he says, are the direct results of ambiguity, and careless wording is like careless shooting.

The lessons work through the army's paper in order. Field messages come first, then the field order, with its estimate, decision, and expression. Later chapters cover the operation order, letters of instruction, the war diary, and the report. Official correspondence and lectures close the course. Ganoe's point throughout is that deciding and phrasing are separate acts: a clear decision does not phrase itself without effort.
71879-the-tarzan-twins:
The Tarzan Twins, by Edgar Rice Burroughs, was published in 1927. The Volland Company issued it at Joliet, Illinois. Grant drew the illustrations. This copy is a seventh edition. Burroughs gives the book to his children, Joan, Hulbert, and Jack. They were brought up on Tarzan stories, he writes. An introduction explains the twins who are not twins. Dick and Doc look as alike as two peas. Their noses, blue eyes, chins, and mouths all match. Yet Dick was born in England, and Doc in America. Their mothers were twin sisters, more alike than peas themselves. One married an Englishman; one stayed home in America.

Each boy takes after his mother, and so after the other. Half their schooling was planned for each country. Africa, unplanned, will teach them instead.
71908-from-trail-to-railway-through-the-:
From Trail to Railway through the Appalachians traces how travel west grew from footpaths to iron roads. Albert Perry Brigham, a geology teacher at Colgate University, wrote the book. It came out in 1907, with many pictures and maps.

Early chapters follow pioneers through the Mohawk and Hudson valleys. Brigham then treats the Erie Canal and the New York Central Railway. Later chapters cover the Pennsylvania Railroad, the National Road and the Baltimore and Ohio. He ends with the cities of the Ohio valley and the south. The book links land, roads and growth in one clear tale. Dozens of views, from canal boats to crack trains, light up the route.
71921-description-of-a-journey-and-visit:
Description of a Journey and Visit to the Pawnee Indians records a Moravian missionary reconnaissance of April and May 1851. The travellers were Brethren Gottlieb Oehler and David Smith. An added part describes the manners and customs of the Pawnee, written by Doctor Smith. The Pawnee lived on the Platte River, a tributary of the Missouri, seventy miles from its mouth.

The answers encouraged them, and they set out from Westfield on the morning of April 22. The narrative crosses the prairie to Fort Leavenworth, a pretty but broken country with bluffs rising above it. At the fort the quartermaster received them courteously and gave a letter to the quartermaster at Fort Kearney. The journey tested whether a mission among the Pawnee should be planted.
72031-attila-and-the-huns:
Edward Hutton's Attila and the Huns, published by Constable and Company in London in 1915, is dedicated to Italy, with the dates A D 401 to 1915 on the dedication page. Hutton, who had written Ravenna, frames the fifth century as an hour of renewed peril, Europe once more fighting the barbarians.

The chapters move from the empire and the barbarians to Attila and the eastern empire, the imperial embassy at his court, and the attack upon the west. His advance from the Rhine to Orleans, the battle of the Catalaunian Plains, and the attack on Italy follow, before his home-coming. The main sources printed at the back are Ammianus Marcellinus, Priscus, and Jornandes.
72115-dogs-as-home-companions:
A F Hochwalt wrote this guide for dog keepers, printed by the Sportsman's Digest of Cincinnati in 1922. Hochwalt had written Dogcraft and books on the pointer, the setter, and the airedale. He gives the book to all who love dogs and keep one or more at home. A scrap of Goldsmith on the dogs of a town heads the gift.

Chapters sort fit breeds into toys, terriers, and mid-sized dogs. Housing, first lessons, food and feeding times, and care follow in order. Hochwalt writes for the amateur who wants a sound, calm house dog. He also answers the cranks who call all dogs a menace and would have them destroyed, a stance he finds in papers worldwide.
72146-hidden-guns:
Henry Patterson wrote this northern story, Hidden Guns, set in the snowbound Trois Lacs country. Its opening claims a record: never within the memory of the oldest voyageur had there been such a snowfall there. All through the last of December and through January the grey clouds hung low and poured down fine crystals without pause.

Two trappers on Canon Creek fought the drifts for days to keep their trap lines clear, then gave up. Jim Henderson, gnarled and grizzled by years in the wilds, dug a tunnel to daylight from their buried cabin. His partner Nick Hartley, a young tenderfoot new to being snowed up, drew the water and wood. Idleness soon soured, and Nick began to complain about the cabin's site.
72326-chains:
Chains gathers the lesser novels and stories of Theodore Dreiser, printed at New York by Boni and Liveright in 1927. Fifteen tales make the volume. Typhoon, The Old Neighborhood and Phantom Gold follow. Marriage for One, Fulfilment, The Victor and The Shadow come near the end. The last two are The Mercy of God and The Prince Who Was a Thief.

The opening story, Sanctuary, begins with the conditions that formed its heroine to the age of fifteen. She grows up in crowded, scummy tenements, in narrow green-painted halls lit by dim gas jets. The floors are bare wood saturated with grease and filth. Outside, block upon block of red tenements swarm with people: longshoremen, wagon drivers, washers of dishes, waiters and janitors. The stories work his lifelong theme: lives chained by poverty, desire and chance.
72346-social-life-in-old-new-orleans:
Social Life in Old New Orleans, being recollections of my girlhood, is a memoir by Eliza Ripley, printed at New York in 1912. She dedicates the book to her children and their children to come. The first chapter treats the New Orleans children of 1840. Children should be seen and not heard, she writes, and in those days they were neither seen nor heard.

They led the simple life, going and coming in their own unobtrusive way, with no ready-made garments for grown-ups, much less for children. The chapters move through schools and teachers of the forties, boarding school, and picayune days. A fashionable function of 1842 and New Year's of old follow. Later pages visit the old French Opera House, wedding customs, and a fancy dress ball at the Mint in 1850.
72466-charles-dickens-and-other-victoria:
Charles Dickens and Other Victorians is a set of book talks by Arthur Quiller Couch. He held the chair of English book lore at Cambridge in his day. A Putnam house of New York and London brought it out in nineteen twenty five. Five talks on Dickens fill the front half of the book scheme. Three talks on Thackeray stand next in the scheme of the set.

A talk on the age as a back cloth stands mid book in the plan. Disraeli, Mrs Gaskell, and the Barsetshire tales of Trollope close the set. The first talk opens in Westminster Hall and its oak roof of old. No four walls hold such a train of grave past, he claims. Worm proof beams and Rufus work frame that cold grand hall.
72538-a-jar-of-jelly-beans:
A Jar of Jelly Beans is a science fiction story by Franklin Gregory, taken from Amazing Stories for February 1960. Justin, a Nobel-winning genius on the faculty of N Y U, talks with his wife Doris in the year 2060. Doris is pregnant, and the world holds ten billion people.

Justin blames the crowding on the generations that ignored the early warnings. Everyone agrees a new frontier is needed to relieve the pressure. Space seems the only place to find one, since the world cannot stretch. Justin thinks the experts miss the obvious. A jar, he says, holds only so many jelly beans, but only in one sense. The other sense is where his answer hides. Gregory builds the tale on that teasing idea. A little child, Justin believes, will finally save the world that the children of men crowded.
72741-oranges-and-lemons:
Mary C E Wemyss wrote Oranges and Lemons, published by Houghton Mifflin at Boston and New York in 1919. Her earlier books are listed at the front: Impossible People, Prudent Priscilla, and People of Popham among them. The tale opens on Elsie Carston. If a bishop asked her whether far-off islands were peopled solely so her brother could govern them, she would say no. But she believed it, the narrator says.

Marcus Maitland, her brother-in-law, cuts the other way. Asked whether God made the hills in India to save white women's complexions, he would say yes, but he did not believe it. Eustace Carston is away learning the art of governing. Elsie, in his absence, governs his children. Wemyss opens her comedy of empire families with a pair of portraits drawn in a page each.
72816-the-case-with-nine-solutions:
The Case with Nine Solutions is a detective novel by Connington. Its contents promise nineteen chapters of inquiry. Sir Clinton is the sleuth at its centre. The first chapter is called The Dying Man. A house next door and Ivy Lodge follow. Two crime scenes are named in the list. Heatherfield and a bungalow both hold deaths.

One chapter is titled The Nine Possible Solutions. A journal, a creditor, and a code advertisement enter next. The Silverdale wills bring the law into play. An informer's murder raises the stakes again. Sir Clinton's double appears near the close. His notebook ends the book in excerpts. Connington wrote fair-play puzzles for keen readers. The nine solutions are the book's bold device. Each must be tested and most must fail.
73136-wigwam-stories-told-by-north-ameri:
Wigwam Stories Told by North American Indians was compiled by Mary Catherine Judd in 1904. Ginn and Company published it at Boston with illustrations by Angel de Cora. Part one sketches various tribes of North American Indians for young readers. Books in the Indian language and things Indians knew before white men came lead that part.

How the Iroquois built their log forts and kept their records follows in the contents. Wampum money, Indian traits, and eye training get sections of their own in the survey. Medicine men, the Indian at home, and the meaning of totems and names fill out the first part. Dakota, Moki, Kickapoo, and Seminole peoples all appear in the tribal sketches. Part two then turns to traditions and myths told by the fireside.
73149-the-pelicans:
E M Delafield opens a novel of English country life in a book issued in New York in 1919. Joseph Hergesheimer praises Delafield's first three novels in a note at the front. The tale begins with Lady Argent telling her son Ludovic that two neighbor girls are to be congratulated on being left orphans.

Rosamund is fourteen and her sister ten or eleven, and their late mother, a musician who died near forty, left them little schooling. Talk across the valley recalls the widow's arrival and the huge grand piano forced in at her small front door. Readers get Delafield's dry, exact comedy of manners, in which kind phrases carry sharp judgments on mothers, neighbors, and the raising of girls.
73189-poems-and-translations:
Poems and Translations, by John Synge, was printed by Maunsel in Dublin in 1911. It reprints the Cuala Press edition of 1909 with additions. A short preface stands before some two dozen poems, and the book's second half gives Synge's versions of older poets.

The first poem, Queens, names queens for seven dog days in Glenmacnass: Etain, Helen, Maeve, and Fand, Deirdre, Lucrezia Crivelli, Judith, and Gloriana, before turning to the living queen before him. Other poems are set in Kerry and Glencullen, with titles like Danny, The Passing of the Shee, and The Curse. The translations take twelve sonnets from Petrarch's Laura in Death, then Villon, Walter von der Vogelweide, and Leopardi's Silvia.
73190-under-the-guns:
Under the Guns is a woman's record of the American Civil War by Annie Wittenmyer. It was published at Boston in 1895, with an introduction by the wife of General Grant. The book is dedicated to the army nurses of the war, and to the women of Iowa who backed the author's work.

The preface is plain about the aim. No history of marches and battles is attempted. The great captains have told that tale. Wittenmyer gives instead the heart histories crowded into her own life from April 1861 to November 1865. Camps and hospitals rose near her home at Keokuk, Iowa, in the first month of the war. She began her rounds at once. On her daily visits she closed the eyes of the first Iowa soldier who died in the war.
73407-camion-cartoons:
Camion Cartoons gathers the letters and drawings of Kirkland Day, who served with a Reserve Mallet camion unit in France during the First World War. His unit landed in France on July 4, 1917, and ran a fleet of some 700 five-ton trucks hauling supplies toward the front. Day wrote home about the daily work of the drivers, the roads, the camps, and the men he served beside, and he paired the letters with cartoons drawn from the same scenes.

The mix of plain letters and jokes gives the book its shape. The cartoons poke fun at army routine, bad weather, and broken trucks, while the letters keep a steady record of what the work felt like from the driver's seat. Read together, they show a supply unit's war, fought with engines and mud rather than rifles, and told by a man who was there for it.
73455-animated-cartoons:
Lutz wrote Animated Cartoons, how they are made, their origin and growth, printed in New York in 1920. A front plate shows the way of making cartoons by cut-outs. Above stand the back scene and the sundered pieces. Below stands the finished scene, one phase of the show by the little cardboard players. Contents open with the start of animated drawings.

The birth of motion-pictures follows. Making animated cartoons, and further points on the making, take the next heads. Movement in the human figure stands fifth, and the gait of beasts sixth. Dead things in movement, mixed matters in making screen pictures, and the camera work follow. Laughing effects and plots come next. The book closes on teaching films and the future. Plates show the thaumatrope, the phenakistoscope, the zootrope, and Reynaud's praxinoscope, the early toys of the art.
73498-my-life-on-the-plains:
My Life on the Plains, or Personal Experiences with Indians, is Custer's own record, printed by Sheldon in New York in 1874. The pieces first appeared in The Galaxy. Custer offers them as personal incidents and sketches, prefaced by a description of the country where the events took place.

Chapter one dissolves a schoolboy myth. The Great American Desert, once bounded by the Missouri, the Mississippi, Texas, and the Rockies, turns out not to exist. Emigrants crossing the great rivers found instead some of the richest land in the national domain, with a pure and bracing climate. The tract, its eastern edge pushed nearly three hundred miles west of the Missouri, is now simply called the Plains.
73641-lives-of-the-electricians:
Jeans wrote these lives of the electricians for Whittaker and Bell at London in 1887. Brewster's saying heads the title page: the electric telegraph is the most precious gift science has given to civilisation. The first series holds three men. Tyndall comes first: the Ordnance Survey, teaching, student life at Marburg, and the discovery of diamagnetism. Radiant heat, slaty cleavage, and the glacier theory fill his middle chapters.

Wheatstone follows, the musician turned electrician. His enchanted lyre was a first telephone; he invented the concertina, measured the velocity of electricity, and fought Cooke over the priority of the needle telegraph. The Dover to Calais cable and the automatic instruments close his life. Morse, the third, waits in the title for his chapters. Jeans wrote biography as the history of an industry: three lives to explain how the world got wired.
73693-vain-oblations:
Vain Oblations is a book of short fiction by Katharine Fullerton Gerould, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in nineteen fourteen. The title story fills the first pages, followed by The Mango-Seed, The Wine of Violence, On the Staircase, The Tortoise, The Divided Kingdom, and The Case of Paramore.

The title story is narrated by a man who shared the four most desperate weeks of Saxe's life aboard ocean steamships. Behind it stands Mary Bradford, a pure-bred New England missionary woman who met the crude physical realities of life alone in the heart of Africa. The narrator insists Saxe did not kill himself and that the last piece of evidence arrived after his death. Gerould's tales test fine consciences against brutal facts.
73761-an-essay-towards-a-theory-of-appar:
John Ferriar, a physician, published An Essay Towards a Theory of Apparitions in London in 1813. He argues that ghosts and spectral sights can be explained by a general law of the human system, as impressions formed in the mind rather than visits from the dead. A preface promises readers more pleasure, not less, from tales of horror once the machinery behind them is understood.

The chapters sort famous cases into kinds. Early chapters weigh a lawyer's argument for witchcraft, the New England witches, and visionaries such as Cardan, Donne, and Jonson. Later chapters turn medical, with distinctions among spectral impressions, old sepulchral remedies, and signs of latent lunacy. Ferriar also reads Hamlet as a case study in hidden madness of this kind.
73910-the-andersons:
Agnes Giberne wrote this tale of a pair of kin, named in its full head as The Andersons: Brother and Sister. A cut at its front bears a cry: they've not got there, they have not come! The list of parts traces the arc of the pair. In rooms let at Brighton stands at its head. Lettice's Dread, a new face, and two maids named Prue and Bertha come next. Then the dread head of their non-arrival, which the cut cries of.

A cot named Quarrington, a call to come, and a trip from Reading to Bristol fill the mid book. A new home, the age of nine and ten years, and a bank note that is gone lead to a find in a strange place. Old names come back, a find is made, and then a crash.
7415-a-shepherd-s-life-impressions-of-th:
W. H. Hudson spent years walking the South Wiltshire Downs, and this book gathers what he saw there. Salisbury Plain opens the volume, followed by Salisbury as Hudson saw it, the village of Winterbourne Bishop, and a shepherd of the downs. That shepherd is Caleb Bawcombe, whose life, memories, and talk fill the heart of the book.

Through Caleb, Hudson shows a vanishing England: sheep on chalk hills, long days in all weather, and a knowledge of land and sky learned by living outdoors. The chapters move with the seasons and with old stories told on winter evenings. It is nature writing of the best kind, built from patient watching and from friendship with one remarkable working man.
74227-the-scientific-pioneer-returns:
Nelson Bond wrote a Lancelot Biggs tale that ran in Amazing Stories in November 1940. Its head note owns the stakes. Time was no bar to Biggs when Horse-sense Hank alone could crack his fix. A drawing shows Biggs formed out of thin air, straight from the future.

The teller calls his own tale silly three times over. A physics man walks off a campus path at half past three and is gone. An observatory chief fades on a stage before twelve hundred students on Friday. The college head then runs, or shambles, to the teller for help. The teller first jokes of oiling his fishing reel. The head calls him a snippet and begs sense.
74271-the-queen-of-the-swamp-and-other-p:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood gathered her short tales in The Queen of the Swamp and Other Plain Americans, issued by Houghton, Mifflin in 1900. She notes that some tales first ran in the Atlantic Monthly, Harper's Bazar, and other journals. She revised them year after year.

Groups are set by state: Ohio, Kentucky, Indiana, and Illinois. The title tale is set in 1846 and opens after a quarterly meeting at George's Chapel in Ohio. Other tales treat a Kentucky princess, the Fairfield poet, and a man from the Spanish War. Catherwood says the tales keep phases of midwestern life that had passed away or survived only in quiet spots.
74323-legends-and-tales-of-the-harz-moun:
Toofie Lauder wrote Legends and Tales of the Harz Mountains, printed in London in 1881. Lauder had written Evergreen Leaves. The book is dedicated, by special permission, to Margherita, Queen of Italy. A long contents list names the legends one by one. The Legend of the Rosstrappe leads, then the Golden Crown in the Bode Kessel and the Seven Springs of Thale.

Legends of the Teufelsmauer, the Wunderstein, and the Regenstein follow, with the lost sketch-book of the Regenstein chapel. The White Stag, the Fisherman of Treseburg, and the twelve knights in the Schöneburg stand in the list. Barbarossa and the Kyffhäuser, the Devil's Mill, and the origin of the Rammelsberg mine near Goslar come in turn. Princess Ilse, the Wild Huntsman, the White Lady, and the bell-founder of Stolberg fill out a store of Harz folk tales.
74356-kittens: Kittens: A Family Chronicle is an animal story by the Danish writer Svend Fleuron, translated by David Pritchard and printed at New York by Alfred Knopf in 1922. The Danish original, Killingerne, was copyrighted in 1920. Fleuron's earlier book Grim, the story of a pike, had been praised as an animal classic in the class of Black Beauty. As its subtitle promises, the chronicle follows a family of cats.
74385-the-venetians:
The Venetians is a novel by the author of Lady Audley's Secret. Simpkin, Marshall published this stereotyped edition in London in 1893. The contents list chapters with quoted verse lines as titles. In the City by the Sea opens the novel at page one. After-thoughts and Fairies follow in the early chapters. The Prelude to some Brighter World stands fourth. Teatime in Arcadia gives a lighter chapter title. Why should he refrain, and He would take his time, come next.

A Face in the Crowd and love and death lines fill the middle. One Thread in Life Worth Spinning stands as a chapter motto. One born to love you, sweet, follows in the list. The Time of Lovers is Brief warns another chapter title. Peggy's Chance names the twentieth chapter plainly. Venice gives the romance its city by the sea. Love in a lagoon city is the tale's element.
74471-two-little-finns:
Two Little Finns is a children's tale by Mary Ropes. The Religious Tract Society published it in London. The story is set in Finland about the year 1816. Chapter titles promise a siege, a ghost, and a council of war. An isle of ghosts stands at the centre.

A woodcutter named Grubert Reuss opens the tale. He lives in a log hut at a forest's edge. His daughter Blonda is eleven and keeps house. His son Tonie is thirteen and rises early to work. Their mother died of fever years before. The family is poor but content. Their food is rye bread, porridge, and forest berries. Hard times have passed, and harder adventure waits.
74594-gena-of-the-appalachians:
Clarence Monroe Wallin sets his novel Gena of the Appalachians in the high hill country he knew well. The book came out in New York in 1910. Wallin gives it to his wife Alma and to the daughters of the hill country.

The tale opens on a cold winter day with the burial of Lucky Joe. Joe had dodged the law for more than forty years, and hill folk feared his name. Chapter heads then move through toil, duty, and school life at college. Gena comes back to the old home and hills, clouds pass, and love seeks its own at last.
74657-sea-yarns:
Sea Yarns is the log of a Cape Cod sea captain in his own words. Captain Joshua Taylor of Orleans tells of his life at sea. The tales start with a first trip on a schooner in 1850. They run through the great age of sail in the United States.

The book moves ship by ship through the posts of his life. A barque takes him to Cape Town and back in one tale. A yacht cruise roams New Zealand and the South Seas in an other. Clipper ships, a wreck in 1867, and a race to New York fill the pages. A tale of sea lions and a tale of a baboon sit among them. Taylor writes as a sailor of the old school, by his own phrase.
74701-where-the-west-begins:
Austin Hall wrote Where the West Begins, a western tale of a cow hand and a cattle king. Hall had told past tales of a love call and an old master. The blurb notes that rank counts for naught with the law man of the land. The tale opens in sage brush and glare.

Billy, a cow hand, waits on a knoll with his pinto horse, named Pinhead. A black car shunts down the dirt road in a trail of dust. Old man Holman, a rich herd lord, is on his way down from town. He is sore since Billy and his horse drink from his water and live on his range. Billy speaks to his horse as a mate and lays out the feud in plain words. A sad note on lost homes runs through the fun of the scene.
74748-straws-and-prayer-books-dizain-des:
James Branch Cabell wrote Straws and Prayer-Books, subtitled Dizain des Diversions, published at New York in 1924 in a third edition. An epigraph from Pope gives the title: beads and prayer-books are the toys of age. The volume belongs to his Biography series, alongside Jurgen, Domnei, and The Cream of the Jest.

Contents open with The Author of Jurgen, then A Note on Alcoves, The Way of Wizardry, and Minions of the Moon. The Thin Queen of Elfhame, Celestial Architecture, and Romantics About Them follow. Readers get Cabell in essay form, witty and self-aware, defending his romances and teasing his critics between the novels.
74759-in-the-tennessee-mountains:
In the Tennessee Mountains gathers stories of mountain life by Charles Egbert Craddock, the pen name under which the tales first appeared. Houghton Mifflin published the book at Boston and New York; the stories were copyrighted in 1884, and Mary N Murfree took the copyright again in 1912.

The first tale, Drifting Down Lost Creek, opens under Pine Mountain, a dark wall of pine that hides Cynthia Ware's valley from the west. Lost Creek itself sinks into the earth beneath the mountain and is never seen again, and Cynthia fancies her own life runs the same course. Other tales give a card game of old sledge at the settlement, an election on Big Injun Mountain, a dancing party at Harrison's Cove, and the haunt that walks Chilhowee. The dialect of the mountain people fills the talk.
74879-woman-under-the-ethnic-religions:
Woman under the Ethnic Religions is Mrs Moses Smith's paper on women and non-Christian faiths. The Woman's Board of Missions of the Interior published it in Chicago in 1898. Smith read it before the World's Congress of Missions. The congress met at the Art Institute in Chicago on October 4, 1893. Her test is Christ's own: by their fruits ye shall know them.

Religion, Smith argues, is the supreme force in history. The worshiper becomes like the being worshiped. Woman moulds society most universally, since she is mother of the boy who fathers the man. A religion's teaching about woman therefore reveals its fruits. Brahmanism receives the first long treatment. It rose among the cultured Aryans of India. Simple nature worship degenerated into caste, priestcraft, and idolatry. Gautama Buddha's reform, around 500 years before Christ, ends with his absorption as Vishnu's ninth incarnation.
75057-dreamikins:
Dreamikins is a children's story by Amy Le Feuvre, issued in London by a tract society office. Le Feuvre had written A Little Listener and Robin's Heritage before this book. She dedicates it to her little niece and godchild Vyvian on the title leaf. Fifteen chapters follow two small sisters in a big country house.

Freda, the elder, is earnest, freckled, and full of schemes to mix fun with use. She once locked the old butler in his pantry to give his legs a rest. Daffy, fair and fragile, dances on her toes and follows Freda's lead in all. The girls have just come to their father's house, let out for years before. A little door, a tea party, and a found playmate open the tale. Chapters ahead hold strangers, a fire, and a parting for the pair.
7510-keith-of-the-border-a-tale-of-the-p:
Randall Parrish, author of When Wilderness Was King, sets this tale on the plains. Its hero rides in at about thirty, slender and long of limb, with broad squared shoulders above a deep chest. He sits the saddle easily in plainsman fashion, yet with an erectness that suggests military training. That combination, soldier and plainsman, drives the story that follows.

The contents promise arrest, an old acquaintance, the one way, an escape, a sand desert, and a wilderness cabin with a girl in it. Mr. Hawley reveals himself, a fight breaks out in the dark, and the trail runs through the ford of the Arkansas toward Sheridan and a marshal. Christie Maclaire and Doctor Fairbain join a plot of conspiracy and pursuit. It is a rattling western of the old school.
75119-report-on-the-geology-of-the-henry:
Gilbert wrote a report on the geology of the Henry Mountains for the United States survey of the Rocky Mountain region, led by Powell. The report came out in Washington in 1877. Gilbert based it on field work done in 1875 and 1876, sent by Powell to study the range without fixed route or method.

Gilbert says the range promised the key to a type of mountain structure then only dimly known. Snow stopped his work two months after it began, yet broad views from the tops showed how the rock layers lie. He spent the rest of his time at the spots that best displayed the odd features of the structure. A front picture of Mount Ellsworth shows uplift alone against uplift worn by erosion. Readers get a landmark study of how these desert peaks were raised.
75421-shell-shock-and-its-lessons:
Elliot Smith and Pear wrote Shell Shock and Its Lessons at the University of Manchester in 1917. Smith led the medical school there, while Pear taught the study of mind by test. Longmans and the University Press put the book out in that war year. The pair say both doctors and lay folk had asked them for plain facts on the ill. They drew on war reports from the British, French, and Russian armies for their account.

Five parts treat the nature of shell shock, its care, and retraining of the mind. Later parts draw broad lessons for care of nerves in war and peace. The book thanks army doctors such as Rivers for help with the draft. It stands as an early bid to treat war strain as a real wound, not as shame.
75422-the-sirens:
The Sirens, an ode by Laurence Binyon, was published by Macmillan of London in 1925. It was first printed by hand at the Stanton Press in 1924, in a limited edition, and revised for this one. Binyon dedicates the poem to Cicely. A prelude in free verse frames the ode proper.

The prelude recalls a soundless night of the poet's youth. Heaven opened height into height, boundless with stars, and dew stood on his face. Through the silence came a hinted sound of waves, felt more than heard, that sought him out. He trembled as a mortal found by a mind in the muteness. The ode that follows takes up the sirens of Greek story, whose song draws men across the deep.
75462-songs-and-lyrics-of-robert-burns:
Songs and Lyrics of Robert Burns holds verse picked from the Scots poets work. William Macdonald chose the songs and wrote the front talk. Two artists of the Flint house drew prints for the fine book. Scant print facts and no year stand in the front of the hosted text.

Banks and braes of the bonnie Doon head the plate list in soft lines. Burns wrote in the Scots tongue, and that speech is kept as first set down. A list of first lines at the end lets fans find each song fast. Love songs, drink songs, and keen Scots wit fill the choice set. The book forms a rich gift print of a most loved song smith.
755-a-lady-s-life-in-the-rocky-mountains:
Isabella Bird travelled the Rocky Mountains in the 1870s and wrote these letters home about her journey. She rode on horseback through Colorado, climbed peaks, stayed in rough cabins, and met miners, settlers, and the famous mountain man Jim Nugent. Her letters describe the land with a sharp, fearless eye.

Bird writes as a Victorian lady who refused to be dainty, enduring cold, danger, and bad roads with good humour. Her account gives a vivid, first-hand view of the frontier West and of a woman travelling alone in it. The book remains a classic of travel writing, prized for its candour, courage, and love of wild country.
75522-the-soldier-s-orphans:
The Soldiers Orphans is a novel by Mrs Ann S Stephens, entered for copyright in 1866 and sold by T B Peterson and Brothers of Philadelphia. Stephens had also written Fashion and Famine, The Old Homestead, and The Heiress. Her tale runs long, through more than twenty chapters.

Early heads name a friend in need, a fair, an old maid, and the death of a soldier. Later heads bring a newsboy, a place found for Robert, and brave young hearts. The tale turns on a poor family driven from a snug home to garret rooms in a poor house. Love, spite, and a hard hearted foe raise the stakes as the orphans fight to rise. Readers of post war tales will find strong feeling and fast turns here.
75737-desultory-thoughts-and-reflections:
The Countess of Blessington set down short thoughts on life in brief heads. Her book came out in New York in 1839. A Latin saw heads it: to live is to think. Life is weighed by thoughts and loves, the front adds. Each head takes one theme in a few keen lines.

She holds that to know life well is a sad prize. It is bought by trials that make us miss our blind days. On being not liked, she says we claim to be not grasped. In truth, we may be grasped all too well, she warns. Gifts hid are worth more than gifts shown, she holds. Smart readers get wit in small, rich doses.
75816-traveling-publicity-campaigns:
Mary Swain Routzahn wrote a study of tours that teach as they roll. Her book came out in New York in 1920. It sits in a set run by the Russell Sage Foundation. Shelby Harrison ran that set of survey books. Trains, tram cars, and trucks bear shows from town to town in it.

Films, talks, and hands-on shows ride those cars to far folk. A back list shows how wide the plan had grown by then. Such tours began a score of years ere this book, she notes. Health, farm, and home themes fill the cars in her tales. Town and farm folk too far for halls gain a school on wheels. Reform men get a new tool's full tale.
75856-the-children-of-dickens:
Samuel McChord Crothers wrote a book on the children of Dickens dated 1925, with art by Jessie Willcox Smith. First pages play with how a child sees old London as a tale city like Bagdad of story. Dickens in his own youth comes next, then Pip at the home of Pumblechook.

David Copperfield, Oliver Twist, and Little Nell each take a full part in the roll of young lives. The Jellyby brood, Sissy Jupe, the Cratchits, and the Dombey young ones fill out the set. Scenes such as Tiny Tim at Christmas and Nell at a wax works show why these young ones still hold readers fast.
76003-minerals-in-rock-sections:
Minerals in Rock Sections is a textbook on naming minerals under the microscope, by Lea Luquer of Columbia University. Van Nostrand published the fourth revised edition at New York in 1913. The full title stresses practical methods, arranged for students in technical and scientific schools. Luquer had taught mineral study at Columbia.

The prefaces trace the book's growth across four editions. The 1913 text keeps the shape of 1908 with small fixes and fresh data. New figures give the bending of light in crystals more fully than before. Luquer points readers to a 1912 work by Wright for exact measures of crystal values. Earlier editions added a method for finding light bending by coloured fringes. Tables of light values were also added for quick reference. The book serves the working study of thin rock slices.
76057-london-parks-and-gardens:
London Parks and Gardens is a survey by the Hon Mrs Evelyn Cecil, who wrote as Alicia Amherst. E P Dutton published it in New York in 1907. Amherst had written A History of Gardening in England. Lady Victoria Manners drew the illustrations. A view of St Katharine's Lodge in Regent's Park fronts the book.

The contents walk London's open spaces in order. Hyde Park comes first, then St James's and Green Parks. Regent's Park and Greenwich Park follow. Municipal parks and south London parks get chapters of their own. Commons and open spaces, squares, and burial-grounds extend the survey. The Inns of Court gardens receive a chapter. Historical gardens and private gardens close the book, with an appendix on Charlton. Coloured plates show crocuses in St James's Park and autumn beds in Hyde Park. Lists of trees and shrubs round out the volume.
76076-affirmations:
Affirmations, by Havelock Ellis, is a book of essays printed in London in 1898. Walter Scott, Limited, issued the volume from Paternoster Square. The preface sets out two ways of looking at books and at the selves books express.

In its rarer aspect, Ellis says, literature is the medium of art, and raises no questions of right and wrong. Such work should be approached as we approach Paradise, for the sake of its joy. He wishes the world could forget all that has been written about its great books. The Bible, he laments, has been stamped into mire by centuries of comment. His own life's work, he says, has been casting off book knowledge to come to life itself. A second kind of writing, the literature of life, stands closer to plain speech.
76282-reuben-roy-s-temptations:
Eglanton Thorne wrote Reuben Roy's Temptations, published in London by the Religious Tract Society. Thorne also wrote The Fishermen's Hero. Twelve chapters follow Reuben from winning renown through partings and the ways of town. An enemy, thrilling experiences, and a discredited story follow.

The first chapter shows Reuben's home: a small whitewashed cottage of four rooms. It always seemed full of children and laundry. His mother was a laundress who worked hard beside his father to keep a numerous family. A garden plot in front lay untidy for want of hands. Readers get a tract society tale of a poor boy's trials in town.
76553-three-millions:
Three Millions, also called The Way of the World, is William Adams's novel of a Baltimore fortune, written under his pen name Oliver Optic. The book came out at Boston with Lee and Shepard. John Hungerford begins business with three thousand dollars. Twenty years of care add the first zero, and twenty more add the second.

After legacies and gifts to charity, three million dollars remain in round numbers. The long chapter list follows the Hungerford and Kingman families through travel, wounds healed and wounds reopened. A smooth doctor named Bilks faces the witness stand. Dick Birch works under a shadow. The tale weighs wealth against the moral and spiritual sums a man can pile up beside it.
76691-goethe-and-schiller-s-xenions:
Paul Carus selected and Englished Goethe and Schiller Xenions in distichs. Open Court printed the second edition at Chicago in 1915. A Goethe motto asks why a man keeps aloof from views. I write not to please you only, you must be learning.

Contents open with the history and poetical form of the Xenions. The history takes thirteen pages, the elegiac distich form follows it. Our purpose, our method, and the distich head the verses. Soul and world pieces run from harmony to human life themes. Zeus to Heracles, folly and insanity, and motives and action stand among the soul pieces.
76772-palaces-and-prisons:
Ann S Stephens wrote Palaces and Prisons, a tale of France in the last king’s days. T B Peterson and Brothers issued the book in Philadelphia in eighteen hundred seventy one. Stephens had filled a shelf of tales, from Fashion and Famine on. A verse to Liberty, in a fair woman’s form, fronts the book.

A countess and a doctor open the tale of court and cell. An Egyptian scarab and King Louis the Fifteenth crowd in fast. The dwarf and the dauphiness mark the court’s strange fringe. Home famine then grinds the poor of Paris in sharp scenes. The Bastille takes the tale’s heart in its deep, dark cells. Count de Mirabeau and Monsieur Jacques plot in those shades. A market woman and a Swiss cottage lighten the grim road. The king’s own work shop shows the monarch at his bench.
76773-of-the-importance-of-religious-opi:
Monsieur Necker wrote Of the Importance of Religious Opinions in French, and J Johnson printed the English version at London in 1788. The translator admits to liberties taken to keep the spirit of the original. Eighteen chapters argue that religious principles hold up public order and private happiness.

Early chapters draw a parallel between laws and opinions and answer the objection that many godless men behave well. Later chapters treat religion in relation to sovereigns, the Sabbath, and public worship. Three long chapters argue that there is a God. Reflections on intolerance and on the morality of the Christian religion close the case. Necker writes as a statesman turned moralist.
76834-the-arctic-legions:
Herries Smith's The Arctic Legions ran in Argosy All-Story Weekly for March 2, 1929. The headnote sets the trap: menaced by the death-dealing hoofs of migrating caribou, Conroy of the Mounted and Yeyik, the half-breed killer, face a struggle for mastery. Corporal Conroy wakes among the Barren Lands rocks as a caribou herd streams past his boulder. Across the stone sits Yeyik, Conroy's own Colt laid on the flat rock before him.

Conroy stretches and yawns, edging a moccasin toward the revolver, until Yeyik shouts his laugh: a babiche tie-string through the trigger guard, passing under his knee, has dragged the gun along undetected. The two trade taunts over the six shells neither dares spend. Smith writes the northern pulp manner: a duel of patience inside a river of deer, with the Mountie's life riding on inches.
76838-error-s-chains:
Frank S Dobbins wrote Error's Chains, how forged and broken. Willey Brothers and Company issued it at New York in 1886. A thirty-ninth edition shows its long reach. Dobbins had lived at Yokohama in Japan. S Wells Williams aided the work with learning. Isaac Hall of Beirut aided it as well.

Williams spent forty years in China, the page says. His Middle Kingdom is China's standard lexicon. He led the American Bible Society as president. The story of the world's worship opens the preface. Odd and curious things fill that story, Dobbins says. Enchanting and revolting parts share it too. Childhood pictures of idols hooked him early, he recalls. Doctor Alexander Duff's father showed such pictures on Sabbaths. A vast comparative survey of religions argues, from a missionary's view, how error chains the nations and truth breaks free.
76936-a-practical-guide-for-making-post-:
Thomas, professor of anatomy in the Hahnemann Medical College of Philadelphia, wrote A Practical Guide for Making Post-Mortem Examinations, sold by Boericke and Tafel in 1873. The book adds directions for embalming the dead and for preserving specimens of morbid anatomy. Its author also lectured on artistic anatomy and edited a journal of homeopathic medicine.

His preface says the work fills a want felt in his practice and teaching. It makes no claim to be a complete work on morbid anatomy. Parts one to three follow the three great divisions of the body: the head, the chest, and the abdomen. Part four treats bones, joints, tumors, the effects of poisons, medico-legal autopsies, and embalming. The guide tells the practitioner what to look for and how to read what the knife exposes.
77100-the-handsome-brandons:
Katharine Tynan writes an Irish family novel in The Handsome Brandons, published at Chicago by A C McClurg and Company in 1901 with twelve illustrations by Gertrude Demain Hammond. Thirty-two chapters move from Castle Brandon and Castle Angry through the Annagassan races, a banshee chapter, a secret room and a Cinderella episode to wedding-bells and the restoration of Brandon. The frontispiece shows Esther at Oona's feet, gazing into the fire.

The narrator counts a family of nine, now seven since Pierce and Freda left, living on nothing at Brandon. She foresees selling the place despite their vows, and hopes some nice English lord might buy it for its beauty.
77117-the-watsons:
Jane Austen wrote The Watsons, a novel left unfinished, here completed in line with her intentions by Edith and Francis Brown. Edith Brown was a great grand niece of Austen. Elkin Mathews and Marrot in London issued the book in MDCCCCXXVIII. Edith gave the book to her father John Hubback, with whom she had written a book on Austen sailor brothers.

Chapter one opens with the first winter assembly in a town in Surrey, set for Tuesday, October thirteenth. A long list of county families is run over as sure to come. Hopes run high that the Osbornes will be there. The Edwards, folk of fortune who keep a coach, invite the Watsons as a matter of course. The Watsons live three miles off, are poor, and have no close carriage. Austen fans get a sharp start on class, balls, and hopes.
77183-cats-and-kittens:
A recitation book fills this item: Cats and Kittens, number thirty-five in a series of readings and recitations, copyrighted at New York in 1906. A front picture shows a four-month-old cat in whose honour the book is published. The contents run to scores of pieces, every one of them about cats.

Poems, fables, stories, songs, and action pieces stand side by side, many signed. Herford, Jerome, Field, and Dumas all appear in the roll, with pieces on Dickens and his kitten, on Dick Whittington, and on the differences between cat and dog. Parodies of famous poems, a cat convention, a cat law-suit, a cats' tea party, schoolboy essays on cats, and a closing address fill out a book made for parlour and platform performance.
77217-social-life-among-the-assyrians-an:
A H Sayce describes daily life among the Assyrians and Babylonians in a small book issued in London in 1893. The volume was number eighteen in the By-Paths of Bible Knowledge series. Sayce taught philology at Oxford and had written on the monuments of the ancient East.

Chapters treat the people, their housing, schooling, marriage, and burial customs in turn. Markets, money-lenders, tenants, slaves, farm laborers, trades, and the religion of the people fill the later chapters. Sayce opens with Ezekiel on Babylonian palace walls, then sets Assyria's limestone hills against Babylonia's flat, canal-cut plain. New digs in the Tigris and Euphrates valleys, he shows, explain the prophet's words. Readers get Bible lands history grounded in fresh finds.
77404-twine-crochet-work-with-illustrati:
Twine Crochet Work, with illustrations, compiled and edited by Marie Louise Kerzman, was published by Henry Bristow at 296 Fulton Street, Brooklyn, in 1883. This is the second edition, enlarged, of number two of a crochet series. The first edition, issued hurriedly out of its regular order, answered a general demand for lambrequin designs.

The introduction explains the re-issue. The work has been carefully re-written to follow the full instructions of number one of the series, How to Crochet. The number of designs has been doubled, with attractive new patterns for lambrequins. Twine, the book says, can be employed widely in household decoration, and has brought the crochet needle into greater use than ever before. Articles that add to a home's attractiveness can be made of twine at little cost, in colors and different sizes.
77563-the-sultan-of-the-mountains:
The Sultan of the Mountains is the life story of Raisuli, written by Rosita Forbes. Henry Holt and Company published it in New York in 1924. Forbes had already written The Secret of the Sahara. A photograph of the author beside Raisuli at Tazrut serves as frontispiece.

Raisuli was a mountain chief of Morocco, half brigand and half prince in repute. The chapters move from his wild land to the man himself in turn. Pride of race and early prowess in war shape the opening portrait. Prison, torture, and escape follow, then the famous taking of two hostages. He rose to be governor of Tangier and built a palace at Azeila. War with Spain, a holy war, and sieges fill the later story.
77597-signs-omens-and-superstitions:
Astra Cielo, author of Fortunes and Dreams, wrote Signs, Omens and Superstitions, issued at New York by George Sully and Company in 1918. The book gathers folk beliefs of many kinds under plain heads. Early chapters sort popular beliefs, wedding customs, and rings, then lucky and unlucky days and seasons through the year, from New Year and Easter to Hallowe'en and Christmas.

Later chapters take signs of good or bad luck, omens tied to children, eggs, charms, and horseshoes. Beliefs tied to the body follow: sneezing, moles, warts, yawning, and the cutting of nails and hair. Cielo writes as a collector, not a scoffer, and the book serves as a handy shelf of the lore its readers half believed.
77675-atoms-and-electrons:
Sullivan wrote Atoms and Electrons as a volume in Doran's Modern Readers' Bookshelf, published in New York by George Doran Company in 1924. The series gathered short, fresh appraisals of things that interest modern men and women. Its aim, in the words the series borrows from James Harvey Robinson, is the humanizing of knowledge.

The series note explains the need it served. Much of history, literature, biography, and science lay hidden from common readers behind forbidding scholarship. These books were to be simple, short, and authoritative, and to stir the wish to know. Companion volumes treated Saint Francis, the Renaissance, Victorian poetry, and everyday biology. Sullivan's subject is the newest physics of his day: the atom broken open, and the electron found inside it. General readers of 1924 got the inside of matter explained by a science writer, not a professor guarding his terms.
77784-the-story-of-the-pennsylvania-germ:
William Beidelman, of the Northampton County bar, wrote The Story of the Pennsylvania Germans, printed at Easton, Pennsylvania, in 1898. Beidelman belonged to the Pennsylvania German Society. A map of the Palatinate during the great emigration opens the book.

The dedication honors Germans exiled from the valleys of the Rhine and Neckar by religious and political persecution. Beidelman tells their origin, history, and dialect in short compass, for descendants who may not know the tale. He corrects magazine writers who claimed the dialect, called Pennsylvania Dutch, was no true speech at all. Visits to the old Rhine country prompted the work.
78011-three-sevens:
Three Sevens is a detective story by Perley Poore Sheehan, copyright nineteen twenty seven. Its contents run to twenty eight chapters, with heads such as Solitary, Headquarters, and By Process of Law. Later heads name a quarry, a gathering storm, and a tigers' den. The scene shifts as far as San Pedro in one chapter.

Chapter one finds its hero, Craig, in a punishment cell. He has at least ten years of prison ahead of him, the text says. A month of that term must pass in the cooler, as the cell is called. He has thought those facts through for long hours and found them barren as stones. A cat, a brand new fact in his world, then draws his mind. The prison cells at San Pedro are described as iron boxes in a dark cellar.
78149-when-love-dawns:
Adelaide Stirling wrote this romance for Street and Smith's New Eagle Series, as its number 448. The line sent out a big new book each week from New York. Its pitch was plain: copyright tales by the best authors, at a low price.

The Eagle list calls itself a matchless set of modern romances. Each book is of full length, good looks, and clear merit, the puff swears. Georgie Sheldon, the line's star, stands at its head in the ads. When Love Dawns takes its place in that flood of cheap love tales. News dealers in all towns sold them, and the post brought them for four cents more to those whose dealer lacked a copy.
78240-many-inventions:
Rudyard Kipling published Many Inventions, a book of short stories, with Macmillan in London and New York in 1893. A line from Ecclesiastes gives the book its name and its motto: men have sought out many inventions. A poem, To the True Romance, stands before the tales.

Fourteen stories fill the table of contents. The Disturber of Traffic opens the book, and A Conference of the Powers and My Lord the Elephant follow. Readers meet The Finest Story in the World, His Private Honour, and A Matter of Fact. The Lost Legion and In the Rukh take the scene to India. Brugglesmith, Love-o'-Women, and The Record of Badalia Herodsfoot carry the middle, and Judson and the Empire and The Children of the Zodiac close the set. Kipling's range is the point: barracks, jungles, London rooms, and the sea, all in one volume.
78348-bonny-bairns:
Bonny Bairns holds verses by Amy Ella Blanchard. Ida Waugh drew the pictures. Worthington issued the book at New York under an 1888 copyright. Its title is Scots for pretty children. A dedication in verse speaks to all bonny bairns. Blue eyes or brown eyes, tangles or curls, all are welcomed. The pictures and stories aim to make children smile and be good. They promise help to sleep and comfort in sickness or fret. Contents list some two dozen short poems, each with its picture.

A Story opens the book: Peggy tells of star children who would not come in. Their mother the moon called, but they stayed to see day begin. What Baby is Like, Two Mammas, and Comfort follow. Hoops, kittens, the old clock, and bed time fill the small pages.
78687-the-coming-of-the-amazons:
Owen Johnson calls The Coming of the Amazons a satiristic speculation on the scientific future of civilization, published by Longmans, Green and Co in 1931. The narrator wakes from a long artificial sleep in a world run by women, revived slowly by doctors who raise his body from ten degrees above zero toward forty. The book is dedicated to Harrie T Lindeberg.

His mind wakes before his body can move. He lies numb, hearing women's voices order saline every half hour, while he tries to recall his friend Doctor Sachaloff. Feeling creeps back like a tingling heat across his skin as the women judge his heart and breathing strong.
78899-by-foul-means:
Patrick Leyton wrote By Foul Means, a mystery tale first held in 1929 and reprinted in New York in the Mystery Library. It opens at a smart London eating place in Piccadilly, where two friends spot Hermione Rodenberg at a near table. She is the rich widow of a South African gold king who died the year before, and her face shows deep grief.

Her friend Frank Daneham claims he alone, with Hermione, knows the true facts of a strange past case. Twenty four parts then move through Ardenmore, a scrap of paper, a light in a tower, smugglers, a clock secret, and two shots. An inspector, a colonel, and a French foe all play a part.
78954-a-little-help-for-hawkins:
A Little Help for Hawkins is a western story by Tuttle, the Hashknife writer, told in rich cow camp dialect. Slim Hawkins, the Cross J outfit's latest burden, fights his pard Chuck out of his trunk.
