The range is a broad, fairly low mass topped by volcanic cones with snow fields and glaciers, Shasta rising to 14,380 feet. The wetter western slopes carry thick conifer forests, where the Douglas fir often reaches 250 feet. In 1910 ten national forest reserves covered nearly 16,000,000 acres of the range. Deer, bears, mountain sheep, and panthers still abounded, and two great railways crossed the range through long tunnels.
britannica-1911-chilblains:
Chilblains, or kibe, in medical Latin Erythema pernio, are a mild form of frostbite affecting the fingers, toes and other parts. They cause a painful swelling with redness and itching in the affected part, the entry explains. Two points in their cause stand out in the account given here. The sores appear at the far ends of the circulation, and rapid change from heat to cold, or cold to heat, usually starts them.

Treatment is both general and local, and the entry gives doses and dressings in detail. Calcium salts help most cases, fifteen grains three times a day, and nitrites help where fingers go dead and white. Washing should be in soft tepid water, with extremes of heat and cold avoided. Ichthyol and formalin serve in the early stage, worn on linen at night, and a named paste is given for the stage where the skin has ulcerated.
britannica-1911-chouans:
Chouans was the name given to smugglers and salt dealers who rose in revolt in western France at the time of the Revolution. This 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article explains the name, a Bas-Breton word for screech-owls. It may come from the cry the men used at night meetings. More likely, it came from a nickname for their leader, Jean Cottereau. He had made contraband salt and had been jailed more than once.

The Revolution ended the inland salt tax and ruined Cottereau's trade. In August 1792 he led peasants to block volunteers from leaving St Ouen, near Laval. His band then lived in woods, in huts and dug-out rooms. From there the Chouans waged guerrilla war on the republic. The revolt spread from Lower Maine into Brittany and across the west. Cottereau's force grew into a small army called La Petite Vendée.
britannica-1911-circeius-mons:
Circeius Mons, now Monte Circeo, is a lone headland on the south west coast of Italy, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its shape. The headland lies about eighty miles south east of Rome. It is a ridge of limestone, some three and a half miles long. At its base the ridge runs about one mile wide, from east to west.

The sea surrounds the headland on all sides but the north. The land to the north sits only fifty three feet above the sea. The summit of the headland, by contrast, rises to 1,775 feet. The source of the name is not sure, the entry says. It has of course been linked with the legend of Circe. One scholar held that the Greek name for the isle of Circe renders a Semitic name, island of the hawk.
britannica-1911-cistercians:
Cistercians is a church order article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about monks also called the Grey or White Monks. The name comes from the colour of the habit, worn with a black scapular. In 1098 Saint Robert, a Benedictine abbot at Molesme, grew unhappy with the loose life there. He led twenty monks to a swampy place called Citeaux, near Dijon.

Count Odo of Burgundy built them a monastery there. They set out to live by the strict letter of Saint Benedict's rule. The next year Robert was ordered back to Molesme, and Alberic took his place. Stephen Harding, an Englishman, followed in 1109 and led till 1134. For some years the new order looked set to fail, with few new men coming. In 1112 Saint Bernard arrived with thirty others. That turning point opens the order's great age.
britannica-1911-claudius-gens:
Claudius was the name of a famed Roman gens, or clan, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The form Clodius was at first a mere variant in spelling, kept later for some members in the late republic. The clan held a patrician house and a plebeian house. The chief men of the first were the Pulchri, and of the second the Marcelli.

The first man named is Appius Claudius, called from Regillum in Sabine land, the founder of the clan. His first name was Attus Clausus, and about 504 years before Christ he settled in Rome with his followers. He was consul in 495 and drove the laws of debt with such harshness that the common folk left the city in protest. The article then works through the great men of the house in turn, with notes on their deeds and their falls.
britannica-1911-collaert-hans:
Hans Collaert was a Flemish engraver born at Antwerp about 1545, noted in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Adrian Collaert, a draughtsman and engraver of note. He worked some years in the studio of his father. Then he went to Rome to make his art more perfect.

His plates after Rubens are held in high esteem, and he left a great stock of work. The best of it named here is a Life of Saint Francis in sixteen prints. It also holds a Last Judgment and ten plates of jewels of fine design from 1581. Scenes of the Dead Christ, of Moses at the rock, and of the raising of Lazarus are named as well.
britannica-1911-commons:
Commons is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on lands held in common. Such lands are a relic of how England was farmed in medieval times. The country was split into vills, or townships. Each had a cluster of houses forming a village. Around the village lay the fields and other lands. The men of the township worked those lands as one common farm. A few small closes near the village stood apart.

Those closes served as gardens, orchards, or paddocks for young stock. The rest of the township lay free of lasting fences. Arable land lay in large tracts split into fields. There were usually three fields in that system. They took wheat or rye, spring crops, and fallow in turn. That three year round ran in constant rotation. Low lying lands were used as meadows for hay. Pastures for grazing stood apart in some townships.
britannica-1911-confolens:
Confolens is a town of south-west France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Charente. It stands 44 miles north-east of Angoulême by rail. Its people numbered 2,546 in 1906. The town sits on the banks of the Vienne where that river meets the Goire. Great age marks its streets and homes.

Steep, narrow streets run between old houses. Two bridges from the 1400s cross the streams. Ruins of a castle from the 1100s still stand. Two churches serve the town, one from the 1000s and one from the 1300s and 1400s. The town holds a subprefecture, a court of first instance and a communal college. Flour, leather, laces and paper form its chief goods. Trade in timber and cattle adds to its work. The entry stays within those facts and gives no siege or event from the town's past.
britannica-1911-continued-fractions:
Continued fractions are a form of expression in mathematics, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines them and sets out their kinds. A continued fraction is built as a chain of fractions within fractions, whose parts may follow any law at all. They may be positive or negative quantities.

The entry sorts them by shape. If the chain ends, it is a terminating continued fraction, and every such chain reduces to a plain rational number. If the chain runs on without end, it is infinite. When the component fractions begin to repeat, from the start or from some fixed term, the fraction is called recurring or periodic. The entry also contrasts English and continental ways of writing the form.
britannica-1911-convulsions:
Convulsions is a medical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The condition shows in abnormal, violent, and spasmodic tightenings and loosenings of the muscles. Together they take the form of a fit. Convulsions may be a sign that flows from varied diseases. In common use, though, the term is narrowed to one kind.

That kind is the convulsions of infants, the entry explains. They come with teething or with other causes that upset a child's nervous system. Treatment must be prompt, it warns, giving a hot bath or chloroform as the means of the day. Convulsions account for a large part of infant deaths, it adds. A second note covers a name given to Jansenist enthusiasts in France. Their fits, born of religious ecstasy, were taken by them as proofs of divine inspiration.
britannica-1911-cowpens:
Cowpens is a town of Spartanburg county, South Carolina, in the north of the state. Its people rose from 692 in 1900 to 1,101 in 1910. The Southern railway serves the town. Its name comes from colonial days on that ground. Cattle were rounded up and branded there in those times, and the name stuck.

Seven miles north of the town lies a famed field of war. The battle of Cowpens was fought there on 17 January 1781, in the War of American Independence. Americans under General Daniel Morgan met British troops under General Banastre Tarleton on that ground. The British were beaten in the fight. A monument rose on the field in 1859 to mark the win. The Civil War left that stone much defaced in time. The town itself dates from 1876 and gained incorporation in 1880.
britannica-1911-creek-or-muskogee-indian:
Creek or Muskogee Indians, a union of North American Indian peoples, are the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They once held most of what is now Alabama and Georgia. The ruling tribe was the Muskogee, whose tongue was widely spoken. Other peoples in the union included the Alabama, Hichiti, Koasati, Yuchi, Natchez, and Seminole.

The Creeks farmed and lived in villages of log houses, and they had a name as brave fighters. In the Creek War of 1813 and 1814 they were beaten in three hard battles. The peace that followed gave most of their land to the United States. In the Civil War they were split and lost much. By 1904 they numbered some 16,000, settled in Oklahoma, and their own rule had all but ended by 1906.
britannica-1911-cremorne-gardens:
Cremorne Gardens, once a famed place of fun by the Thames in Chelsea, London, are recalled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The ground was first held by the earl of Huntingdon, who built a great house here. It passed through more than one set of hands. One lord with the Cremorne name made it far more fair.

It was then sold and turned into a paid place of fun. It drew crowds from eighteen forty five to eighteen seventy seven. It never won the high flair of Vauxhall, its great rival. In the end it was such a pain to those who lived near that its grant to run was not renewed. The site was soon built over with homes. The name lives on in a road name. The entry is a brief, sad arc of a lost night garden of London.
britannica-1911-crow-indians:
Crow Indians, also called Absarokas, are a Native people of Siouan stock. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives their range and repute of that day. Their name comes from a kind of hawk, the entry says. About eighteen hundred then lived on a reservation in southern Montana.

Their old range spread east and south from the Yellowstone River. No land for hundreds of miles was safe from their raids. They were famed as raiders and horse stealers among neighbors. With whites they shunned open war yet robbed when chance served. The entry calls them tall and athletic, with very dark skin. Short as it is, the piece shows how white writers of 1911 framed the tribe.
britannica-1911-crowe-eyre-evans:
Eyre Evans Crowe is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Crowe was an English journalist and historian who lived from 1799 to 1868. He began work as a writer for the London newspaper press. He wrote for the Morning Chronicle and later gave much work to the Examiner and the Daily News. Of the Daily News he was chief editor for some time before his death. His chosen field was the history and politics of other lands.

The article lists his books on foreign statesmen and on Greece and Turkey. He also wrote on the reigns of two French kings. His chief work was a history of France in five volumes, printed between 1858 and 1868. It rested on original sources, which he studied during a long stay in Paris. He died in London in February 1868.
britannica-1911-cumberland-mountains:
The Cumberland Mountains, more rightly the Cumberland Plateau, form the westernmost of the three great divisions of the Appalachian uplift in the United States. Many small ranges make up the plateau, which runs from Pennsylvania to Alabama. It reaches its greatest height, about 4,000 feet, in Virginia. Its east face drops steeply into the great Appalachian Valley, while the west slope breaks roughly down. Coal in many places and fine marbles lead its mineral wealth.

Cumberland Mountain parts the waters of the Cumberland and Tennessee rivers. Cumberland Gap, where Kentucky, Virginia, and Tennessee meet, became a main path for settlers crossing into Kentucky and Tennessee. In the Civil War both sides fought to hold that gate into Tennessee. The entry praises the scenery of forest valleys and rugged gorges as among the finest of the range. It closes with the mountain people and the schools founded for them.
britannica-1911-dahl-hans: Hans Dahl was born in 1849 and is a Norwegian painter of landscape and genre scenes. The brief 1911 Britannica note places his birth at Hardanger. After a spell in the Swedish army he studied art at Karlsruhe and at Dusseldorf. His work shows much humour, though his colour is judged hard and rather crude. He settled in Berlin in 1889, and his pictures are very popular in Norway.
britannica-1911-delaware-indians:
Delaware Indians, the English name for the Leni Lenape, are the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They are a people of Algonquian stock. When whites first met them they were settled on the banks of the Delaware river. The French called them Loups, or wolves, from their chief clan sign.

The article traces two centuries of loss and movement. The Dutch began trading with them early in the seventeenth century. William Penn then bought large tracts of their land, and war followed, the Delawares holding they had been cheated. With the help of the Six Nations, the whites forced them west of the Alleghenies. They were placed on reserved land in Ohio in 1789, then moved to Missouri in 1818. In 1866 they accepted lands in what is now Oklahoma and gave up their tribal tie. They numbered some 1,700.
britannica-1911-enns:
Enns, a town of Upper Austria south east of Linz by rail, is given a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It held 4,371 people in 1900 and stands on the river Enns near its meeting with the Danube. The town has a castle from the fourteen hundreds, a Gothic church, and a town hall of 1565. Near by lies the monastery of Saint Florian.

That house is one of the oldest and largest religious houses of Austria. Founded in the six hundreds, it was held by Benedictines till the middle of the ten hundreds, then passed to the Augustinians in 1071. Its present buildings, among the most magnificent in Austria, went up between 1686 and 1745. Its library holds over seventy thousand volumes, with valuable manuscripts and a fine coin collection. Enns itself is one of the oldest towns in Austria, near the site of Roman Laureacum.
britannica-1911-fens:
The Fens are the subject of a region entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. They form a district in the east of England with a distinct history and traits. The region lies west and south of the Wash. It spreads across Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire, and Norfolk over a vast area of low flat land.

Though low and cut by countless water courses, the region is not a simple river mouth. The entry explains it as a bay of the North Sea that has silted up over time. The Wash is the last remaining portion of that old bay. That insight frames the account of drainage, farming, and settlement that follows in the full entry.
britannica-1911-fielding-william-stevens:
William Stevens Fielding (1848-) is a Canadian journalist and statesman born in Halifax, Nova Scotia, on 24 November 1848. From 1864 to 1884 he served on the staff of the Morning Chronicle, the chief Liberal paper of the province. He worked in all parts of newspaper life. In 1882 he entered the local assembly as Liberal member for Halifax. From 1884 to 1896 he was premier of the province.

Fielding had fought against Confederation in the 1860s. As late as 1886 he won a provincial vote on a pledge to seek repeal of the union act. In 1896 he became finance minister in the Dominion cabinet of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He took a seat in the House of Commons for Shelburne and Queen's county. In 1897 he brought in a new tariff that gave British goods a favoured rate, later raised. He also laid a surtax on German goods.
britannica-1911-flint-implements-and-wea:
Flint tools and weapons are worked stones left by early peoples. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells how their study changed views of human age. Finds in river gravel beds drove that change. For years few scholars thought people had lived in very deep time.

In 1841 a French scholar found a cut flint near Abbeville in old sand beds. More finds followed across England, France, and many other lands. The stones turned up in gravel, burial mounds, shell heaps, and lake homes. High gravel beds held tools from an age shared with the mammoth. By 1859 the proof won over the world of science. The entry shows how plain stones reset the story of early man.
britannica-1911-floris-frans:
Frans Floris (1520–1570), whose true name was Frans de Vriendt, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Flemish painter, one of a large family trained in art in Flanders. His father Cornelis was a stonecutter who died at Antwerp in 1538. The boy began as a learner of sculpture, then gave up carving for painting. At twenty he went to Liège and took lessons from Lambert Lombard.

That path, from a stonecutter's yard to the school of a master linked with the art of Italy, lifted Floris among the best known painters of his land and time. The life is worth reading for what it shows about how art was learned in the Low Countries. Skills passed from father to son within one family. A young craftsman could also cross from stone work to the brush when his gift showed itself.
britannica-1911-foster-stephen-collins:
Stephen Collins Foster (1826-1864), American song and ballad writer, was born near Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, on 4 July 1826. He was the youngest child of a merchant of Irish descent who sat in the state legislature. Stephen showed early talent for music, playing the flageolet, guitar and banjo, and he picked up French and German. At thirteen he wrote a first song, and at sixteen Open thy Lattice, Love. At seventeen he entered his brother's firm in Cincinnati, composing all the while.

In Cincinnati Foster wrote Old Uncle Ned and O Susannah, then took up song-writing as a profession. His chief successes were songs for the Christy minstrels: Old Kentucky Home and Old Folks at Home among them. Old Folks at Home is said to have brought him 15,000 dollars. He wrote words and music for most of his songs. Old Black Joe appeared in 1861.
britannica-1911-foundations:
Foundations, in building, are the works that spread a structure's weight equally over the ground. A building's loads gather at set points on piers and columns. The foundations must spread those loads out, bringing the pressure down to an average the soil can bear. Care is needed to stop the soil escaping sideways, or a bed sliding on sloping ground. The work must also guard against damage from the weather, frost and damp acting on the buried masonry.

The soils of ordinary practice, rock, gravel, chalk, clay and sand, differ widely in the weight they can carry. No English building act fixes the load allowed on each, though the New York building code does. The long technical article treats kinds of foundations, depths and footings in many soils. The hosted file opens with the end of the Fould article before reaching this subject.
britannica-1911-gallaudet-thomas-hopkins:
Gallaudet, Thomas Hopkins (1787–1851), an American educator of the deaf, was born in Philadelphia on the 10th of December 1787, of French Huguenot ancestry. He graduated at Yale in 1805 and studied theology at Andover, licensed to preach in 1814. Resolved instead to teach deaf mutes, he spent 1815 and 1816 in Europe studying the methods of Sicard at Paris and of Braidwood and Watson in Britain. With Laurent Clerc he opened a school for deaf mutes at Hartford in 1816, backed by a congressional land grant.

The Hartford school was the first of its kind in the United States and a model for those that followed, and Gallaudet led it until ill-health forced his retirement in 1830. He died at Hartford on the 5th of September 1851. His son Edward Miner built the Columbia Institution at Washington into the first college for deaf mutes, with power to grant degrees from 1864.
britannica-1911-gislebert-of-mons:
Gislebert of Mons (about 1150-1225) was a Flemish chronicler. The 1911 Britannica entry makes him a clerk who held church posts at Mons and Namur, and served Baldwin V, count of Hainaut, as chaplain, chancellor or notary. The count employed him on important business.

After 1200 Gislebert wrote the Chronicon Hanoniense, a history of Hainaut and the lands around it from about 1050 to 1195. The entry calls it specially valuable for the later 12th century and for the life and times of Baldwin V. It then lists the chronicle's editions, in the Monumenta Germaniae historica and in later Belgian and French printings. Studies of the chronicle's worth as a source for constitutional history are named at the close.
britannica-1911-gliddon-george-robins:
George Robins Gliddon, a British student of ancient Egypt who lived from 1809 to 1857, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Devonshire, the son of a merchant. His father was United States consul at Alexandria, and the boy was taken there at an early age. Gliddon later served as United States vice consul in Egypt.

In Egypt he took a keen interest in the old monuments and remains. He went on to lecture in the United States, where he stirred wide interest in Egyptology. His chief work was Ancient Egypt, printed in 1850. He also wrote on the cotton of Egypt and on the harm done to its monuments. With Nott and others he later wrote books on the races of mankind. He died at Panama in 1857.
britannica-1911-gorgon-gorgons:
Gorgon and Gorgons, in the 1911 Britannica, form a myth entry on the terrible faced figures of Greek tale. Homer speaks of one Gorgon, her head set in the middle of the shield of Zeus. In the Odyssey she is a monster of the underworld. Hesiod makes them three sisters: Stheno, Euryale, and Medusa, daughters of the sea god Phorcys.

They are drawn as winged young women with snakes for hair and tusks like boars. Medusa alone could die, and Perseus cut off her head, from whose blood sprang Pegasus. Her head, which turned all who saw it to stone, went to Athena's shield and was set on walls as a charm. Later art softened Medusa into a lovely maiden dead in calm sleep.
britannica-1911-grisons:
The Grisons, or Graubünden in German, is a Swiss canton. It is the most easterly canton and the largest in area. Its 2,753.2 square miles are also the most sparsely populated. The whole canton is mountainous. Glacier groups ring the Tödi, Piz Bernina and Piz Linard. It holds the three main sources of the Rhine. It also holds the upper Inn valley, the Engadine.

Forests and mountain pastures form the chief source of wealth. The lower meadows keep a fine breed of cows. Bergamasque shepherds rent the upper pastures each summer. Mineral springs at St Moritz and Schuls draw visitors. Davos, Arosa and the Engadine attract growing numbers of strangers. A long historical section follows the canton's leagues. It traces dealings with Austria and France. It ends with entry into the Swiss confederation.
britannica-1911-hals-frans:
Frans Hals (1580?–1666) was a Dutch painter born at Antwerp. At Haarlem he died in 1666. As a portrait painter he stands second only to Rembrandt in Holland. Extraordinary talent and quickness marked his work. Improvidence marked his handling of money. He served in Haarlem's military guilds. He chaired the Painters' Corporation there in 1644. Drink and low company were among his failings.

His pictures mirror every stratum of Dutch society. Officers' banquets and sharpshooter groups are his most famous works. Itinerant players and singers fill his low-life scenes. Gentlefolk's portraits are true and noble. Fishwives and tavern heroes speak even more expressively. Debt ruined him in 1652. A baker's suit forced the sale of his goods. The town later paid his rent and firing. An annuity of 200 florins came in 1664. His widow died obscurely in a hospital.
britannica-1911-helvetic-confessions:
The Helvetic Confessions are two documents of the Swiss Reformed churches. They express the common belief of those churches. The first is also called the Second Confession of Basel. Bullinger, Leo Jud, Megander, Myconius and Grynaeus drafted it in 1536. Bucer and Capito of Strassburg added their hands. Zürich objected to the Latin draft's Lutheran phrasing. Leo Jud's German version won acceptance instead. Both versions were adopted on 26 February 1536.

The Second Helvetic Confession was Bullinger's private work of 1562. He revised it in 1564. Elector Friedrich III had it translated and published. Swiss churches found the first confession too short and Lutheran. The second spread far beyond Switzerland. Scotland adopted it in 1566, Hungary in 1567. France followed in 1571 and Poland in 1578. Only the Heidelberg Catechism rivals its authority. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Helvetic Confessions entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-herzog-hans:
Hans Herzog (1819–1894) was a Swiss general, born at Aarau. He became an artillery lieutenant in 1840, then spent six years travelling, England among his stops, before joining his father's business in 1846. His first active service came in 1847, as an artillery captain in the short Swiss Sonderbund war. In 1860 he left trade for a purely military career, as colonel and inspector-general of the Swiss artillery.

In 1870 Herzog was commander-in-chief of the Swiss army, which held the frontier in the Jura during the Franco-German War. In February 1871 he concluded the Convention of Verrières with General Clinchant. Under it the remains of Bourbaki's army, which had fled into Switzerland, were disarmed and interned. In 1875 he became commander-in-chief of the Swiss artillery, which he did much to reorganize. He helped reshape the other branches of the army as well. He died in 1894 at Aarau, his native town.
britannica-1911-huns:
Huns is a name given to at least four peoples, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out with care. Their identity cannot be regarded as certain in any of the cases. First are the Huns who invaded the East Roman empire from about AD 372 to 453. They were most formidable under the leadership of Attila in that age.

Second are the Hungarians or Magyars, who crossed the Carpathians into Hungary in AD 898. Third are the White Huns, who troubled the Persian empire from about 420 to 557. Fourth are the Hunas, who invaded India during the same period of time. The text holds that the third and fourth of these tribes are in not much doubt the same people. It is quite likely that the Magyars descend from the horde that sent forth the Huns of the fourth century.
britannica-1911-huysmans:
Huysmans is the name of four Flemish painters who joined the Antwerp guild in the sixteen hundreds, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica treats them in one entry. Cornelis the elder, apprenticed in 1633 and a master by 1636, stayed obscure. Jacob learned from Frans Wouters and later crossed to England, near the end of the reign of Charles the Second.

In England Jacob rivalled Lely as a portrait painter to the fashionable world. He painted Queen Catherine of Braganza, and his portrait of Izaak Walton shows a wish to copy the styles of Rubens and Van Dyke. Jan Baptist, born in 1654, left little but a dated landscape and a long list of apprentices. His elder brother Cornelis the second was the one talent of the name that won wide praise. He painted chiefly woodside views, with backgrounds half Italian and half Flemish.
britannica-1911-hyperboreans:
Hyperboreans were a mythic people tied to the worship of the god Apollo. The 1911 Britannica article notes that Homer does not name them. Herodotus says they stood in Hesiod and in an old epic of the Theban cycle. In the tale, maidens from their land bore gifts to Apollo at Delos, with five men as guards. When the envoys did not come back, the gifts were wrapped in straw. Each land then passed them to the next, till they reached Delos at last.

Much of the piece weighs what the name itself may mean. One view makes the word a Greek form for those who carry gifts across. The folk sense, dwellers beyond the north wind, set their home in a far land of sun and bliss. There Apollo could take men who had lived a pure life. The place could not be reached by land or sea.
britannica-1911-impatiens:
Impatiens is a plant article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a group of herbs grown for their blooms. The plants are found most often in the hills of warm Asia and Africa. Some kinds also grow across the north temperate zone and in South Africa.

The article notes the spurred, uneven blooms in purple, yellow, pink, or white. The name comes from the ripe seed pod, which bursts and flings its seeds out. Four kinds get close treatment. Touch-me-not bears yellow blooms in wet hill ground in Wales and the north of England. The garden balsam comes from India. A scarlet kind from Zanzibar needs warmth and a glass house in winter.
britannica-1911-imperial-cities-or-towns:
Imperial Cities or Towns is the English name for the Reichsstadte of German history, treated in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Such a town owed duty to no lord save the emperor, or German king. The first of them stood on the land of the crown and grew up around royal palaces. A town under a prince, by contrast, was a Landstadt.

The entry follows how many towns won this free rank in the middle ages. Some got it by gift or purchase, some by force, and some when great houses died out. More lay in the south than the north, and the rank was lost far more fast than it was won. Mainz, for one, was taken back by its archbishop in 1462.
britannica-1911-jains:
Jains is a faith entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes the followers of Jain thought in India, a group apart from the main Hindu path. Most Jains live in towns and work as traders. The wealth of many gives the group weight well past its count.

The entry gives a census count of more than a million souls. Rich shrines and temple hills show that wealth in stone and craft. The faith grew from bold thought in the Ganges valley in old times. For long years a rival faith cast a deep shade over it. When that rival faded, the small Jain group still stood firm in India.
britannica-1911-juel-jens:
Jens Juel (1631–1700) was a Danish statesman, born on the 15th of July 1631. He began as a diplomat in the train of Count Christian Rantzau, whom he followed to Vienna and Regensburg in 1652. In August 1657 he was sent to the court of Poland, and on his return he was made a privy councillor.

His rise was secured when his uncle Hannibal Sehested made peace with King Frederick III. Acting for Sehested, Juel closed the peace of Copenhagen with Charles X of Sweden. After the Danish change of rule in 1660 he served as minister at Stockholm for eight years. The chancellor Griffenfeldt sent him in 1672 and again in 1674 as envoy to Sweden. The talks spoke of closer union between the two northern kingdoms. Their real aim was to gain time for a wide web of alliances and to weaken Sweden.
britannica-1911-kohlhase-hans:
Hans Kohlhase was a German merchant of Kölln in Brandenburg, a man of disputed character who lives on as the hero of Heinrich von Kleist's novel Michael Kohlhaas. In October 1532, on his way to the Leipzig fair, servants of a Saxon noble, Günter von Zaschwitz, seized his horses. The delay cost him trade at the fair, and on his return he refused the small sum asked for the horses' release and claimed heavy damages instead.

Denied redress by the elector of Brandenburg and by the courts, Kohlhase issued a formal challenge, a Fehdebrief, against Zaschwitz and the whole of Saxony. With a band of followers he robbed travellers, burned villages and plundered towns until a price was set on his head. In March 1540 he and his chief partner, Georg Nagelschmidt, were seized, and on the 22nd of that month both were broken on the wheel in Berlin.
britannica-1911-livingstone-mountains:
Livingstone Mountains, a band of highlands in German East Africa, are described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The range forms the east border of the rift valley of Lake Nyasa. It stands at the north end of that lake. In part it has the flat top of a plateau more than the sharp crest of a true range.

The article maps the range from a steep scarp in the north to the Ruhuhu valley in the south. The ridge next to the lake falls almost sheer to the water. One peak near the lake rises to near seven thousand nine hundred feet. Farther north the range widens and holds its top peak, near nine thousand six hundred feet. Flat-topped hills of sandstone cap the east half of the range.
britannica-1911-macneil-hermon-atkins:
Hermon Atkins MacNeil, an American sculptor born in 1866, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Chelsea, Massachusetts. He taught industrial art at Cornell University from 1886 to 1889. He then studied in Paris under Henri Chapu and Falguiere, two teachers.

Back in America, MacNeil helped Philip Martiny prepare sketch models for the Columbian exposition. In 1896 he won the Rinehart scholarship and spent four years in Rome. In 1906 he became a National Academician. His first key work was The Moqui Runner, followed by A Primitive Chant and The Sun Vow. All three are figures of the North American Indian, a theme he returned to often. His chief work is the sculpture for a large memorial arch at Columbus, Ohio, in honour of President McKinley. In 1909 he won a commission for a soldiers and sailors monument at Albany.
britannica-1911-mahommedan-institutions:
Mahommedan Institutions is a religion article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the ruling forms of Islam. Of all of them, the article says, the caliphate is the oldest and the most basic. It sends the reader to the Caliphate entry for the history. Here it treats the office's origin and nature.

Mohammed held full rule over his people as a prophet guided by God. He led the public prayers, acted as judge, and ruled. If he took counsel with others, the last word stayed his own. He was, in effect, the state. On his death a leader was set in his place with like power, though without the gift of prophecy. That leader was called the successor, or caliph, of the Prophet. He was chosen by the Muslims, as Arab tribes had always chosen their chiefs.
britannica-1911-makart-hans:
Hans Makart is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an Austrian painter born at Salzburg in eighteen forty. His father kept watch at the royal castle there. The boy entered the art school at Vienna when its taste ran cold and strict.

The entry says his love of rich colour marked him as a poor hand at line work. The school cast him out as a youth with no gift. In Munich a new teacher saw his worth and trained him fast. Big lush scenes then made his fame in a few short years. An emperor bought one famed love scene and called him back to Vienna in honour.
britannica-1911-mandaeans:
Mandaeans, also known as Sabians, Nasoraeans, or St John's Christians, are an eastern sect of great antiquity treated in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The article calls them almost the only surviving example of a certain kind of religion. Their faith mixes Christian, heathen, and Jewish elements. Its type is essentially that of ancient Gnosticism.

The Mandaeans live in the marshy lands of South Babylonia, above all near Basra, and in Khuzistan. They speak the languages of the places where they live, Arabic or Persian. The language of their sacred books is an Aramaic dialect. It stands closest to that of the Babylonian Talmud and uses a script recalling old Palmyrene. The sect has been known to the West since the mid-seventeenth century. Missionaries then began work among them at Basra. Later travellers and scholars added fuller accounts of their customs.
britannica-1911-massicus-mons:
Massicus, Mons, a mountain ridge of ancient Italy, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the land of the Aurunci, on the border of Campania and Latium. It runs south west from the volcanic system of Rocca Monfina to the sea. It parts the lower course of the Liris river from the plain of Campania.

The ridge is of limestone, capped with later volcanic masses, and was once an island. Its highest point is 2,661 feet above the sea. It was very famous in ancient times for its wine. A narrow coast road passed at its foot, guarded by the town of Vescia. That town ceased to exist in 314 before Christ, after the defeat of the Ausones. Its successor, Sinuessa, rose on the coast as a station on the Via Appia. Virgil joined Horace there on the famed journey to Brundusium.
britannica-1911-matins:
Matins is a church article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin term tied to the morning. In church use it names one of the set hours of prayer in the Roman Breviary. It was first meant to be said at midnight, the morning watches.

In practice the hour often shifted. Matins might be said at dawn, with lauds recited or sung after it. Outside monasteries, the office is usually said the afternoon or evening before. The word also names the public service held on Sunday mornings before mass. In the Church of England, matins has a further sense. Since the Reformation it means the order of public morning prayer. The short entry untangles one word across two churches and many centuries of prayer.
britannica-1911-maxim-sir-hiram-stevens:
Hiram Stevens Maxim, an Anglo American engineer and inventor born in 1840, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Sangerville in Maine, he trained with a coachbuilder as a youth. In 1864 he entered the machine works of his uncle in Massachusetts. Four years later he became a draughtsman at iron works and shipbuilding yards in New York.

About that time he made several inventions tied to lighting by gas, the entry says. From 1877 he was one of many inventors seeking a lasting electric lamp that glowed. He brought in a widely used process for treating carbon threads in vapour. In 1880 he came to Europe and soon turned to a machine gun. His aim was a gun loaded and fired by the force of its own recoil.
britannica-1911-memlinc-hans:
Hans Memlinc, a Flemish painter who lived from about 1430 to 1494, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His art gave lustre to Bruges in the years of its decline in trade and power. The records of Bruges are silent as to his birth and schooling. His name was spelt in many ways by old writers, which clouds who he was.

A document found in 1889 says he came from the church principality of Mayence and died at Bruges in August 1494. He likely served his apprenticeship at Mayence or Cologne, then worked under Rogier van der Weyden. He came to Bruges only about 1467, already a skilled artist. Tales that he arrived wounded from battle and was nursed by monks there are fiction, the entry says. He did paint for the Hospitallers of the city, all the same.
britannica-1911-merovingians:
Merovingians is a 1911 Britannica article on the first dynasty to reign over the Franks. The name comes from Merovech. He was one of the first kings of the Salian Franks. He succeeded Clodio in the middle of the fifth century. He soon became the centre of many legends.

The chronicler called Fredegarius tells one such tale. A queen sat once by the seashore. A monster came out of the sea. By that monster, the tale says, she became the mother of Merovech. The text calls this myth an attempt to explain the hero's name. That name means the sea-born. At the great battle of Mauriac, in the year 451, Frankish troops stood in the Roman army. There Aetius checked the invasion of the Huns. The article thus opens the history of a royal house with fable and fact side by side.
britannica-1911-mons:
Mons, called Bergen in Flemish, is a town of Belgium in the province of Hainaut described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of that province and stands on a small river called the Trouille. The count in 1904 was 27072 people. Mons was the capital of the old countdom of Hainaut in past ages.

English history knows that link through the marriage of Edward the Third to its countess Philippa. Countess Waudru founded the town in the eighth century, the entry says. Charlemagne then owned it as the capital of Hainaut, and it has kept that place ever since. Not till the eleventh century did the counts make it their fixed home. Before that they held the castle of Hornu and left Mons to its abbey and church.
britannica-1911-mont-dore-les-bains:
Mont-Dore-les-Bains, a watering place in central France, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands in the department of Puy-de-Dôme at a height of 3,440 feet. The town sits on the right bank of the Dordogne, not far from its source. It lies 31 miles by road from Clermont-Ferrand. Its people numbered 1,677 in 1906.

Twelve thermal springs, known to the Romans, supply the town's cure. The waters hold soda, iron, and arsenic, and are used for drinking and bathing. Hot baths mark the treatment, said to help chest and nerve complaints. The season runs only from mid-June to mid-September, since the valley climate is severe. The bath-house was rebuilt in the early 1890s. Relics of the Roman baths are kept in the park along the river. South of the town rises the Puy de Sancy, the highest peak of central France.
britannica-1911-mordvinians:
Mordvinians, also called Mordva or Mordvins, are a people of Russia. The 1911 Britannica entry counts them at about one million souls. They belong to the Ural-Altaic stock of peoples in the east. Their home lies in the middle Volga lands of the empire. Small groups of them spread south and east from that core.

Their roots in the Volga basin run back to high antiquity. One great branch, the Erzya, may match a tribe Ptolemy named long ago. Russians raided their lands as early as the 1100s in war. After Kazan fell, Russian settlers poured in and took much ground. Today their villages sit mixed among Russian ones, a small share of all.
britannica-1911-myrobalans: Myrobalans are the sour fruits of several kinds of Terminalia tree, covered in a brief plant entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The trees are large, lose their leaves each year, and belong to the Combretaceae family. The chebulic or black kind comes from Terminalia Chebula and has smooth fruit. The beleric kind has five sides with grey down. In India the fruits were used a great deal for dyeing cloth and for tanning hides, and they were shipped abroad for the same uses.
britannica-1911-nestorians:
Nestorians were followers of a teaching tied to the name Nestorius. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces their church in Syria and Persia. One leader was Ibas, head of the school of Edessa. He became bishop there in 435 and spread the teaching.

A synod cast Ibas out, but Chalcedon pardoned him in 451. His pupil Barsumas planted a school at Nisibis in Persia. When Rome shut the Edessa school in 489, its men scattered. They crossed Asia as eager missionaries of their faith. Persia welcomed them as a shield against Byzantine power. Their church let even bishops wed, by a rule of 499. A patriarch of the East ruled them from the Tigris. Monkish life held on beside that loose rule for centuries.
britannica-1911-north-barons:
North, Barons is a family article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It traces the English title of Lord North of Kirtling. The title was created in 1554 for Edward North, a successful lawyer. He had served as clerk of the parliament and as chancellor of the court of augmentations.

The entry follows the title from father to son. Roger North, the second baron, was a noted courtier and soldier under Queen Elizabeth. His eldest son died before him, so the line passed to a grandson. Dudley North, the third baron, was born in 1581 and succeeded at nineteen. He was educated at Cambridge, married in 1599, and travelled in Italy. He also campaigned in the Netherlands in 1602. The article gives readers the skeleton of a noble family's rise over three generations.
britannica-1911-old-age-pensions:
Old-age pensions are traced through a century of British debate in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The article opens with early plans from the 1700s for state payments to the aged poor. Writers such as Francis Maseres and Thomas Paine put schemes forward. The idea then faded, and came back strong late in the next century.

Canon Blackley's plan asked each young worker to pay ten pounds to the state. In return the state would pay a weekly sum in sickness and a pension after seventy. A select committee in the 1880s reported against the sickness part of the plan. The pension idea itself lived on, backed by a league and by a committee led by Chamberlain. By 1892 the promoters had dropped force and turned toward aid for those who saved on their own.
britannica-1911-oraons:
The Oraons are a native people of Bengal in India. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says they call themselves Kurukh. Their home is the Ranchi district, with groups in nearby states. Others have scattered to tea gardens in Jalpaiguri and Darjeeling. Their numbers pass three quarters of a million. Tale says the tribe migrated from the west coast of India. Near 600,000 people spoke their tongue in 1901.

The entry gives their build in the era's blunt style. They average five feet two in height, with dark brown skin. Their tongue is harsh and kin to Tamil. They revere the sun and own a high god, Dharmi. Evil spirits, they hold, thwart his good designs. They burn their dead and keep the ashes in an urn. The urn hangs outside the dead person's hut. It waits for the set burial season of the year.
britannica-1911-papuans:
Papuans are the subject of a survey entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name comes from a Malay word for frizzled or woolly hair. It was given to the people of New Guinea and the isles of Melanesia. The entry says the pure type was found in the north west of New Guinea.

The text looks at where Papuan peoples lived, from Flores in the west to Fiji in the east. It weighs their roots and notes that scholars had not settled the question. Traits such as hair, raised scars, and beliefs are used as clues. The entry shows early views of race and kinship in that part of the world.
britannica-1911-paulicians:
Paulicians were an evangelical Christian church spread over Asia Minor and Armenia. Their sect entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The church spread from the fifth century onward in those east lands. The patriarch Nerses the Second first notes them in a letter of five fifty three.

Leaders of the sect bore names drawn from the New Testament books. Constantine was martyred in six eighty four under a bid to crush the sect. His killer Simeon was so moved that he joined and led the church. He too was martyred, in six ninety, under Justinian the Second. In seven fifty two many Paulicians were moved to Thrace as a shield.
britannica-1911-pelasgians:
Pelasgians is the subject of a peoples entry in the 1911 Britannica. The name was used by Greek writers of old. It named a folk held to have lived in Greek lands first. The entry sorts old claims by the date of each writer. That care shows some claims start late in time. Late birth does not prove a claim is false, it warns. In the poems of Homer such folk aid Troy.

Their town is called Larissa in those poems. A camp site by Troy is named in one book. The Odyssey places such folk in Crete as well. They stand there with native and settler folk side by side. No sign tells which class they fall in there. Two more lines call a district and a god by their name. The entry weighs each scrap of proof in turn.
britannica-1911-philadelphians:
Philadelphians were a sect of Christian mystics founded in London in the late seventeenth century. The 1911 Britannica article traces the group to John Pordage, rector of Bradfield. In 1652 he drew a small circle of readers of Jakob Boehme around him. Chief among them was Jane Lead, a woman of strong mystic gifts. She kept a diary of her visions from 1670, the year the society took firm shape.

Lead wrote the Laws of Paradise for the group. The rules aimed to spread the kingdom of God by a pure life and by love for all men. Members held fast to hidden divine secrets and looked for the second coming of Christ. Her books, turned into Dutch in 1693, won links in Holland and Germany. The sect still faded fast after its confession of 1703.
britannica-1911-pirmasens:
Pirmasens is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in the Bavarian Palatinate, in Germany. It stands forty miles west of Spires, on a branch rail line. The count of 1905 gave it 34,002 people. The only buildings of note are the town hall and the main Protestant church.

That church holds a fine monument to Louis the Ninth, landgrave of Hesse-Darmstadt, who made the town his home. The town's staple trade is the making of boots and shoes. Musical instruments, leather, and machines are also made there. The town takes its name from Saint Pirmin, said to have preached the faith there in the eighth century. It passed to Hesse-Darmstadt in 1736. In September 1793 the Prussians beat a body of French troops near the town.
britannica-1911-praetorians:
Praetorians, the emperor's bodyguard under the Roman empire, are explained in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The name reaches back to the early republic, when a praetor was a commander of the army. A general's quarters in camp were thus called the praetorium. His bodyguard was the praetorian cohort, or cohorts when there were several.

Under the empire the name settled on the imperial bodyguard. Founded by Augustus, it held nine cohorts of a thousand men each. Some part of it was always with the emperor, in Rome or elsewhere. In the year 23 Tiberius gathered the force into fortified barracks on Rome's eastern edge. One cohort in turn, dressed as civilians, served at the emperor's house on the Palatine. The men were volunteers from Italy or Italianized districts. They had better pay and shorter service than the regular army, under two or more praetorian prefects.
britannica-1911-prestonpans:
Prestonpans is the subject of a burgh entry in the 1911 Britannica. The burgh lies in Haddingtonshire in Scotland. It stands on the Firth of Forth east of Edinburgh. Its count in 1901 was just over two thousand souls. It serves as a small resort by the sea shore. A mile east lies the site of a famed battle. That battle was fought in September of 1745.

Prince Charles Edward won a full win there that day. His Highlanders routed the royal troops of Sir John Cope. A colonel died a hero death at that fight. A ballad song made the rout of Cope well known. Salt works by the shore once thrived in the town. Those pans were laid down as early as 1185. Brick, tile, and brew trades now serve the place. Coal fields near by and fisheries add to its work.
britannica-1911-ribbons:
Ribbons are narrow webs, most often of silk, no more than nine inches wide. Their trade entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. They serve to bind and tie dress, and for many plain and fine uses. With tapes and fringes they form a branch of the textile trades.

The key tool is a loom that weaves many narrow webs at once. Modern frames can hold as many as forty webs in one run. Such looms were at work in Danzig in the late sixteenth century. Use at Leiden in sixteen twenty sparked riots by hand weavers there. Towns across Europe then banned the loom at times for years.
britannica-1911-sabaeans:
The Sabaeans of south Arabia are sifted in a study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Their old name for the folk of Yemen was Saba. The first word of them comes in the Hebrew Scriptures. A list of Joktan's sons in Genesis names the peoples there. Many of those names match stones and Arab maps, the entry shows. Sheba, Hazarmaveth, and Joktan all find their matches in the south.

Some great names on the stones miss the old list, though. Those peoples may have risen to fame at a later date. Saba itself may first have named groups of trading men. The root word in the stones means to make a trade trip. Posts and towns of those traders lined the desert roads north.
britannica-1911-sabians:
Sabians are first named in the Koran as a faith group of Babylonia. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica links them to a semi Christian sect, the Elkesaites. Their name likely means those who wash themselves, in Aramaic roots. Rites of washing stood out as a mark of the group.

Mohammed listed them with Jews and Christians as holders of a book. That status won them a tolerance not given to heathens. A second group at Harran later took the same name for safety. Threatened in 830, they claimed the name to shield old star worship. The entry is careful to keep those two groups apart throughout.
britannica-1911-saint-albans:
Saint Albans is a small city in Franklin County, Vermont, near Lake Champlain. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it on a plain below hills with wide views. Rail lines and shops served the town, and farms around it focused on dairy work. The town made butter and condensed milk for sale.

Its past holds sharp drama for a quiet place. In October 1864 a band led by Bennett H Young raided the town from Canada and robbed three banks. The men were caught in Canada but were never punished for the raid. In later years Fenian groups also used the town as a base.
britannica-1911-salutations:
Salutations, the set forms of greeting on meet and part, are the subject of a study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin term for wishing health. In strict use it names words that are spoken. Yet the piece takes in the acts of the body as well.

Old forms among wild folk can last on, near unchanged, in high custom. The warm hug at a meet is one such case, seen from island folk to the tales of Genesis. The kiss, though, is unknown to half the world, the entry says. In its place, folk greet by scent, with noses pressed close. That is the way from Polynesia to Lapland. The Persians, by Herodotus, kissed on the mouth if equal, on the cheek if not.
britannica-1911-selachians:
Selachians, also called Elasmobranchii, are treated in the 1911 Britannica as a subclass of fishes holding the sharks and rays. A shark's body runs spindle shaped, while a ray's is pressed flat for life on the sea floor. The hammerheads stretch the head out at the sides, and saw fishes push it forth as a long flat blade. Tail, chest fins, and the male claspers all get close notice.

The mouth sits as a curved slit below the head in most kinds. Gill slits stand open, each with a flap that lets water pass out but not in, five in most kinds. The basking shark guards its gill mouths with long rods that strain tiny food from the water. There is no swim bladder, and a spiral valve winds through the gut.
britannica-1911-shenandoah-valley-campai:
Shenandoah Valley Campaigns is a war article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about fighting in Virginia during the American Civil War. The valley saw action again and again. Twice, the article says, those actions rose to the rank of full campaigns with great weight in the war as a whole.

The piece first sets out why the valley mattered. It was rich farm land, full of crops, cattle, mills, and works, so the army that held it could feed itself from it. For the South it was also a source of new troops. A paved road ran from Lexington through Staunton and Winchester to Martinsburg, giving the South a path into Maryland. Rail lines let troops from Richmond reach the valley fast. Strasburg lay almost due west of Washington, which made the North fear a force massed there.
britannica-1911-sloane-sir-hans:
Sir Hans Sloane (1660-1753) was a British doctor and collector born in County Down, Ireland. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica stresses his boyhood love of natural objects. That taste led him to medicine in London, Paris, and Montpellier. He took his medical degree at Orange in 1683 and returned with many plants.

In 1687 he sailed to Jamaica as doctor to the duke of Albemarle. In fifteen months he gathered about eight hundred new plant species there. His books on that trip filled two large volumes in time. He led the Royal Society and the College of Physicians in turn. He was the first doctor to gain a hereditary title.
britannica-1911-spillikins:
Spillikins, also called Jackstraws, is a game of great age in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is played with a set of thin sticks of wood, bone, or ivory, three to six inches long. The sticks are often carved to look like weapons and tools of many kinds. They are thrown in a heap at random on the table.

Players then take turns to draw sticks from the heap one by one. The aim is to free each stick without moving any other in the pile. The player who gains the most sticks wins the game.
britannica-1911-st-albans:
Saint Albans is a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in Hertfordshire, England. It stands twenty miles north west of London, on main rail lines. Its count rose from 12,898 in 1891 to 16,019 in 1901.

Most of the article deals with the great abbey church on the hill. A church rose where Saint Alban was slain, most likely in 303. King Offa founded a house of Benedictine monks there in 793. The Norman church, begun under Abbot Paul of Caen, was blessed in 1115. Its tower, transepts, and part of the nave still stand. Later abbots rebuilt the west front and added a lady chapel. The town became the seat of a bishop in 1877.
britannica-1911-stans:
Stans is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Swiss town. It is capital of Nidwalden, the east half of Unterwalden canton. The town stands amid orchards on a plain. That plain lies at the north foot of the Stanserhorn. It sits near fifteen hundred feet above the sea. An electric railway links it to its port, Stansstad. That port lies on the south shore of Lake Lucerne. Engelberg, with its great abbey, lies not far off.

A count from 1900 gives the town 2798 people. All spoke German and all were Roman Catholic. Stans was the home of the Winkelried family. A modern monument there honours Arnold von Winkelried. He is the storied hero of the battle of Sempach. In 1481 a holy man composed a strife at Stans. In 1798 many folk were massacred there by the French. The entry joins place, memory, and faith in one sketch.
britannica-1911-summons:
Summons is the subject of a law entry in the 1911 Britannica. In English law it means a call from high power. It can call a man to attend at a set time. It can call him to do some public duty. It can also mean the paper that holds that call. Such a paper may state what neglect will cost. Spoken calls came before writ calls in England.

Roman law shows the same path of growth in form. The age and weight of the form show in old tales. A church court caller stands in the Canterbury Tales. The word serves for calls to attend parliament too. In church and wedlock courts a kin word, citation, is kept. A chief rule of justice backs the whole form. No court should judge till all sides can be heard. Civil steps in the High Court are then set out.
britannica-1911-svane-hans:
Hans Svane (1606–1668) was a Danish statesman and churchman, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his two callings. He was born on the twenty seventh of March 1606 at Horsens. His father was burgomaster of that town. His mother was a daughter of the historian Hans Svaning, whose name the son took in altered form.

At Copenhagen, Svane gave himself to the study of Oriental languages. Between 1628 and 1635 he completed his education abroad. He studied at Franeker, Wittenberg, Oxford, and Paris in those years. After seven years away, he came home to a chair of Oriental languages at Copenhagen. Promotion came slowly in that post, the entry says. In 1646 he turned to theology instead. His old patron, now a bishop, made him a doctor of theology that year.
britannica-1911-tatra-mountains:
The Tatra Mountains are the subject of a place entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. They are the highest group in the central Carpathians and the core of the whole chain. They lie between four rivers named in the entry. The group is sharply defined and stands apart from its neighbours.

The range rises like a giant wall from a high plateau above the sea. Its peaks reach more than eight thousand feet in height. The range runs through Hungarian counties and into Galicia. Its length and varying width are both given in the entry. Mean height figures help readers grasp the scale of this wall of rock.
britannica-1911-tausen-hans:
Tausen, Hans, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of the lead man of the Danish Reformation. Born at Birkende in Funen in 1494, he was a bright peasant lad. He ran from the plough young and became a friar at Antvorskov. He read at Rostock and taught there and at Copenhagen.

He knew Latin and Hebrew well and turned the books of Moses into Danish. In May 1523 he went to Wittenberg to study under Luther's sway. A year and a half later his house called him back home. His open love of Luther's teaching got him jailed at Antvorskov. He was then sent to Viborg, where he preached from gaol. The town folk there took up his cause with zeal.
britannica-1911-trade-unions:
Trade Unions, combinations that regulate the relations of workmen and masters, are the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry begins with the United Kingdom and its law. By English common law such combinations were, with few exceptions, held to be illegal. They were treated as conspiracies in restraint of trade, against public policy.

Those who took part in them could be prosecuted and punished by fine and imprisonment on conviction. The offence was the same in law whether masters or workmen committed it. In practice, though, the law's force fell on workmen far more than on masters. A workman alone might lawfully refuse to labour for any pay or hours he pleased. Yet when two or more joined and agreed to work only on set terms, their agreement was void. Worse, it was a criminal offence under the common law of the day.
britannica-1911-united-states-the-popula:
Population and social conditions in the United States are treated in a section of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The section opens with the growth of the nation in land terms. At independence, the folk owned the land from the Gulf to the Great Lakes. Florida alone was excepted, and the land ran west to the Mississippi.

Real settlement, though, clung to a strip along the Atlantic shore. Its depth inland varied a great deal, from mere shore posts for fishing to farm land that reached the hills. On average it ran some two hundred fifty miles deep. Four paths led west through gaps in the mountain barrier. Small groups had already settled past the hills, near Pittsburgh, in Kentucky, and in Tennessee. Their sites were set by river routes.
britannica-1911-ural-mountains:
Ural Mountains form a chain that runs from the Arctic Ocean south. The 1911 Britannica entry traces them near to the Caspian Sea in length. Men have long held them as the line that parts Europe from Asia. Russians call them simply Kamen, which means stone, or Poyas, a girdle. The name Urals may come from a Turkic phrase for isle peaks.

The true build of the range is still dimly known, the entry admits. Shocks at sundry times have thrust its parts up at sundry angles. Some folds strike north west, and others strike north east in trend. The chain reaches its top heights in a zone that runs north south. At both ends the folds split into clear, distinct chains of hills.
britannica-1911-valens:
Valens is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an East Roman emperor. He ruled from 364 to 378, the text notes. His brother Valentinian raised him to the throne at age thirty six. The two then split the empire into East and West for good. Valens had served in the guard of the emperor Julian. He did not share the soldier's gift of his father. His father had risen from the ranks to high place.

A revolt led by Procopius shook the second year of his reign. The rebels drew support from Constantinople and from Gothic chiefs. Valens thought of talks, but the revolt soon fell apart. His ministers and generals stood firm and saved his rule. In 366 he cut the taxes of the empire by one fourth. The move won him favour, though Goths loomed on the Danube.
britannica-1911-valentinus-and-the-valen:
Valentinus, the leading figure of the Gnostic movement, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. By one account he was born on the coast of Lower Egypt. He was raised and educated at Alexandria. He then travelled to Rome to teach.

The article fixes his stay at Rome between about 135 and 160. He came under one pope, flourished under the next, and stayed into a third's time. Justin Martyr had already attacked him in an earlier work against heresy. That proves his teaching was abroad by about 140 at the latest. Polycarp, visiting Rome, won back a few of his followers to the church. A later writer claims Valentinus himself had sought the bishopric of Rome. On losing it to a confessor, he is said to have left the church in anger. The article treats that tale as doubtful gossip of the early church.
britannica-1911-zoological-gardens:
Zoological gardens, places where wild animals are kept for view, are covered in a 1911 Britannica article. Their main aim is the joy most people take in seeing rare and fine beasts up close. They also teach natural history and supply study material for museums. Some earn money as pleasure grounds or sale yards.

The piece traces their roots far back. The first garden with clear records was set up in China near 1100 before Christ. Greeks and Romans kept many wild beasts, but for death in the arena. Kings later kept private menageries, such as one at Woodstock under Henry the First. Those grew into the public gardens of modern times.
britannica-1911-zwiedineck-von-sudenhors:
Hans Zwiedineck von Südenhorst, a German historian who lived from 1845 to 1906, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Frankfurt on the Main, he studied at the university at Gratz and became a professor there in 1885. He died at Gratz in November 1906, and the entry is built around his books.

His works cover village life in the seventeen hundreds, Prince Hans Ulrich von Eggenberg, and the policy of Venice in the Thirty Years War. He also wrote on Venice as a world power, on war scenes from the days of the Landsknechte, and on public views in Germany in the age of Louis the Fourteenth. Later books deal with Archduke Johann and with Maria Theresia. He ran a large series on German history, wrote two parts himself, and edited a journal of general history, a full career in print.
california-and-the-californians:
David Starr Jordan, president of Stanford University, wrote California and the Californians as a short essay of interpretation. The Californian, he begins, loves a state that loves him back. Outside criticism, however aimed, flies wide of the mark. Yet Californians may say hard things about themselves that strangers may not.

Jordan lists the charges cheerfully: sleepy commerce, gambling industries, shabbiness, and saloon politics. Then he answers them from the land itself. Scenery, climate, and freedom of life are the three sources of California's charm. From Siskiyou to San Diego he surveys missions, sierras, valleys, and surf. The essay is brief, fifty pages of prose, and reads as a founding president's defence of his adopted state against Eastern condescension.
canadian-crusoes-a-tale-of-the-rice-lake:
Catharine Parr Traill wrote a tale of lost children on the Rice Lake Plains, printed at London in 1852. Agnes Strickland set the book in order. Harvey drew the plates. Traill had won her name with The Backwoods of Canada. Settler children of the Plains get the book, signed at Oaklands, Rice Lake, in October 1850.

Truth backs the tale, the preface holds. Men's hearts beat fast for lone souls who fight for food, it grants. Pride and rank sink to nought in that sight. Cold and hunger, the gaunt foes, drive the stakes. Backwoods craft — fire, food, and shelter won by small hands — forms the stock. Kin love in wild ground gives the book its warm core, as the gift line to settler youth vows.
carolina-chansons:
DuBose Heyward and Hervey Allen joined forces for a book of poems subtitled Legends of the Low Country, published in 1922 and dedicated to John Bennett. Groups of verse treat pirates, the Sewee Indians, Lafayette's landing, and the legend of Theodosia Burr, alongside a poem on the first submarine and its last crew.

Other sections honour Edgar Allan Poe and the gardens along the Ashley River. Legends of the Cooper River follow. A group written in dialect voice gives the book a different register. Prose notes at the back explain the history behind the poems, and a bibliography lists sources. Charleston's coast, marshes, and old stories supply nearly every page.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-leri:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Lérins describes an island monastery off Provence, on Saint-Honorat island, a league off Provence's coast. St. Honoratus founded it early in the fifth century, living first as a hermit before followers gathered from Roman Gaul and Brittany alike.

Through the fifth, sixth and seventh centuries Lérins exerted considerable influence, until Saracen raids made monkish life unworkable or shaky for two hundred years. Restored in the eleventh century, the abbey gained estates, churches and privileges from popes, counts of Provence and kings of France. Its monks also defended the coast against Moorish incursions from Algeria through the Middle Ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on St. Albans describes a Hertfordshire abbey. Offa, King of the Mercians, founded it about 793. Bede, writing early in the eighth century, already speaks of a church of wonderful workmanship, fine enough for the martyrdom it honoured. Offa's monastery grew beside that church, which he repaired with papal approval.

Willegod, the king's kinsman, became abbot, and by 1000 the old church again stood dilapidated. Abbots Ealdred and Eadmer gathered materials from Roman Verulam's ruins, and Abbot Paul of Caen began the new church in 1077, completing the whole in eleven years. Adrian the Fourth later freed St. Albans from bishops' control and ranked it first among English abbeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abecedarians:
The Abecedarians were a sect of Anabaptists who scorned all human learning, holding that God enlightens his chosen people inwardly and gives them needed truth through visions and ecstasies. They rejected every other path to knowledge and claimed that salvation required ignorance even of the first letters of the alphabet, which gave the group its name. Study of theology struck them as a kind of idolatry, and they treated learned preachers as men who falsified God's word.

In 1522 Nicholas Storch and Zwickau's prophets began preaching this teaching at Wittenberg, mixed with other errors. Carlstadt was drawn to it and put it into practice so fully that he surrendered his doctoral title to work as a street porter. For a while he preached the new teaching to Wittenberg's people and students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-janss:
Abraham Janssens was a Flemish painter born at Antwerp about 1573 who probably died there about 1631. Also known as Janssens van Nuyssen, he likely took that name from his mother's family to set himself apart from other artists named Janssens. He was a pupil of Jan Snellinck and entered the Guild of St. Luke as a teaching master in 1601. He married the next year and raised a family, and his daughter Anna married Jan Breughel the younger.

Houbraken started a story that Janssens bitterly opposed Rubens, but his work is the only authority for that legend. The entry judges Houbraken hostile to Janssens. In fact Janssens was a respected contemporary of Rubens, spoken of warmly by fellow artists in Antwerp. In colour's splendour and composition's vigour, only Rubens surpassed him in his day, and many of his pictures were engraved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acclamation-i:
Acclamation is one of three valid forms of papal election, alongside scrutiny and compromise. The method rests on the constitutions of Gregory XV, confirmed by Urban VIII. Acclamation, also called quasi-inspiration, consists in all cardinals present unanimously proclaiming one candidate Supreme Pontiff without casting votes. Since it must happen without prior consultation or negotiation, it is viewed as proceeding from the Holy Ghost.

Recent examples anchor the account. Clement X, formerly Cardinal Altieri, was elected in 1670 after the crowd outside the conclave cried Altieri Papa, a cry the cardinals confirmed. Innocent XI, elected in 1676, was surrounded in the conclave chapel and, despite his resistance, had every cardinal kiss his hand and proclaim him pope. The entry cites Ferraris, Wernz, De Montor, and Keller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acts-of-roman:
Acts of Roman Congregations is the term for documents, also called decrees, issued by the Roman Congregations under powers conferred by the pope. The entry treats the subject under six heads: kinds, authority, use, manner of preservation, accessibility, and collections. In kinds, these bodies grant privileges and dispensations, issue ordinances, give true readings of law, and decide cases between contending parties, though not every body holds all these powers.

Decrees are for single cases or church-wide, by whether they address individuals or the whole church, and most deal with discipline, explaining, enforcing, or dispensing from positive church laws. Some deal with doctrine, declaring a doctrine untenable or an act unlawful against divine law. In authority, these decrees are supreme in a sense, coming from the highest church tribunals, but not wholly supreme, since the Congregations are distinct in law from the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advocates-of-:
Advocates of Roman Congregations, ecclesiastical or lay, know canon and civil law and plead causes before Rome's ecclesiastical tribunals. The learning required is exceptional and profound. Beyond thorough jurisprudence, canonical and civil, they must know theology and history, sacred and profane. Frequent references to councils, canons, and papal decrees demand deep and varied learning covering languages ancient and modern.

A Roman advocate differs from an ordinary legal pleader in several ways. He does not establish facts in a case, since that is the procurator's business. He assumes the facts given him to be true and builds his legal argument on them, freed from tempting distortions of testimony. He pleads always before learned judges, not a jury, so his language must be sober, refined, clear, and precise. His fee is fixed, win or lose, and consistorial advocates must defend the poor free of charge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aeons:
Aeons is the term Gnostic heresiarchs used for spiritual powers arising by progressive emanation from the eternal Being. Together they form the Pleroma, the unseen spiritual world, as distinct from the Kenoma, the visible material world. The word aeon, aion, means age, the ever-existing, or eternity, and came to denote the divine eternal power and its personified attributes.

From there it extended to successive emanations from divinity, seen as needed links between spiritual and material worlds. The concept traces to a philosophy holding divinity incapable of contact with matter or evil. The wish was to square that view with Christian belief in God's direct action in creation and redemption. Jewish angelology and Hellenic systems of go-betweens suggested a series of lesser heavenly powers, each less perfect the further from the supreme deity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agents-of-rom:
Agents of Roman Congregations look after their patrons' affairs at the Roman Curia. The name comes from Latin Agens in Rebus, matching Greek Apocrisiarius. Such agents first appear not at Rome but at Constantinople's imperial palace. There bishops, given church and state's close tie and the lack of canons on mixed matters, needed men to watch their interests at court.

Until the French Revolution, French prelates kept like agents at St. Denis's royal court. Today bishops or private persons employ agents in the pontifical courts, temporarily or permanently. Their chief business is pressing patrons' cases forward. For favours such as dispensations they prepare supplications and call repeatedly on officials until an answer comes. They rank next before the notaries, and their pay rests wholly on employers' will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexian-nuns: The Alexian nuns, or black sisters, began early in the fifteenth century as religious women affiliated to the Alexian Brotherhood. They adopted the Rule of St. Augustine and took up the Brothers' bodily works of mercy. Their dress is black: a mantle of matching colour and a white cap gave them their common name. The black, or Cellitine, sisters now have their mother-house at Cologne, and they have no houses in the United States and Canada.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexians:
The Alexians, also called Cellites, are a religious congregation that began at Mechlin in Brabant in the fifteenth century, during the ravages of the Black Death. Certain laymen joined under a man named Tobias to help the plague-stricken, without taking vows or adopting a rule at first. The institute took its name from St. Alexius, and its brothers devoted themselves to burying the dead and nursing the sick.

The Alexian Brothers run four hospitals in the United States. The first, built at Chicago in 1866, burned in the great fire of October 1871 and was rebuilt the next year, and the second, raised at St. Louis in 1869, covers an acre with wards for the insane, nervous diseases, and inebriety. Bishop Vaughan of Salford invited the brothers to England in June 1875, and the Bishop of Middlesborough brought them to his diocese in 1884.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-algonquins:
The Algonquins were probably once the largest North American tribes, roaming between Kentucky and Hudson Bay, and between the Atlantic and the Mississippi, perhaps further still.
