Kingsley preaches as a Broad Church clergyman and social reformer, joining moral earnestness to scientific curiosity. Readers of Victorian preaching will find these sermons muscular, humane and characteristic of their author.
doe-osti-17084193-p-clap-bridging-aeroso:
Lekha Patel and a large Sandia team present P-CLAP in report SAND2026-26735, printed September 2026, a method for carrying aerosol detail across model scales. Aerosols are tiny airborne particles that affect climate, yet global models cannot track each particle group in full detail. Statistical learning, bound by physics rules, is their bridge.

Parts of the project build compact generative summaries of aerosol populations and rebuild full states from partial observations. A method named AeroMELD keeps the shape of a particle population intact under mixing and grouping, with exact rules for combining populations. Later chapters couple a detailed particle model, PartMC, into grid boxes of the E3SM Earth system model and verify the transport math.
doe-osti-2573934-symmetries-strings-and-:
Final technical report DOE-UCLA-0025534, by Thomas Dumitrescu of UCLA, closes a grant that ran only seven months, September 2024 to March 2025, though three years were proposed. The topic is strongly-coupled gauge theories, systems like quantum chromodynamics where the usual perturbative math fails. Two themes organize the work: confining strings, and phases with their transitions.

One paper treated quantum electrodynamics in two space dimensions plus time, a strongly coupled cousin of the familiar theory. Using anomaly matching and the Vafa-Witten theorem, the team argued the theory breaks its chiral symmetry by condensing a monopole operator. A second study finished the case of SU(N) gauge theory with two adjoint quarks. By way of a deformed supersymmetric relative, it found strong evidence the theory confines and breaks chiral symmetry for every number of colors. String solutions were also built with graduate students, in both plain and supersymmetric settings.
doe-osti-2574384-integrated-system-for-m:
Project report DE-FE0032302 for the DOE iM4 program lays out an integrated system for watching methane emissions across the natural gas supply chain. The authors are Julio Danin Lobo Neto, Doug Baer, Sneha Neupane, and colleagues. The deliverable is an engineering, design, deployment, and operating plan rather than a single instrument. Its quarry ranges from super emitters, above ten kilograms per hour, down to small chronic leaks.

Sensors of every scale feed the system. Satellites and aircraft sweep regions, while stationary, vehicle, drone, and walking surveys work the local scale, continuously or on rounds. Data streams flow into a Centralized Cloud Information Center, which analyzes, maps, and shares results with stakeholders. The center also layers in asset data from ArcGIS databases, so a detected plume can be matched against known equipment. Sections cover requirements, algorithms, testing and validation, and the rollout plan.
doe-osti-2574600-nuclear-astrophysics-th:
Final technical report DE-SC0020435, by Francois Foucart of the University of New Hampshire, reports simulations of colliding neutron stars. Mergers are among the most violent events in the universe, shining across the spectrum and ringing in gravitational waves. They also fling out neutron-rich matter that forges about half of the heavy elements, including most gold, platinum, and uranium, through rapid neutron capture.

Modeling such an event means solving Einstein's equations together with fluid motion, magnetic fields up to ten quadrillion gauss, and neutrino radiation. The project's focus was Monte Carlo transport, tracking neutrino packets through the wreckage so their heating and composition effects are captured faithfully. What telescopes see depends on the ejecta's mass, makeup, shape, and speed, and those same traits set the element yields. Better merger models therefore serve both dense-matter physics and the cosmic origin story of the elements.
doe-osti-2583516-predicting-fuel-propert:
Project 5 of NREL's fuels agreement with ExxonMobil is reported in NREL/TP-2A00-94890, dated April 11, 2025. Robert McCormick was the laboratory's contact. The question is predictive. Given a new bio-derived molecule that could go into diesel, can its engine behavior be known before an engine ever burns it? The project studied biofuel molecules in the diesel range. Some came from ExxonMobil's technology portfolio. All were chosen to span the space of possible chemistries.

Bench-scale tests anchored the modeling. Two prototype biofuels were measured for autoignition behavior and soot precursor formation. Those data feed general rules linking fuel traits to performance and emissions. The rules cover today's spray-combustion engines and future designs where mixing patterns change the links. A sound rulebook lets fuel developers screen candidates on paper. Costly engine testing is then saved for the molecules that deserve it.
doe-osti-2997612-effects-of-srppf-ars-ef:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-STI-2025-00614, by Katherine Broadwater, Hoang-Kim Pham, and Brinley Swanson, dated September 2025, stress-tests a grout recipe against messy real-world feed. The grout, a magnesium oxysulfate mix, will solidify liquid effluent from the Savannah River Plutonium Processing Facility's aqueous recovery system. The standard mix is 28 percent reactive magnesia, 10 percent magnesium sulfate, and 62 percent dead-burnt magnesia by weight.

The standard batch mixed in 18 minutes, peaked at 100.5 degrees Celsius, and set in 60 minutes, with leachate near pH 9.4. Trials then varied feed temperature, caustic level, nitrate load, and trace metals, using cerium and lanthanum compounds as stand-ins for plutonium and americium. Warming the feed between 30 and 40 degrees Celsius sped the reaction only slightly, lifting peak heat by no more than 6 degrees. The recipe looks tolerant of the swings the plant expects.
doe-osti-2998953-laser-calibration-syste:
Maria Domenica Galati of the University of Pisa reports in FERMILAB-TM-2919-STUDENT on her summer internship with the Muon g-2 experiment at Fermilab. The experiment measures how muons wobble in a magnetic field, aiming to pin their anomalous magnetic moment to 0.14 parts per million. That is four times sharper than the earlier Brookhaven result. Small errors in detector gain or lost muons could spoil such precision.

Galati's first task replaced the old NIM logic units in the laser calibration system with a programmable FPGA board. That system flashes laser light to keep the experiment's calorimeters honestly scaled. Her second task studied lost muons, particles that leave the storage ring before decaying, in both real data and computer simulations. Supervised by Marco Incagli and Anna Driutti, she closes by hoping to refine the data-to-simulation comparison further.
doe-osti-2999888-an-exploration-into-ele:
Sebastian Chavarria's design journal, LA-UR-25-30434, issued 21 October 2025 from Los Alamos, compares tungsten welding electrodes with different elemental additions. In TIG welding, the tungsten tip must strike an arc reliably at low current. Makers dose the tungsten with rare-earth or thorium oxides to help. Chavarria tested four blends head to head: 2 percent thoriated, ceriated and lanthanated, plus a proprietary mix sold as Tri-Mix WS2.

Every electrode shared one geometry, 0.040 inches thick and 2 inches long with a fine flat tip. An automated Miller welding system fired spot welds on stainless steel 304 and on molybdenum. Current stepped upward until ten clean arc starts in a row were achieved. The 2 percent lanthanated electrode started most reliably on stainless steel. The thoriated type lagged, struggling to strike and giving poor arc character. Weld size, depth and grain structure were also checked where allowed.
doe-osti-3002172-mpex-ai-digital-twins:
Gary Staebler, Rhea Barnett, Mark Cianciosa, and colleagues at Oak Ridge and Lawrence Livermore lay out a fusion software project dated September 13, 2025. The project builds AI digital twins for MPEX, the Material Plasma Exposure eXperiment. MPEX is a steady-state linear plasma device that will blast material samples with plasma like that hitting a fusion reactor's exhaust wall. Its targets include heat flux of 20 megawatts per square meter.

A digital twin is a live computer copy of the machine, used to guide control before and during runs. The planned AI hot spot controller would steer heating and particle sources to hold extreme conditions safely. The report assigns roles across groups: plasma turbulence, heating models, machine learning sampling, and materials modeling. A budget table splits about two million dollars per year among the teams.
doe-osti-3006950-cyber-conservative-oper:
Four Idaho National Laboratory authors, Patience Yockey, Sam Chanoski, Benjamin Lampe, and Virginia Wright, set out a defensive playbook in this September 2025 guide. It adapts conservative operations, a practice power grid operators use during storms, to moments when a cyber threat looms instead. Bulk power systems are the main setting, though the steps fit other control systems too.

The guide walks through planning ahead, staging extra controls and countermeasures, and moving through watch and warning stages as a threat sharpens. Suggested steps range from added staff and closer monitoring to switching off digital assets the plant does not need. Grid operators can use it to keep critical functions running while riding out a cyber event.
doe-osti-3009500-the-institute-for-nucle:
Final report for DOE award DE-SC0022075, from Michigan State University, covers the INSIGHT institute at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams, September 2023 to August 2025. The cover page names Paul Gueye as principal investigator. INSIGHT coordinates the national nuclear physics traineeship effort and runs its own training at FRIB.

An evaluator surveyed and interviewed students and mentors across the traineeship cohorts, and a final evaluation report followed in June 2025. A pilot summer school, NuPEERS2024, brought fifteen undergraduates from minority-serving institutions to Dillard University for three days of lectures and hands-on work. Participants later landed places in graduate programs from Texas A&M to UC Riverside.
doe-osti-3010135-synthesis-of-aerosol-cl:
Final technical report for DOE award DE-SC0021250, by Paquita Zuidema, covering August 2020 to September 2025, synthesizes aerosol-cloud work over the southeast Atlantic. The puzzle is why smoke drifting off Africa absorbs so much more sunlight there than smoke elsewhere.

The answer starts with black carbon: it makes up 15 to 40 percent of the aerosol mass, born in dry, flame-efficient grass burning. Over Ascension Island, organic aerosol fell by about half relative to black carbon during the trip. In the June to October 2017 LASIC record, black carbon cores grew about 10 percent across the burning season, and June's slow, low transport made the smoke most water-loving.
doe-osti-3011818-accelerating-floating-p:
Intel AMX hardware speeds floating point matrix work in a National Renewable Energy Laboratory study by Weslley da Silva Pereira. The report tests the tile matrix unit on single core multiplication first, then mixed precision routines through Intel MKL. As of oneAPI 2024.1, MKL offers only one mixed precision GEMM routine using AMX, the bf16 bf16 f32 variant.

A blocked triangular matrix multiplication built on that GEMM kernel serves as proof of concept in the TLAPACK library, version 0.1.2. The aim was showing mixed precision gains beyond GEMM in generic scientific codes. Enabling AMX inside PyTorch and TensorFlow is covered for the Kestrel system.
doe-osti-3011888-standardized-croas-key-:
Key legal provisions in carbon removal offtake agreements are compared across contract templates in a November 2025 slide deck by Sushmita Jena and Mark Greenfogel of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. Templates reviewed include Frontier Climate, 1pointfive, and the IETA primary and secondary forms. Provisions on methods, registries, and monitoring, reporting, and verification vary in how much say they give the buyer.

Volume terms contract a set amount of credits per year at a fixed price, with shortfall fixes ranging from pro-rata cuts to paying replacement cost. One template holds a recourse pool as reversal security across the project's life. Termination rights and rights of first offer are also compared.
doe-osti-3012527-plant-enhanced-degradat:
Lawrence Livermore final report LLNL-TR-2013173, by Mimi Yung, Buddhinie Jayathilake, Allison Yorita, and T. Halvorsen, covers PEDOMETER, a DARPA CERES project run with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory from April 2024 to September 2025. The idea was to pair plants with engineered soil microbes that break down munitions compounds such as TNT left in training ground soil. Safety rested on keeping the altered microbes dependent on the plants.

One team engineered a kill switch in the bacterium Pseudomonas putida, testing regulators that sense chemicals roots release, so the microbes would die without plant signals. A second team built an electrochemical TNT sensor using coated electrodes. Sensor films grew too thick past 50 deposition cycles and hid the TNT signal at 6000 parts per billion, setting a clear design limit.
doe-osti-3015899-national-laboratory-of-:
Vincent Westfallen, Wenqi Zhang, and Reiko Matsuda-Dunn of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this January 2026 report, NLR/TP-6A40-98374, for Pennsylvania's Public Utility Commission. It is a deep dive into how well the state's electric distribution systems, the local pole-and-wire networks, bounce back from storms and other disruptions. The work was done with the commission's Technical Utility Services Bureau.

The team compared Pennsylvania practice with other jurisdictions and looked at how performance should be measured. One finding is that new resilience metrics are practical for Pennsylvania, because the measures set out in the report use data the state's distribution companies already collect. A second line reviews investment choices seen elsewhere. Regulators reading it get a menu of metrics and spending options tied to records utilities already keep, rather than new reporting burdens.
doe-osti-3020368-ab-initio-molecular-dyn:
Garnet K. Chan's final technical report for DOE award DE-SC0019390, from the California Institute of Technology, sums up theory work on modeling molecules better than density functional theory allows. That method is the standard tool for quantum chemistry, but its errors limit what it can foresee. Chan's group built methods that raise accuracy while cutting cost, using machine learning and better algorithms.

The work produced 18 publications. One line of results, molecular orbital machine learning, gave energies and forces of high accuracy at a cost much lower than conventional density functional theory. Those accurate force fields made it possible to simulate hydrogen atoms scattering off surfaces, work published in Science in 2019. Other advances covered transcorrelated Hamiltonians treated with density matrix renormalization group methods. The report frames the gains as orders of magnitude in both speed and accuracy.
doe-osti-3022662-gold-catalyzed-polymeri:
A University of Southern Mississippi final report by Jason Azoulay closes DOE award DE-SC0021161, a 2020 to 2023 project turning gold-catalyzed small-molecule reactions into polymer synthesis. Gold catalysts perform distinctive changes on unsaturated compounds. The project asked whether those reactions could be run on bifunctional monomers. The aim was to build entirely new macromolecular structures rather than single molecules.

Goals included extending gold-catalyzed reactions between molecules to polycondensations of diverse nucleophiles. The team also pinned down the mechanisms at work. It used the chemistry to make new classes of aromatic plastics. Sustainability runs through the design brief. The target polymers were chosen so they can be taken apart selectively after use. That feeds recycling and upcycling rather than landfill. The report also records graduate training and conference talks the award supported.
doe-osti-3028166-engineering-scale-demon:
ION Clean Energy of Boulder, Colorado, reports Project Enterprise under award DE-FE0031950, submitted March 2026, with Erik Meuleman as principal investigator and Kenneth Kwan Jew as the report's named author. The project ran its transformational carbon capture solvent at engineering scale on flue gas from a natural gas combined cycle plant. Gas plants are a hard capture case because their exhaust is dilute and oxygen-rich.

Over the 2025 campaign, the ICE-31 solvent captured 2,500 tonnes of carbon dioxide and reached capture efficiencies as high as 99.4 percent. At that rate the treated gas leaving the absorber held about 250 to 300 parts per million of carbon dioxide, less than ambient air. The solvent stayed stable in the high-oxygen stream with very little makeup. Earlier work packages covered a monoethanolamine baseline, where foaming limited the regenerator, and the ICE-21 solvent.
doe-osti-3364112-chargex-ocpi-recommenda:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-25-85597, by Benny J. Varghese and Casey W. Quinn and dated September 2025, collects ChargeX recommendations for the Open Charge Point Interface. OCPI is the open protocol that lets charging networks share data so electric vehicle drivers can roam between networks with one account. The recommendations come from the ChargeX Diagnostics taskforce work of June 2025.

The report targets practical friction. Billing records called Charge Detail Records vary in format between operators. Timestamps follow no single standard across regions. Error codes from vehicles do not reach the people who could fix faults. Fixes are proposed version by version, through OCPI 2.2.1. Guidance also looks ahead to vehicle-to-grid charging. Operators who adopt the recommendations should see cleaner billing and faster troubleshooting.
doe-osti-3366076-xcel-energy-s-electric-:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-ACT-10156, by Brian O'Neill and prepared with Xcel Energy in June 2026, benchmarks the utility's carbon reduction path against climate scenarios. The Paris Agreement aims to hold warming well below 2 degrees Celsius, pursuing 1.5. The study updates an earlier analysis using the newest database of global emissions pathways consistent with those limits.

All pathways are expressed relative to 2005 emissions for comparability. Vetted scenarios, those matching recent global trends, sit higher in the near term, 2025 to 2030, then fall more steeply before 2050 than outdated ones. Xcel's planned trajectory is plotted against the sector pathways for the United States and North America. The authors caution that every pathway leans on assumed technology deployment and policy choices that reality may not follow.
doe-osti-3369034-equivalent-equilibrium-:
SAND2026-21834, a Sandia National Laboratories report printed in May 2026, by Thomas P. Hughes works out when ion distributions inside an ion source or an ion beam can be treated as equal to each other. Ion sources often hold ions with more than one charge-to-mass ratio, from mixed charge states and mixed atomic or molecular species. Hughes shows that under set conditions, one distribution can stand in for another, which makes the math far simpler.

The report treats the ions two ways, by tracking paths and by distribution functions, for single-species and multi-species cases. It then covers non-neutral equilibria, space-charge-limited current, and perveance in diodes and beams, plus matching rules for a diode fed by a plasma source. Particle-in-cell runs with the Aleph code test the results.
doe-osti-3374722-bioaerosol-profiling-wi:
Atmospheric Radiation Measurement report DOE/SC-ARM-26-018, dated June 2026, covers the BIOPOP campaign on open-path sensing of living particles in the air. Maria Zawadowicz and Chongai Kuang of Brookhaven ran the study. A. Vakhtin of Mesa Photonics was co-investigator. The targets were coarse biological particles, chiefly pollen grains and fungal spores. Flights ran in mid and late summer, when such particles peak.

Open-path imagers watched a free air volume rather than sucking air through an inlet. The payload sized particles from about ten microns up to a thousand. Ground gear, an aerodynamic particle sizer and a fluorescence sensor, ran beside it for contrast. That pairing let the team measure inlet losses in the standard tools. It also mapped how bioaerosols spread with height in the boundary layer, a factor in cloud studies.
doe-osti-3377897-utilities-role-in-major:
Jamie Cutlip-Gorman of the National Laboratory of the Rockies explains what utilities owe their customers when the grid goes down. The slides are dated April 23, 2026. The deck first sorts utilities by structure. Investor-owned utilities are for-profit and regulated by state public utility commissions. Cooperatives are not-for-profit and member owned. Municipal utilities are publicly owned by local or state government.

Obligations during an outage turn on that structure and on state law. Utilities must work to minimize interruptions and mitigate losses with reasonable effort. But they are not obligated to keep service running through emergency events such as storms or cyber attacks. Nor must they reimburse spoiled food. The deck closes with mutual aid agreements. Under them, utilities share crews and equipment under a set process after damage is assessed.
doe-osti-3377900-assessment-of-energy-te:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-6A20-99846, dated June 2026, assesses energy technology options for the island of Molokai, Hawaii. The authors are Evan Rosenlieb, Jayaraj Rane, and Mahalia Hunt of the laboratory, with Kyle DeSomber of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. Three options are analyzed for the island grid: floating solar, pumped storage hydropower, and backup energy systems.

The floating solar section is careful about claimed cooling gains. Many studies measure output only at the module, leave the inverter load ratio unclear, or float panels in direct contact with water in ways real installations do not. Setting those designs aside, one cited review found floating solar efficiency gains between 0.1 percent and 4.45 percent. The report weighs such evidence for each option before comparing them for Molokai.
doe-osti-3380278-assessment-of-energy-te:
Slides dated March 2026 present the Molokai energy technology assessment to the island community that commissioned it. Evan Rosenlieb, Jayaraj Rane, and Mahalia Hunt of the National Laboratory of the Rockies worked with Kyle DeSomber of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. The analysis ran through the Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project, with a community team of Sustainable Molokai, the Molokai Clean Energy Hui, Ho'ahu Energy Cooperative Molokai, and Shake Energy.

The deck carries the study's key takeaways to stakeholders and community members, and points readers to the full report for detail. It advances three priority projects picked through the Community Energy Resilience Action Plan: floating solar, pumped storage hydropower, and backup energy systems. Plain definitions of terms such as net present value are included so residents can judge the numbers themselves.
doe-osti-3391627-best-practices-for-grid:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38474, Best Practices for Grid Communications, distills what a modern grid's communication networks must do. Carol M. Larvick, Angie Kelic, and Samuel D. Olsen are among the contributors named in the evidence record. The report opens with the transition driving everything. The grid is moving from a centralized, producer-controlled network to a distributed, consumer-interactive smart grid.

A working smart grid needs sensors everywhere in transmission and distribution. They must share data with consistent, well-defined latency and higher bandwidth. Flow must run two ways between utilities and the customers who are now also producers. That data has to reach distributed or cloud computing to become action. Secure communication is treated as critical throughout, not an afterthought. Without it, the report argues, the smart grid vision fails operationally, not just on paper.
doe-osti-3509103-an-infrared-database-of:
Pacific Northwest final report, dated December 2025, builds an infrared database of optical constants for aerosol spectrum calculations in the PICARD program. Tracy Baker, Thomas Blake, Jeremy Erickson, Timothy Johnson, Schuyler Lockwood, and Tanya Myers wrote the report. The constants, called n and k values, state how materials bend and absorb light.

Values were derived by several methods and cross-checked where possible. One check compares fused silica results from reflectance and ellipsometry tools. A Kramers-Kronig transform turns reflectance spectra into constants. Sensor modelers can compute aerosol signals from vetted constants instead of scattered lab values.
doe-osti-3625657-studies-of-localization:
Fermilab note FERMILAB-FN-1303-STUDENT, dated August 5, 2026, is by Braden Bulla and Joshua L. Barrow. Bulla links to Danville Area Community College and Fermilab, and Barrow to the University of Minnesota. The work concerns GENIE, the event generator used to model neutrino hits on nuclei. A known mismatch sits between GENIE output and MicroBooNE data on transverse kinematic imbalance, a measure of sideways momentum that does not balance.

The team changed GENIE's intranuclear routines so particle positions inside the nucleus guide each step. Both main cascade models were tested, in their 2018 and 2025 forms. Checks showed the new position handling worked as planned. Yet the imbalance curves moved only a little, far short of the gap with MicroBooNE data. Making the model's insides more consistent thus did not solve the mismatch. Its source stays open, which shapes where model work should go next.
doe-osti-3684110-cultivation-ready-impro:
MicroBio Engineering's final technical report, submitted September 8, 2026, closes the CRIAS algae project under award DE-FE0032189. John R. Benemann was principal investigator. Partners were New Mexico State University, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, Los Alamos, and Heliae Development. The project ran from February 1, 2023 to January 31, 2026. Its aim was algae strains ready for ponds that use carbon far better than current practice.

Four small raceway ponds ran at wastewater sites in San Luis Obispo and Las Cruces. The green alga Scenedesmus obliquus grew on bottled carbon dioxide at both sites. Las Cruces also ran on simulated flue gas. The design paired strains that tolerate high pH with a gas transfer system built for dilute flue gas. The federal target for carbon use efficiency was fifty percent, with the team aiming at seventy or more. Cost studies modelled farms at two scales.
doe-osti-3895873-from-design-to-ocean-de:
National Laboratory of the Rockies deck, dated August 11, 2026, distils lessons from putting a small wave energy device in Hawaiian waters. Thirteen laboratory staff are named, alongside five from the Hawai'i Marine Energy Center. The SURF-WEC is a one-metre-square flap that swings with the surge and drives a hydraulic power take-off. Three goals steered the project: learn deployment needs, evaluate the take-off, and share open data.

The deck's headline number is seventy-seven lessons, with thirty-one told in full. Permitting alone took about two years across federal and state agencies, even for a kilowatt-scale device. Wide, early permits with optional gear included are the standing advice. Dry commissioning on land, with every team present, caught faults cheaply. Three clear goals blocked scope creep at hard crossroads. The authors stress the set is field experience, not a standard or a recipe.
domestic-manners-of-the-americans:
Frances Milton Trollope sailed from London on November 4, 1827, with her son and two daughters, and this account of the United States, first published in 1832, grew out of that stay. The family reached the mouth of the Mississippi on Christmas Day. Thirty-four chapters trace their route and the life they found along it.

Trollope watches American manners with a sharp, often tart eye. River towns, cities, churches, theaters, and dinner tables all pass under her gaze, and she praises or blames as she sees fit. A set of chapters admires the Capitol at Washington, with its grand terraces and fronts. British readers took the book as a bold report on a young republic, and Americans smarted at its frank tone. The hosted text keeps the full run of her sharp, detailed witness.
dream-life-a-fable-of-the-seasons:
Donald G. Mitchell, known to readers as Ik Marvel, shaped a man's life as a fable of the seasons in Dream Life, issued by Scribner in New York in 1876. A new preface prints Washington Irving's letter blessing the dedication, in which Irving jokes that the LL.D. after his name was urged on him against the stomach of his sense. The book had been Mitchell's for twelve years by then.

Parts follow the hero from a boyhood with his Aunt Tabithy through school dreams, a friend made and lost, cloister and college days, and first love. Manhood brings pride, hope, and the wide, crushing future that one moonlit passage dreads. Mitchell writes in a soft, musing voice, half story and half reverie. The charm is the mood: a life seen as weather, with each season's light on the same fields of home.
early-israel-and-the-surrounding-nations:
The Reverend A. H. Sayce, professor of Assyriology at Oxford, sets Israel among its neighbors in a book from Service and Paton of London in 1899. Seven chapters cover the Israelites, Canaan, the nations of the south-east and north-east, Egypt, and Babylonia with Assyria. Sayce wrote as a scholar of the new cuneiform finds, eager to test the Bible against the monuments.

The first chapter traces Israel's origin to Ur of the Chaldees. Abraham stands as father not only of Israel but of Ishmaelites, Midianites, Moab, Ammon, and Edom. All dwell, he says, in one family belt from Palestine to Arabia. Later chapters weigh Egyptian art, where Old Empire sculptors carved the hardest stones into living likenesses. The book reads the Hebrew story inside the wider ancient East that diggers were then uncovering.
early-plays-catiline-the-warrior-s-barro:
Henrik Ibsen's Early Plays gathers Catiline, The Warrior's Barrow and Olaf Liljekrans, translated from Norwegian by Anders Orbeck. The volume belongs to the Scandinavian Classics series, founded in the belief that familiarity with northern literature would help Americans understand Scandinavians.

Ibsen himself insisted that his dramas were not isolated accidents, and the introduction stresses the orderly development of his genius from these early works onward. Catiline shows the young Ibsen already wrestling with rebellion and fate, while the other plays display his romantic, national phase. Readers tracing Ibsen toward Peer Gynt and the later masterpieces should start here.
earthwork-out-of-tuscany-being-impressio:
Maurice Hewlett gathers impressions and translations from Tuscany in Earthwork out of Tuscany, a small book given to his father. An opening note explains the folk belief behind the pieces. Wells, groves, farmsteads, and pine woods in the hill country round Perugia, country folk hold, are still haunted by tame spirits of the soil itself.

Hewlett renders old Italian tales and lyrics in a rich, archaic English. One scene rests in a garden shade while a dark-eyed boy sings a ballad to his lute. The girl at whose feet he crouches laughs and blushes, and dares not raise her eyes. Tales of saints, lovers, and saucy priors follow in the same key. The book is less a guide than a mood: Italy seen as a land where the old gods never quite left the fields.
edison-his-life-and-inventions:
Frank Lewis Dyer, general counsel for the Edison laboratory, and Thomas Commerford Martin, past president of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote this authorized life of Thomas Edison. The contents run from the age of electricity and Edison's pedigree through his Port Huron boyhood and telegraph years. Boston, the stock ticker, and quadruplex telegraphy follow.

Later chapters cover the phonograph, the long hunt for lamp filament, Menlo Park memories, and the building of a complete lighting system. The authors had Edison's papers and cooperation, so technical claims come with inside detail. Their account of ore-concentrating work shows his optimism under staggering requirements. The biography remains a primary source on Edison's methods, if an admiring one.
eight-cousins:
Louisa May Alcott sent a delicate orphan to be raised by science and cousins in Eight Cousins. Rose Campbell, lately bereaved and brought up on salons and sickrooms, arrives at the Aunt Hill in Boston to live under her guardian, Uncle Alec, a sea-surgeon with theories. His prescription scandalizes the aunts: fresh air, plain food, loose dresses, work, and the company of her seven boy cousins, from steady Archie to baby Jamie.

Rose blooms under the regimen, and the cousins' scrapes and festivals fill the year. Alcott writes reform into a family story: health, dress, and girls' education argued through affection rather than lectures. Eight Cousins followed Little Women and shares its faith that love, properly administered, is a kind of medicine. Rose's progress from invalid to manager delights still.
el-estudiante-de-salamanca-and-other-sel:
George Tyler Northup of the University of Chicago edited this school text of José de Espronceda, Spain's foremost lyric poet of the nineteenth century. A life at the front gives the facts: Espronceda was born on March 25, 1808, the year of Spain's revolt against Napoleon, to Andalusian parents of noble stock. Notes on his verse craft follow.

The centerpiece is El Estudiante de Salamanca, the wild tale of Don Félix de Montemar in four parts. Shorter pieces join it: the Pirate's Song, the Cossack's Song, the Beggar, a sonnet, and the elegy A Teresa. The pirate's chant rings through the mid-text: sail, my vessel, without fear, for twenty prizes have been taken and a hundred nations have bowed. A vocabulary, built largely by Emily Cox Northup, closes the book. Students meet Spanish Romanticism at its most defiant.
elizabethan-sea-dogs-a-chronicle-of-drak:
William Wood chronicles Drake and his companions in Elizabethan Sea-Dogs, dated 1918. His prefatory note argues the point of the book at once. Citizen, colonist, and pioneer came to America, he writes, but the sea-dogs prepared their way and won the English right of way into Spain's New World under Elizabeth.

Twelve chapters run from England's first look west to Drake's end. Life afloat in Tudor times, Hawkins and the fighting traders, and Raleigh's vision of the West all get their due. Drake's encompassment of all the world has a chapter, and the Armada another. In one fight scene, Drake cuts every cable in a harbor and leaves it a pandemonium of drifting ships, chasing news of the great treasure ship bound for Panama. Wood writes brisk imperial history for young readers.
eminent-victorians:
Lytton Strachey remade biography in Eminent Victorians, dated 1918, with four lives: Cardinal Manning, Florence Nightingale, Dr. Arnold, and General Gordon. A preface thanks Sir Edward Cook's Life of Florence Nightingale as an honourable exception among sources, while warning that his own study works from a decidedly different angle.

Manning opens the set, born in 1807 and dead in 1892. Strachey grants his practical ability, and pictures him as a medieval church-statesman reborn: had he lived earlier he might have been an Innocent, not a Francis or an Aquinas. The Nightingale life shows her on the brink of death for months, extorting the means to carry out her commission's report. Strachey's irony is cool and surgical. He punctures Victorian sage worship with a raised eyebrow, and the four portraits still read as the sharpest short lives of their age.
evergreens:
Jerome K Jerome begins Evergreens by pitying the shrubs of his title, so dull beside snowdrops, crocuses, and summer roses. Evergreens stand cold and hard while everything else puts on gladness, he writes, and seem dowdier as the garden brightens. The image becomes a way into memory, youth, and the people who stay faithful out of season.

The sketches drift from garden meditation to remembered scrapes, including two proud young men trapped in an undignified position and unwilling to call the family down for help. Jerome mixes the joke with genuine sentiment about spring and lost years. Readers who like his gentle, wandering essays will find the evergreen a fitting emblem for his tone.
familiar-quotations:
Bartlett's Familiar Quotations collects phrases that became household words in English. John Bartlett first made the collection without thought of publication. His preface explains its object in plain terms. It shows what our language owes to many authors for familiar phrases.

An English work on a like plan supplied many additions, Bartlett notes. Quotations were taken from the original sources for accuracy, he claims. Complete indices of authors and subjects serve the reader. The author index runs from Addison and Akenside through Bacon, Bunyan, and Bryant. This copy is a New York issue from Hurst and Company. Bartlett hopes favor will earn a worthier future edition. The book became the standard American quotation treasury.
fast-in-the-ice-adventures-in-the-polar-:
Ballantyne's Fast in the Ice tells of a brig trapped in the Polar Seas. R. M. Ballantyne wrote the adventure, and the record dates it to 1863. Chapter One opens many years after the brig sailed from a British port. That brig never came back, the narrator states at once.

Cheers, wishes, and waved handkerchiefs marked her leaving Old England. Storms battered her, frost stiffened her rigging, and ice rasped her hull. She was forced onto a shore where winter reigns nearly all year. There she lay frozen in for two long years. Her starving crew forsook her on that coast. Ballantyne frames the tale as a wreck that may still lie unvisited.
five-sermons:
Whipple speaks to his church in Five Sermons, printed in 1890. Henry Benjamin Whipple was Bishop of Minnesota. The five pieces come from set days. They mark the opening of the General Convention in October 1889, and the Faribault celebration of the centennial of Washington's inauguration. A third was given at the Missionary Council at Washington the year before.

An address at Lambeth Chapel, at the first session of the Lambeth Conference on July 3, 1888, stands among them. The sampled pages dwell on the African bishops in that company. One had gone from Africa to a university, taken honors, and gone back as a bishop. Whipple thought of the man who carried the cross up the hill to Calvary. Bishop Smythies, off on foot into the interior, drew his tears. The sermons show a missionary bishop's wide heart and plain speech.
flatland-a-romance-of-many-dimensions:
Edwin Abbott Abbott, an English schoolmaster and church scholar, wrote Flatland: A Romance of Many Dimensions in 1884. He published it under the name of its hero, A Square. The hero lives in Flatland, a world of two dimensions. There men are shapes with many sides, and women are straight lines. Rank follows geometry in a strict social ladder.

A Square dreams of one-dimensional Lineland. Then a Sphere from three-dimensional Spaceland visits him. The Sphere lifts him out of his world to see it from above. Back home, no one will believe him. He is jailed for preaching a third dimension. Abbott mixes math with satire of Victorian class and sex roles. The tale also puzzles over how hard it is to picture what lies past our own senses.
flowers-and-flower-gardens-with-an-appen:
Richardson gossips about gardens in Flowers and Flower-Gardens, printed at Calcutta in 1855. David Lester Richardson was principal of the Hindu Metropolitan College. He warns the reader in his preface that the book is no scientific treatise. It is, he says, mere gossip in print on a pleasant subject, though he hopes it will not be useless.

He wrote for India, and says a good deal on the mythology and language of flowers for that reason. An appendix adds practical instructions for the Anglo-Indian flower-garden. The sampled pages sing the daisy. Richardson quotes Chaucer's praise of the flower that softens all his sorrow at dawn. Then he gives Burns his place, with the poem to a mountain daisy turned up by the plough. The book mixes verse, lore, and garden craft.
food-for-the-lambs-or-helps-for-young-ch:
Orr wrote this small devotional book for new converts, whom he calls Christ's lambs. Its chapters take up mortality, fruit-bearing, dress, and the little foxes that spoil a young faith. Some pieces are borrowed from other writers, among them essays on spiritual decline and seeking first the kingdom of God. Poems close several sections, including one that remembers a little boy taken to heaven on a winter evening.

Charles Ebert Orr signed his preface at Federalsburg, Maryland, in September 1904. He kept the book short on purpose, judging that a small volume gets read more readily than a large one. His hope, stated plainly, is that its sayings lift readers toward a higher and holier life.
forest-and-frontiers-or-adventures-among:
Gordon-Cumming's hunting adventures open with an attack on four patriarchal lions. The scene lies in the African interior, near the junction of the Mariqua and Limpopo rivers. He had resigned his army commission at the Cape of Good Hope to hunt full time. Five years of exploring and shooting wild beasts fill the account.

The compiled pages range far beyond Africa. One passage, drawn from Humboldt, watches jaguars emptying river turtles from their shells with supple paws. Alligators, herons, and vultures join the list of the turtles' enemies. Roualeyn Gordon-Cumming was billed on his title page as the most daring hunter of his day.
george-du-maurier-the-satirist-of-the-vi:
T. Martin Wood surveys the art and character of George du Maurier in this 1913 book, with forty-one illustrations. Du Maurier drew the famous Punch cartoons that mocked Victorian fashion, art talk, and smart society. Late in life he also wrote novels, among them Trilby. Wood divides the study into the artist's world, his art, his work as an author, and his life.

Plates show his work from early magazine drawings to his illustrations for Wives and Daughters. Wood shows how du Maurier's weak eyesight and French training shaped his fine line. The book captures a man who watched his age with a kind, amused eye. Art lovers get both a life story and a gallery of the drawings that made his name.
ghazali-confessions:
Al-Ghazali, the great Muslim thinker of Baghdad, wrote his Deliverance from Error near the end of his life, around 1100. Claude Field's version appeared under the title The Confessions of Al-Ghazzali. Ghazali had been the most famous teacher in Baghdad.

He tells how doubt about all knowledge drove him to quit his post and wander. Years of Sufi practice, he says, gave him the certainty that books could not. The short work reshaped Islamic theology and is still read as a classic of spiritual searching. Many call it the finest autobiography in medieval Islam.
govdocs-archive_org-fer-latin-american-l:
Knights of Lucifer gathers Latin American luciferian and Hyperborean writings by several hands, including L. Wotan, Ignacio Ondargain, Piedra Iberica, Orlando Croy Romero, and Geburah Michel Lycanon. The compilation comes from the esoteric underground of the Spanish-speaking world.

The pieces treat Lucifer as a bringer of light and a rebel against the Christian order, mixed with Hyperborean myth about a lost northern homeland. Such texts circulate in small esoteric circles rather than through bookshops. The collection is held as an archive item, without endorsement, as a sample of that Latin American fringe literature.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AssassinationsR: nsia-AssassinationsRacist Assassinations De Gaulle CIA: the made public government document on killing plots against de Gaulle and the CIA's role. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIACubans_CIA_C: Myra MacPherson, an Associated Press writer, titled her piece on the Bay of Pigs' long aftermath The Last Casualty of the Bay of Pigs. The failed 1961 invasion of Cuba by CIA-trained exiles left prisoners and widows. It left a wound in Cuban-American politics that lasted decades, and MacPherson's article returns to that aftermath. It is preserved as a single article among the archive's CIA and Cuba clippings, from the years when the invasion's story was still being settled.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FensterwaldBern:
Joseph Berger wrote about a new book on the Kennedy assassination by Bernard Fensterwald, titled Coincidence or Conspiracy. Fensterwald built his book around three people. Each of the three had intriguing encounters with both Lee Harvey Oswald and Jack Ruby, the two men at the center of the Dallas story.

A book built on such crossings invites readers to judge the pattern for themselves. Coincidence or planned connection is the question the title poses. Berger's article presents the book and its three figures to readers weighing that question, part of the large literature the assassination produced.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Mexican-America:
Peter Nabokov reported for the Washington Post on December 16, 1968, that Reies Lopez Tijerina had been acquitted. Tijerina led a land-grant movement in New Mexico. The charges grew out of a 1967 raid on a courthouse, in which his followers went looking for a district attorney they meant to arrest.

The raid made Tijerina a national figure in the Chicano movement. His acquittal, on the charges Nabokov covers, was a courtroom victory after a trial that drew wide attention. The article records the verdict and the reaction of officials, who were stunned by it. It preserves a turning point in a movement that tied modern protest to old Spanish land grants.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NewOrleansExcha:
Chris Shearouse wrote about Exchange Alley in New Orleans, in an article titled 'Change in Exchange: Dilemma in an Alley.' The alley was born in 1831 as Exchange Passage. Shearouse covers the debate over its future: what to keep, what to change, and who decides.

Old alleys in the French Quarter carry two centuries of commerce in a few yards of brick. Articles like this one appear when a landmark's fate is argued in public. Shearouse gives the alley's history and the present dispute together. The piece is local journalism about preservation, filed in these papers because the alley also belongs to the Oswald story's New Orleans geography.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Translations_Tr: Called 'Translations,' this declassified US government document rests in the Internet Archive's govdocs collection. Translated from what, by whom, and when - the catalog is mute. No public text located. A task-word for a title, awaiting its papers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_CDC:
Starting in Havana, American diplomats began reporting strange illnesses with no clear cause. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention spent two years on an epidemiologic investigation of those incidents. Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, posted in February 2021, on the CDC report.

The report left the medical mystery unresolved, as the posting's title says. That non-answer is itself the news: a long, formal study could not settle what hurt the diplomats. Readers interested in the Havana Syndrome debate get the government's own investigative record rather than rumor or press summary.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
The National Security Act of 1947 built the machinery of modern American power. Rachel Santarsiero compiled this briefing book, number 799, published in July 2022 for the law's seventy-fifth anniversary. The statute established the CIA and the National Security Council.

It also laid the foundations of the Department of Defense. The posting calls the law's effect a complete overhaul of the executive branch. It transformed how foreign policy was made and powered America's global engagement through the Cold War and beyond. Anyone reading declassified records works inside institutions this single act created, which makes its anniversary set a useful map of the whole system.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_COU:
A new documentary film, COUP 53, examines the 1953 overthrow of Iran's Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq. Malcolm Byrne edited this briefing book, posted in August 2020, around a startling item the film features. It is a recently recovered interview with a former MI6 operative.

In that interview, Britain's Secret Intelligence Service is tied to the 1953 kidnapping of Tehran's chief of police. A kidnapping of the capital's police chief was no side detail in a coup; it removed a man who could have resisted. The posting links film research with the declassified record, each strengthening the other.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_Doc:
Relations between Iran and the United States from 1978 to 2015 fill this National Security Archive collection. Those years run from the last period of the Shah's rule, through the revolution and hostage crisis, to the nuclear deal era. A documentary set spanning that whole arc is rare.

Most accounts treat those decades as separate stories: revolution, war, sanctions, talks. A single collection lets readers trace the same two governments across all of them. The value is continuity. Claims made in one decade can be checked against the paper of the next, which is exactly what a relations archive should allow.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Preoccupations with West Germany's Nuclear Weapons Potential: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated entry, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
When Bill Clinton took office in January 1993, Boris Yeltsin's Russia was the new partner the United States had to learn to work with. The National Security Archive's electronic briefing book covers the first six months of that relationship. It is built on declassified records of the summits the two presidents held at Vancouver and in Tokyo that year.

The records show joint diplomatic work and a strikingly personal element: Clinton backed Yeltsin directly in his fight with the Russian parliament. That support helped set the tone for years of American policy toward Moscow. For readers, the papers capture a brief season when Washington treated Russia's shaky new democracy as a project worth personal risk from an American president.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_chile-cold-war-he:
Henry Kissinger shaped American foreign policy in the 1970s, and few figures of that era draw stronger praise or sharper blame. Under the heading Power by Any Means Necessary, the National Security Archive assembled a declassified dossier on his record. It is drawn from the secret files of the governments he dealt with, and of the one he served.

A dossier built from declassified papers lets readers test the legend against the memos. Kissinger, often shortened to HAK in the files of the time, left an unusually full paper trail across wars, coups, and secret diplomacy. The collection's value is that it argues with documents rather than opinion, giving critics and defenders alike the same evidence to work from.
graded-lessons-in-english-an-elementary-:
Alonzo Reed and Brainerd Kellogg's Graded Lessons in English is an elementary English grammar, famous for its sentence diagrams. The book teaches pupils to analyse sentences by placing words on a heavy horizontal line for the main clause, with vertical, diagonal and dotted lines for modifiers and subordinate parts.

Lessons proceed step by step, so that a child learns parts of speech, sentence structure and correct usage together, rather than by rote rules alone. Generations of American schoolchildren learned grammar from Reed and Kellogg, and their diagrams became a classroom institution. Teachers and historians of education will find this volume the classic statement of the diagramming method.
great-possessions:
David Grayson, the pen name of Ray Stannard Baker, writes of his country life in Great Possessions. The chapters open with The Well-Flavoured Earth, and turn on smells, green growing things, and places of retirement. One head reads Follow Your Nose! Another warns No Trespass. A good apple gets its own chapter, and so does a trip to the city.

Grayson finds his wealth in soil, seasons, neighbors, and work done by hand. An old stone mason, an auction of antiques, and a man named Bill Richards, styled His Majesty, fill the later pages. The close treats living in the country as a chosen art. The book's quiet claim is in its title: the great possessions are not bought. It is a gentle classic of American back-to-the-land writing.
great-singers-second-series-malibran-to-:
Ferris made this second series of Great Singers in 1881 as a companion to the first, which ran from Bordoni to Sontag. The same limits guide him, he says: only singers who stand without dispute in the front rank get sketches, with lesser lights brought in where a great life needs them. He also gives notice, in several pieces, to a few of the greatest men singers. The series opens with Malibran.

Maria Malibran died young after a fall from a horse, and her blaze of fame sets the tone. The sketches run on through the age of Jenny Lind's rivals to Theresa Titiens, the great dramatic soprano of London. Ferris quotes those who heard them, since no record of their voices could exist. The pair of volumes together gives a full gallery of opera's early stars.
half-portions:
Edna Ferber published Half Portions in 1920, a book of nine short stories. The first, The Maternal Feminine, opens on Aunt Sophy Decker, whom the world files as a spinster. She is unmarried and fifty, stylish stout in blue serge. Broad-toed health shoes and a small, astute hat complete the portrait. Ferber says you would have to coin a term to describe her, or fall back on the dictionary. The tale turns that dry label inside out.

Old Lady Mandle, a long-distance call, and a story in dialect stand among the rest. Ferber writes of working women, mothers, and the Jewish and German folk of her native Midwest, with warmth and a sharp comic ear. The title hints at lives served less than their due. These stories show the craft that would soon make her one of America's best-loved novelists.
handy-dictionary-of-poetical-quotations:
George W. Powers compiled his Handy Dictionary of Poetical Quotations at New York in 1901. His preface states the aim. The book is a ready reference to the most familiar stanzas and lines of the chief English poets. A few selections come from Continental writers. Some less familiar modern pieces are added, which may in time become classic. A portrait of Longfellow leads the book.

The entries run by theme, so that a speaker hunting a line on love, death, or spring can find it fast. Powers notes that the few great poets of the language have struck nearly every chord of human sentiment that verse can show. Such dictionaries stood on every parlor shelf in the age of elocution. This one is a fair specimen, handy in size and catholic in taste.
happy-hawkins:
Robert Alexander Wason put a cowboy at the center of Happy Hawkins and let him tell the tale in dialect. Happy, born in Indiana, ran west as a boy hunting Indians and found hunger instead. Lunch counters, silent ranch bosses, and open ranges school him. His nickname fits: humor carries him through work, fights, and love alike.

The Diamond Dot ranch gives the story its home ground across thirty chapters. Happy convinces a cook, rides under fire, sets a broken leg, and drifts off whenever restlessness calls. A lasso duel, a winter at Slocum's Luck, and questions over Chinese labor mark the middle episodes. Barbie, the ranch girl, slowly turns the comedy toward courtship, discovery, and a wedding day. A final reckoning and an afterglow chapter close the wanderer's account. Western readers who like talk, ranch routine, and a soft heart under the slang will enjoy Happy's company.
human-nature-and-other-sermons:
Joseph Butler, Bishop of Durham, preached the sermons gathered in this Cassell volume of 1887, and the introduction gives his life from his birth at Wantage in 1692. Butler argued his way from a Presbyterian upbringing into the Church of England, took his Oxford degree, and in 1718 became preacher at the Rolls Chapel in London. The sermons on human nature that open the book were preached there.

Butler's argument in those sermons is moral anatomy. Human nature is a system of appetites, affections, self-love, benevolence, and, ruling over all, conscience. Self-love and benevolence are not enemies; each passion has its proper object and place. The later sermons take up charity, resentment, and the love of God. Few English sermons have been argued over so long by philosophers.
hunted-down-the-detective-stories-of-cha:
Charles Dickens opens Hunted Down, his 1860 detective tale, through a retired life assurance manager who claims to have seen more romances in thirty years of business than most men. A smooth client named Slinkton wins his trust, then suspicion, as a young lady's death and an insurance policy come together. The manager sets himself to hunt the man down.

A drunken associate named Beckwith, brandy saucepan in hand, becomes an unlikely instrument of exposure. Dickens builds the short novel from office observation rather than police procedure, making the detective an amateur of character. This edition, from Hard Times and Reprinted Pieces, collects Dickens's contributions to crime writing, a field his Inspector Bucket had already transformed.
in-and-out-of-three-normandy-inns:
Anna Bowman Dodd wrote this travel book on three inns in Normandy, in northern France. Chapters move through Villerville, along an old post road, and to Dives and Honfleur. Landladies, a village, a mussel bed, and a Norman household get close attention. Dodd frames the folk she meets as wholly their own.

Later parts stage two banquets at Dives, with talk after dinner. A duchess praises an old friend's youth at Les Rochers as twilight falls. Seventeenth-century scenes are revived beside nineteenth-century ones. Readers get a warm, detailed stay with Norman hosts and guests.
indian-heroes-and-great-chieftains:
Charles A. Eastman, a Dakota Sioux doctor and writer known also as Ohiyesa, wrote Indian Heroes and Great Chieftains, published in 1919. Eastman profiles the Native leaders he most admired, telling their lives from inside the world that produced them. His pages carry Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse of the Sioux, Red Cloud, Spotted Tail, and Little Crow.

He crosses the continent for others: Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce, Geronimo of the Apache, and the Shawnee and Sac and Fox leaders of older wars. Eastman writes as a bridge figure, educated in white schools yet loyal to his people's honor. The book set out to give young readers, Native and white alike, heroes told truly, and it still reads with quiet force.
inquiries-and-opinions:
Brander Matthews published Inquiries and Opinions in September 1907, dedicating it to Henry Arthur Jones. Essays open with literature in the new century, read first at St. Louis in 1904. An apology for technic and a piece on invention and imagination follow. Poe and the detective story get their own inquiry.

Mark Twain's prose is praised for a huge vocabulary with few dead words. Matthews says Twain speaks only when he has something to say, and says it sharply. Maupassant, Ibsen, and the modern novel and play close the set. The book is a working critic's views on craft.
intentions:
Oscar Wilde gathered his four great critical dialogues and essays as Intentions, first published in 1891 and reprinted by Methuen in 1913. The Decay of Lying opens the book in a Nottinghamshire library, where Vivian argues that art should not copy life because life copies art. Cyril plays the straight man and loses beautifully.

Pen, Pencil, and Poison studies the forger Wainewright as an artist in crime. The Critic as Artist, the longest piece, claims criticism is itself creative, and The Truth of Masks defends costume and paradox in Shakespeare. Wilde's epigrams here became the doctrine of the aesthetic movement, argued with a learning that keeps surprising readers who expected only wit.
jan-of-the-windmill-a-story-of-the-plain:
Jan of the Windmill, a story of the plains by Juliana Horatia Ewing, follows a baby left with a miller's family and raised beside the sails. Ewing's tale appears here in a fifth edition from London, dated 1890, with eleven illustrations by Helen Paterson Allingham. The contents promise a windmiller's wife, strangers at the mill, and a payment of ten shillings a week for the little Jan.

Chapter headings trace the boy's growing up in plain village terms. He works as a nurse boy, minds pigs, and learns beside Abel, the miller's man, who plays schoolmaster over a spelling column. A pocket book and a family Bible carry a five pound reward and a buried question about his birth. Visitors bring a tiny lady with a grand name and a cure for whooping cough. Kindness, class, and a foundling's secret carry the story.
jimmie-higgins:
Jimmie Higgins is a novel by Upton Sinclair, the American writer known for exposing social wrongs. Its contents page alone maps Jimmie's whole path in twenty chapter titles. He meets a candidate, hears a speech, and debates the issue. Then he strikes it rich, helps the Kaiser, and goes to jail.

Later chapters send Jimmie back to nature, face to face with an owner, and into open war. He meets a patriot, dodges trouble, and takes the road. The titles then turn sharp: Jimmie turns Bolshevik, meets a tempter, and wrestles with him. At last he takes the plunge and puts on khaki. Sinclair builds a working man's political education into a story.
journals-of-australian-explorations:
Journals of Australian Explorations gathers the expedition journals of Augustus Charles Gregory and his brother Francis Thomas Gregory. Both men were fellows of the Royal Geographical Society and gold medalists of it. The Brisbane government printer issued the volume in 1884. Its preface explains that readers kept asking for journals long out of print.

Earlier, the journals had appeared only in fragments. This volume collects them whole, for reference and for the permanent record. It leaves the brothers' first impressions unchanged, even where later knowledge corrected them. The first journal covers the 1846 expedition east and north of Swan River. A settlers' expedition under A. C. Gregory in 1848 follows. Together they trace early attempts to open Australia's unknown interior.
judith-of-the-plains:
Judith of the Plains is a novel by Marie Manning, published by Harper and Brothers in 1903. Twenty chapters carry the story, opening simply with Town. Judith works as postmistress, as one chapter title announces. Leander and his lady, the Rodneys at home, and Mrs. Yellett and her 'government' fill the early cast.

The plot moves onto the horse-thief trail and into a cabin in the valley. A round-up, a wolf hunt, and the land of the red silence follow. Mary spends her first day in camp, and Judith adjusts the situation. Cloudburst, hanging threats, and a final ball close the contents. Manning writes a Western of ranch life with a capable heroine at its center.
keith-of-the-border-a-tale-of-the-plains:
Keith of the Border: A Tale of the Plains is a Western novel by Randall Parrish. Thirty-six chapters carry it from The Plainsman to The End. Early chapters stage a sudden arrest and a desperate escape. A ride through sand and desert leads to a wilderness cabin and the girl there.

Keith crosses the ford of the Arkansas and reaches the marshal of Sheridan. Christie Maclaire enters as one who believes in him, and a message from the dead complicates his case. An Indian raid, a duel in the desert, and a single shot raise the stakes. The final chapters bring forgiveness and a last interview. Parrish writes fast frontier adventure around a wronged plainsman clearing his name.
life-of-charles-dickens:
Frank T. Marzials wrote this Dickens life for the Great Writers series. Walter Scott published it in London in 1887. Marzials acknowledges a heavy debt to Forster's life of Dickens. He also used the letters edited by Dickens's family.

Charles Dickens was born on February 7, 1812. Happy Chatham days gave way to family troubles and London hardship. His father entered the Marshalsea, and Charles worked in a blacking business. Marzials compares the boy's isolation with David Copperfield's story. Kitton's Dickensiana lightened Marzials's labor considerably, he acknowledges. Young Charles felt isolation keenly during the blacking warehouse months.
lives-of-the-three-mrs-judsons:
Arabella M. Willson wrote these lives of three missionary wives. Ann, Sarah, and Emily Judson each married the same missionary. All three served as missionaries to Burmah in turn. Lee and Shepard published the book in Boston.

Congress copyright records date its entry to 1855. Portraits of Ann and Emily Judson illustrate the volume. A verse epigraph praises their self-denying band of workers. They counted life cheap to fulfil their ministry, it says. Miller, Orton and Mulligan first entered the copyright in 1855. Charles Dillingham later sold the New York edition.
love-among-the-chickens:
Love Among the Chickens is an early comic novel by P. G. Wodehouse. In his dedication, Wodehouse thanks his friend W. Townend for giving him the stuff. Sixteen years before, he says, they were sprightly lads at school together. The stuff Townend gave him became a chicken farm by the sea.

A young writer joins his friend's hopeless chicken venture on the coast. Hens, eggs, and farm chaos fill the days there. Amid the squawking, the young man falls in love. Wodehouse keeps the tone light, bright, and full of jokes. The book shows his high spirits long before his fame peaked. It is vintage early Wodehouse, warm and very funny.
men-like-gods-dover-thrift-editions:
H. G. Wells published this utopian novel in 1923. Its hero, Mr. Barnstaple, is a tired journalist who takes a holiday drive in 1921. He and several other motorists are suddenly swept three thousand years into the future. This Dover edition reprints the original Macmillan text.

The travelers land in a world remade along Barnstaple's own ideals. Crime, poverty, war, disease, and bigotry have all vanished there. Wells uses the visit to test his hopes for science and social planning. The novel asks whether ordinary modern people could bear such a perfected world, or would spoil it.
missionary-work-among-the-ojebway-indian:
The Reverend Edward F. Wilson tells here how he came to work among the Ojibway of Canada. His contents trace the journey: first experiences, arrival at Sarnia, and work at Kettle Point. He records Indian names given to the missionaries and a Christmas spent on the reserve. The bishop's visit and a first trip to Garden River follow.

Later chapters describe baptisms of pagan Indians and the Red River expedition. Wilson meets Chief Little Pine and winters in Algoma. His account preserves detail about Ojibway life, language, and customs in his era. Mission memoirs like his remain sources, read critically, for nineteenth-century Indigenous history around the Great Lakes.
modern-italian-poets-essays-and-versions:
William Dean Howells wrote these essays on Italy's modern poets, adding his own English versions of their verse. The contents begin with the Arcadian shepherds of the eighteenth century. Giuseppe Parini, Vittorio Alfieri, and Vincenzo Monti follow. Ugo Foscolo and Alessandro Manzoni anchor the Romantic generation.

Howells gives Giacomo Leopardi a place among the later names. Giuseppe Giusti, Giovanni Prati, and Aleardo Aleardi continue the line to his own century. Silvio Pellico, famous for his prison memoir, appears as a poet here. Howells, America's leading novelist-critic of his day, introduced English readers to Italian poetry he had loved since his consulate at Venice.
more-toasts-jokes-stories-and-quotations:
Marion Dix Mosher, a Rochester public librarian, compiled this handbook in 1922. The H. W. Wilson Company published it at New York. At 552 pages it promises jokes, stories, and quotations for speakers. The contents open with an essay on the importance of humor.

That essay, reprinted from the Nineteenth Century, calls humor a divine gift. It deals, the essay says, with a mystery pleasantly woven into daily life. Toasts fill the body of the book, with an index for finding them fast. Banquet speakers and toastmasters of the 1920s kept such compilations at hand, and librarians like Mosher built them for reference shelves.
mother-carey-s-chickens:
Kate Douglas Wiggin opens this family story with the petrels called Mother Carey's chickens. The birds flit from wave to wave like swallows over the sea. Mother Carey herself heads the first chapter, and her chickens the second. A chapter called The Common Denominator introduces the family's shared life.

Then comes The Broken Circle, and the Careys' flitting, or move, to Beulah. Cousin Ann, a service on the threshold, and a housewarming mark the new home. Nancy's idea and Nancy's coming out carry the eldest girl forward. Wiggin, author of Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, writes of a widowed mother holding her brood together with cheer.
my-literary-passions:
William Dean Howells maps his reading life in this 1895 book. The contents begin with the bookcase at home. Goldsmith, Cervantes, and Irving mark his early loves. First fiction and drama follow, then Scott and Pope.

Uncle Tom's Cabin, Ossian, and Shakespeare each get a chapter. Dickens, Thackeray, Dante, and Tolstoy mark later stages. He ends with new names like Zola, Hardy, and Galdos. Howells tells how each book formed his taste and craft. The memoir is a reader's autobiography, warm and exact, showing how one boy's shelf became an American man of letters.
nasa-tm-19650015349-1964-publications:
Compiled by the Materials Division at Marshall and dated January 30, 1965, this volume lists NASA publications from 1964. The entries are technical notes from across the agency's programs. Subjects run from materials and propulsion to spacecraft and engineering development work of many kinds.

A yearly list like this one served as a finding aid. Researchers could scan one volume to see what the agency had released. They could then order the notes that mattered to their own work. As a record, it also freezes one busy year in place. The range of titles shows how wide NASA's technical work had become by 1964.
nasa-tm-19660020445-an-approximate-solut:
Peter Ralph Kurzhals submitted this work in May 1966 as a doctoral thesis at Virginia Polytechnic Institute. His subject is the motion of a rotating spacecraft of any shape. Real spacecraft tumble or spin in complex ways, pushed by small uneven forces. Kurzhals offers an approximate analytic solution for that motion, with disturbance effects that can vary over time.

Exact solutions exist only for simple, tidy shapes. Flight vehicles are neither simple nor tidy. An approximate solution that handles arbitrary shapes fills a real gap. Disturbance functions stand for the small torques that slowly change a spin in flight. Thesis work of this depth, done inside the space program, fed directly into attitude control practice.
nasa-tm-19680013932-biosatellite-2-opera:
John W. Dyer of NASA's Ames Research Center presented this account of Biosatellite II operations in February 1968. The spacecraft carried living specimens into orbit so scientists could study how space flight affects life. Dyer explains how the mission was planned, flown, and recovered using services that already existed.

The craft weighed about 950 pounds and rode a two-stage Delta launch vehicle. About half its weight sat in the reentry vehicle that returned the specimens to Earth. Batteries supplied power, since the smooth craft carried no solar panels. Gas jets and gyroscopes held rotation very slow, keeping forces on the specimens small during the flight.
nasa-tm-19680016151-morphological-studie:
Webb Haymaker of NASA's Ames Research Center reviews studies of laminar lesions in the brain in this essay, prepared in 1967. The cerebral cortex has six thin layers, or laminae. Researchers asked whether one layer could be destroyed while the others stayed intact.

If one layer alone could be removed, its role in cortical electrical activity could be tested. An early study used proton radiation on cats to damage a narrow zone of cortex. That work, reported ten years earlier, showed selective damage was feasible. Haymaker surveys the morphology, or physical form, of such lesions. Dose and tissue volume factors shape how the damage develops in the cortex.
nasa-tm-19700009336-low-frequency-cosmic:
Four Goddard Space Flight Center researchers, J. K. Alexander, L. W. Brown, T. A. Clark, and R. G. Stone, wrote this preprint on low frequency cosmic noise. Cosmic noise is the steady radio hiss arriving from our own galaxy. Their question is what that hiss reveals about the local system of stars and gas near Earth.

Working from galaxy-wide radio measurements, the team estimates how thermal electrons are spread through nearby space. They also estimate the glow from fast electrons spiraling in magnetic fields, plus the flow of low energy cosmic ray electrons. Their radio figures run far above direct measurements, by about a hundredfold. They suggest strong solar effects or an uneven cosmic ray spread could explain the gap.
nasa-tm-19710023966-the-degeneration-of-:
H. Volland and H. G. Mayr of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in August 1971, numbered X-621-71-331. It concerns Hough functions, the mathematical shapes that describe atmospheric tides in the lower atmosphere. The authors ask what happens to those shapes high in the thermosphere, where dissipation takes hold.

Heat conduction, viscosity, and drag between neutral air and ions all modify the Hough functions as height increases. The paper shows they ultimately degenerate into spherical harmonics above about two hundred kilometers. That degeneration changes the latitude structure of the tidal modes and how waves travel upward. In particular, the twice-daily tidal mode becomes nearly trapped above about one hundred sixty kilometers, explaining its apparent absence in upper thermosphere dynamics.
nasa-tm-19720007680-review-of-magnetic-f:
Norman F. Ness of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this review in November 1971, numbered X-690-71-465, on magnetic field observations in the magnetosphere. By then satellites were routinely mapping Earth's magnetic bubble and its boundaries. Ness gathered the recent observations into one account of what they showed.

The review describes improved pictures of the magnetosphere, magnetosheath, plasma sheet, and bow shock, and how storms distort them. Observations of the polar cusp region support the idea that particles reach the plasma sheet through the polar neutral points. Distortions there suggest currents flowing along field lines far from Earth. The plasma sheet's field reversal region proved more complex than simple single neutral line models. No clear solar cycle change in magnetosphere structure was detected.
navy-boys-behind-the-big-guns:
Halsey Davidson wrote Navy Boys Behind the Big Guns as a sea adventure for boys. Its subtitle is Sinking the German U-Boats, which places it in the First World War. George Sully and Company published it in New York, with pictures. Davidson had written other Navy Boys books before this one.

A front picture shows gunners stripped for action, alert as panthers, by their guns. The series list names Navy Boys After the Submarines and Navy Boys Chasing a Sea Raider. Sea fights, convoys, and prizes fill those titles. Young readers of the war years got their navy's fight told as fast, brave action close to the guns.
new-tabernacle-sermons:
T. De Witt Talmage preached the sermons in New Tabernacle Sermons at the Brooklyn Tabernacle. George Munro published volume one in New York in 1886. Talmage had already issued Crumbs Swept Up and The Abominations of Modern Society. A portrait of the preacher fronts the book.

Sermon titles range from Brawn and Muscle to The Pleiades and Orion. The Queen's Visit, Vicarious Suffering, and The Lord's Razor follow. Windows Toward Jerusalem, The Great Assize, and The Road to the City keep the biblical frame. One late sermon takes up capital and labor. Talmage spoke to city crowds on faith, duty, and the day they lived in.
options:
O. Henry gathered sixteen short stories in Options, one of his late collections of tales built on surprise endings and city-and-country contrasts. The table of contents names pieces such as The Third Ingredient, The Hiding of Black Bill, Supply and Demand, Buried Treasure, The Higher Pragmatism, Best-Seller, and Rus in Urbe.

The opening story, The Rose of Dixie, starts in Toombs City, Georgia, where a stock company has raised a hundred thousand dollars to found a magazine. A committee calls on Colonel Aquila Telfair, a man of learning, family, and Southern tradition, to beg him to edit it. O. Henry sets the scene in the colonel's inherited library of ten thousand volumes, and the comedy of old South meeting new publishing begins.
osage-traditions:
James Owen Dorsey was a missionary-linguist for the Smithsonian's Bureau of Ethnology. He recorded Osage Traditions in Indian Territory in January 1883. A secret society of seven degrees guarded the people's traditions, he learned. His short stay allowed only fragments. Initiated Osage men gave him parts of two traditions.

Red Corn, of the Tsiu washtake gens, dictated the first tradition. He had it from Sadekihe. Red Corn's own story fills much of the introduction. A white man adopted him. He studied at a Jesuit college in Missouri. Later he practiced as an Indian doctor, known to whites as Bill Nix. The pamphlet preserves sacred tradition and the tale of its telling.
our-churches-and-chapels-their-parsons-p:
A. Hewitson, writing as Atticus in the Preston Chronicle, surveyed every place of worship in Preston. Churches, chapels, parsons, priests, and congregations all came under his eye. He reprinted the sketches as a book in 1869. His preface warns readers that a lively spirit runs through the descriptions, which may offend the phlegmatic, the sad-faced, and the puritanical.

Hewitson promises the solemn their facts, the facetious their humour, and the analytical their criticism. The work embodies a fuller history of each Preston place of worship than any yet published, he claims. The town's Anglican, Catholic, and Dissenting clergy helped generously. Genial humour, he insists, only makes the dry enumeration palatable.
out-with-gun-and-camera-or-the-boy-hunte:
Edward Stratemeyer, writing as Captain Ralph Bonehill, sent his boy hunters into the mountains in Out with Gun and Camera, the fourth volume of the Boy Hunters Series.
